Thus, then, the Maccabees are martyrs of Christ. Consequently, it is not out of logic or importunate, but, on the contrary, very convenient, for Christians to be the ones who particularly solemnly celebrate their feast day. Do Jews celebrate something similar? It is known that the basilica dedicated to the holy Maccabees is located in Antioch, that is, in the same city that receives its name from the same persecuting king. In fact, they had to suffer Antiochus, the impious persecuting king, and in Antioch the memory of his martyrdom is celebrated, so that the name of the persecutor and the memory of the crowner resonate at the same time. Such a basilica is property of the Christians, the Christians being the ones who built it. Therefore, celebrating his memory corresponds to us in law and in fact; Thousands of holy martyrs have imitated among us, throughout the world, their passions. Eorum ergo memoriam celebrandam nos habemus, nos tenemus: apud nos passiones eorum millia per orbem terrarum sanctorum martyrum imitata sunt. Nemo ergo dubitet, fratres mei, imitari Machabaeos; ne cum imitatur Machabaeos, putet se non imitari christianos. Prorsus imitationis affectus ferveat in cordibus nostris. Discant viri mori pro veritate. Discant feminae, from matris illius tanta patientia, ineffa-

They were the ones he wasn't afraid to lose. These each suffered their own passion, she suffered it in each one witnessing them. Mother of seven martyrs, she became a martyr seven times. He did not separate himself from his children seeing them suffer and joined them with his death. He watches over them all and loved them all. She suffered in her eyes what everyone else suffers in their flesh; Not only was he not afraid, but he even exhorted them. 7. The persecutor Antiochus judged this mother as one of many. "Persuade," he said, "your son not to die." And she answers him: «I will certainly persuade my son to live by exhorting him to die; "You want to persuade him to die by forgiving his death." What an answer! How pious, how worthy of a mother! How it oscillates between the spiritual and the carnal! Son, have mercy on me, he says. Son, have pity on me, who carried you for nine months in my womb, who breastfed you for three months and made you reach this age; take pity on me. Everyone was waiting for words like these: "Listen to Antiochus and do not abandon your mother." She, on the other hand, said: «Obey God, do not abandon your brothers. Even if it seems like you're abandoning me, that's when you're not abandoning me. I will have you again where I will no longer fear losing you. "Christ will keep you for me where Antiochus will not be able to take you." Theme: Happiness in this life, eternal happiness. Location: Unknown. Date: August 1, feast of Saints Maccabees. Around the year 417.

1. What a great spectacle it is before the eyes of our faith! We have heard and even seen with our hearts that a mother wanted her children to leave this life before her. What desires so contrary to those of human custom! In fact, all men want to precede, not follow, their children in leaving this life; She, on the other hand, wanted to die later. He did not lose his children, but sent them ahead; Nor did he focus on the life they left, but on the one they began to possess. They stopped living where they would once die and began to live a life without end. Talking about her as a spectator is an understatement, since we have been filled with admiration, above all, to see her as an entertainer. She was more fruitful in virtues than in children when she saw those in whom she herself fought fight; By defeating all of them, she herself won. Unique woman, unique mother, how the Church has put before our eyes the only holy mother, who everywhere exhorts her children to die for the name of the one who conceives them and gives them birth! IN SOLEMNITATE SS. MACHABAEORUM, II

CAPUT I.—1. Mater Machabaeorum in filiorum passione quam fortis. Magnum spectaculum positum is before oculos fidei nostrae. Aure audivimus, corde vidimus optantem matrem ante se finiré istam vitam filios suos: longe contrariis votis consuetudini humanoe. Omnes enim nomines filios suos ex hac vita migrando praecedere volunt, non sequi: illa autem optavi posterior morí. Non enim amittebat filios, sed praemittebat; nec intuebatur quam vitam finirent, sed quam inchoarent. Desinebant enim vivere, ubi quandoque fuent morituri; et incipiebant vivere, sine fine victuri. Parum est fuesse spectatricem, mirati sumus potius hortatricem. Fecundior virtutibus, quam fetibus: videns certantes, in quibus omnibus ipsa certabat; et in omnibus vincentibus ipsa vincebat. Una mulier, una mater, quomodo nobis ante oculos posuit unam matrem sanctam Ecclesiam, ubique exhortantem filios suos pro illius nomine morí, de quo

From the martyrs, like a seed thrown previously, the harvest of the Church flourished. Where did this come to man? The salvation of the righteous comes to them from the Lord, who is their protector in the time of tribulation. 2. We have seen and know that, during their tribulation, the Lord was the protector of those three men who walked through the fire without suffering any harm and who praised the Lord without the slightest injury. Where man was cruel, he calls her merciful. We have seen and know how the righteous have received salvation from the Lord, so that, thrown into the fire, they converted with their lives that cruel king whom they had irritated with their word. He, in fact, believed in his God, and published an edict according to which anyone who blasphemed against the God of Sidrach, Misach and Abdenago would go to death and his house would be plundered. How different the first and second orders! What was the first? "Perish who does not worship the golden statue." And the second? "Perish who blasphemes against the true God." Remaining immovable, those faithful men transformed the unfaithful. His firmness in faith did not allow him to remain in perfidy. Evidently, their salvation came from the Lord. The Lord was present when they praised him, unharmed, in the midst of the flames. According to this, where was the Lord when the Maccabees, despite confessing to him, eos concepit et peperit? Sic sanguine martymm impletus orbis praeiactatis seminibus seges Ecclesiae pullulavit. Unde hoc homini, nisi quia salus iustorum a Domino, et protector eorum est in tempore tribulationis (Ps 36,39)? 2. Deus non tantum tribus pueris, sed etiam Machabaeis adfuit. Cur three pueri ab ignibus líberantur, Machabaei consumuntur.—Vidimus, novimus protectorem Fuisse Dominum in tempore tribulationis trium virorum illorum, qui ambulabant inter ignes innoxios, et Dominum sine ulla laesione laudabant. Ubi homo saeviebat, flamma parcebat. CAPOT II.—Vidimus, novimus quemadmodum salus eorum iustorum a Domino Fuit, ut in ignem mit[1381]terentur, et illum asperum regem, quem loquendo irritaverant, vivos converterent. Credidit quippe in eorum Deum, et proposuit edictum, ut quicumque blasphemaret Deum Sidrach, Misach et Abdenago, in interitum iret, et domus eius in direptionem (Dan 3:96). Quam dissimilis iussio primae iussioni! Qualis prima iussio? Pereat qui statuam auream non adoraverit. Qualis secunda? Pereat qui Deum verum blasphemaverit.

Fideles homines non mutati, infidelem hominem mutaverunt. Illum in perfidia stare non permiserunt, quia ipsi in fide stetetunt. Salus ergo illorum I manifested to Domino Fuit. When illi non ardebant et laudabant, aderat Dominus. When isti ardebant, confitebantur, tamen moriebantur, ubi erat Dominus? An forte Affirmation of Tertullian (Apologetic 50), which we have already seen appear in this volume (serm.286,5).

did they burn and die? Were those righteous and these sinners? Not long ago, when his passion was read, we heard how they confessed their sins, and recognized that they suffered all those evils because God was angry with their own sins and those of their parents. What to say about the others? Read it, and you will see that they also confessed their own sins, recognizing that their sufferings were deserved. Equally just and equally aware of their sins, and just precisely because they recognize their sins. Irreprehensible, therefore, for not being liars. If we say, John states, that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth does not reside in us. If, on the other hand, we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us and purify us from all iniquity. It is, therefore, typical of the just to recognize sins, and typical of the proud to defend personal merits. 2. Both were, therefore, just who equally confessed their own sins, equally gave glory to God and were equally willing to die for his law. Why were some saved from the fire and the others consumed by it? Did God assist one having abandoned the others? No way; Furthermore, he assisted both, some openly and the others secretly. He delivered some visibly, others he crowned invisibly. True, those were delivered from death, but they remained in the temptation of this life; they were delivered from the fire, but reserved for other dangers; They defeated a single tyrant, but they would still have to fight the devil. My brothers, understand illi iusti erant, isti peccatores? Audivimus enim istos paulo ante, cum passio eorum legeretur, confiten peccata sua, et dicere quoníam omnia illa ¡ráscente Domino sibi, sed et paterno merit paterentur (cf. Mach 7). Quid illi? Legite, et videbitis etiam ipsos peccata propria confiten, et dicere se merit perpeti. Aequaliter iusti, confessores aequaliter peccatorum; et ideo iusti, quia confessores aequaliter peccatorum. Ideo irreprehensibiles, quia non mendaces. Si enim dixerimus, ait Ioannes, quia peccatum non habemus; nos ipsos decipimus, et sales in nobis non est. Si autem peccata nostra confessi fuerimus, fidelis est et iustus, qui dimittat nobis peccata, et emundet nos ab omni iniquitate (1 lo 1,8-9). Ad iustos ergo pertinet confessio peccatorum: ad superbos pertinet defensio meritorum.

Pariter ergo iusti peccata confitentes, pariter Deo gloriam dantes, pariter pro eius legibus morí parati. CAPUT III.—Quare illi ab ignibus liberantur, isti ab ignibus consumuntur? Ergo illis Deus aderat, hos deseruerat? Absit: immo utrisque adfuit; illis in aperto, istis in occulto. Illos visibiliter liberabat; istos invisibiliter coronabat. Illi quidem de morte liberati sunt; thirst in huius vitae temptatione manserunt: ab igne liberati, ad pericula reservati; one

as Christians that you are. The liberation of the Maccabees was better and safer. Those three men passed one test, but all the others remained; These put an end to this life, which is all a temptation. Then, by divine decision, hidden no doubt, but just, Nebuchadnezzar deserved to be converted, and Antiochus to harden; The one found mercy, the other increased his pride. 3. But to what extent and to what extent did he raise his pride? I saw the wicked rise above the cedars of Lebanon. As far as? For how long? I passed by, and noticed that he was not there; and I asked for him, and his place was not found. Fairly; You looked for it and you didn't find it, because you passed by. Do you want to see that the wicked does not exist? Do you want to see that neither he nor his place is found? Happens. Why do I say: "Come in"? Don't be scared, because I didn't say you should die. You thought I had said: "Pass away from this life," and you were scared precisely because you have not passed away. What do you mean you haven't passed? That you have not passed, lifting your heart above the seduction of temporary happiness; You have not passed over the flattery of the flesh nor over the temptations of the world, which solicit the heart and inspire fear of human miseries. Consequently, you think that happiness is found in this world and that there is no calamity in it. The happiness of the kingdom of heaven has not touched your heart nor has its refreshing air descended on your ardor. When they tell you: "The happiness of this world is false,"

Although you do not dare to proclaim it, I nevertheless see what is hidden in your heart; perhaps you twist your mouth, sneer and mock, while saying to yourself: "Oh, how well it is for me here! How things will go for me afterwards, I don't know. It is no small thing to say that you ignore it; And thank goodness if you don't add this other thing: Short and boring is the time of our life, and there is no return when man comes to his end, and no one is known to have returned from hell. At least say you don't know. The confession of ignorance is a stepping stone towards science. I'm going to talk to you starting from this supposed concession: «I don't know what will be after death; "I do not know completely whether the righteous are to be happy, and the sinners unhappy, or whether neither one nor the other are to exist." However, even if you ignore it, you will never dare to say that the sinners will be happy and the righteous will be unhappy. Even if you suspect that neither one nor the other will exist, you will never dare to say that after death the wicked will be in a good situation, while the righteous will be involved in evil. Not even your ignorance can suggest such things to you. You can, therefore, say: "I do not know whether after death the righteous will be happy and the wicked miserable, or whether both will exist without sensitivity. Oh, that I could do well here while I live and feel! You're seeing that you haven't passed yet. You have not yet passed over these thoughts of earth, dust, smoke, vapor, carnal and mortal. Therefore it seems to you that the wicked rises above the cedars of Lebanon; That's why you look for its place and find it: because you haven't passed by.

tyranno victo, adhuc certaturi cum diabolo. Fratres mei, sicut christiani intellegite. Machabaei melius et tutius liberati sunt. Ab illis tribus viris, ceteris remanentibus, illa una temptado superata est: ab istis ista vita finita, quae tota tentatio est. Deinde divine judicio, occulto procul dubio, sed tamen íusto, Nebuchodonosor meruit convertedí, Antiochus meruit obdurarí. Ule invenit mercym, iste auxit superbíam. CAPUT IV.—3. In eos qui congratulatem in hac vita esse censent, ac de altera vita dubitant.—Sed quantum et quo usque auxit superbiam? Vidi impium exalt super Libani cedars. What did you use? quamdiu? Transivi, et ecce non erat: et quaesivi eum, et non est inventus locus eius (Ps 36,35.36). Bene: quaesisti, et non invenisti; quia transisti. Vis videre impium non esse? vis quaerere eum, et locum eius non ínvenire? I passed. What I mean, Transí? Noli expavescere; non dixi: Morere. Putasti enim me dixisse: Transí de hac vita; et ideo expavisti, quia non transisti. Quid est, non transisti? Non transisti erectíone cordis temporalis [1382] felicitatis ilécebras; non transisti blandimenta carnis, non transisti suggestions saeculi cor titulantes et immittentes timorem miseriarum humanorum. Ideo in hoc mundo putas esse congratulatem, in hoc mundo non putas esse calamitatem. Felicitas regni caelorum non tetigit cor tuum, non inde aspersa est aestibus tuis aura refrigerii. Quando tibi dicitur: Falsa est felicitas mundi; etsi non audeas ita dicere, video tamen in

corde tuo, forte os torques, subsannas, irrides, et dicis tibi: O si hic mihi bene sit! post quid futurum sit nescio. Et non est parum quia vel nescio dicis; ne forte etiam hoc dicas: Exiguum et cum taedio est tempus vitae nostrae, et non est reversio in fine hominis, et non est qui agnitis sit reversus ab inferís (Wis 2,1). Vel nescio dec. Confessio ignorantiae, gradus est scientiae. Sic ergo te alloquar, tanquam mihi dicas: Nescio quid post mortem futurum sit; prorsus Ignoro an beati futuri sint iusti, et miseri peccatores; an utrique pariter non sint futuri. Illud tamen quamvis nescias, non audebis dicere post mortem blessed future peccatores, miseros iustos. Non potes dicere, illos etsi suspicaris pariter non Futures, in meliori tamen statu Futures impíos, et iustos in malis post mortem Futures. Nec ignorantia tua tibi potest suggerere hoc. Ergo potes dicere: Utrum bene sit post mortem iustis, et male post mortem impiis, an utrique pariter sine sensu futuri sint, nescio. Or if hic mihi bene sit, cum vivo, cum sentio! Vides quia nondum transisti. Istas, inquam, istas cogitationes terrenas, pulvereas, fumeas, vaporeas, carnals, mortales nondum transisti. Ideo tibi videtur impius exaltari super cedars Libani; ideo quaeris locum eius, et invenís, quia non transisti.

4. You look for its place and you find it, but here. It has its place in this century. God, who knows everything in advance, would not have created it in vain, nor nourished it in vain, or made the sun rise upon it, or let the rain fall; In vain would the great patience of God have condescended to him, being an evil man and living badly. All this has not been done in vain: he has his place here, although we cannot find out in its entirety; God, who knows how to arrange everything, knows everything. Ignoring other things, what function did this miserable Antiochus, for example, have here? Through him the people of God were scourged and tested; Thanks to him these young saints were crowned. So he had his role. He was bad, but he who cannot be bad made good use of him. As bad men use good creatures badly, so the good creator uses bad men well. Whoever created the entire human race knows what to do with it. The goldsmith carries the gold, weighs it and measures it. The painter knows where to place the color black so that a beautiful painting results. And won't God know where to put the sinner so that creation is ordered? If God in his patience had not kept sinners alive during past times, how would so many faithful people be born today? Some bad people are left alive so that good ones can be born from them. Good by the grace of God, for the entire mass of sin is condemned. What is more evil than the devil? And yet, how much good did God bring out of his evil? The blood of the redeemer would not have been shed for

our salvation except for the wickedness of the deserter. Read the gospel and read what is written in it: The devil entered the heart of Judas so that he would betray Christ. The devil and Judas were evil; as the organist, so the organ. The devil, then, misused his own vessel; The Lord used them both well. They both intended our ruin; God deigned to make it a salvation for us. 5. Judas handed over Christ, and was condemned; Judas, who betrayed him, is condemned; The Father gave the Son, and he is glorified. He handed over, I repeat, Judas to the teacher, and he is condemned; The Son also gave himself, and is praised. We all know when Judas betrayed Christ; Perhaps you are waiting for me to tell you when the Father gave up the Son. You also know this, but I will say it again so that you remember it. Listen to what the Apostle says referring to the Father: Who did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all. Listen to him also regarding the Son: Who loved me, he said, and gave himself for me. He sees that there are already two who handed him over: the Father handed over the Son, the Son handed over himself, but both were saviors, because both were creators. So what did Judas do? What good did he do? He did no good, but good came out of him. In fact, Judas does not say: "I will hand over Christ to free the human race." In the person of Judas he gave greed to Christ; in God, mercy. To Judas

CAPUT V.—4. Mali hic suo loco in usus bonds positi.—-Locum eius quaeris, et invenís; thirst hic. Habet locum suum in hoc saeculo. Non enim frustrate Deo praescio crearetur, aut frustra nutriretur, aut frustra super eum sol oriretur, et pluvia funderetur, frustrate ei malignant et male vivirti tanta Dei patientia parceretur. Non est hoc frustra: habet hic locum suum. Et si non omnia possumus nos invenire: sed Deonota sunt omnia, qui novit cuneta disposere. Ecce, ut de aliis taceamus, qualem locum hic habuit iste miser Antiochus? Per eum populus Dei fiagellatus est et probatus: per eum isti sancti iuvenes coronati. Ergo habuit hic locum suum. Malus erat; See bene illo usus est, qui malus esse non potest. Sicut enim mali nomines male utuntur creaturis bonis: sic Creator bonus bene utitur hominibus malis. Novit quid inde agat, qui totum creavit humanum genus. Aurifex portat, aurifex appendit, aurifex librat. Pictor novit ubi ponat nigrum colorem, ut sit decora pictura; et Deus nescit ubi ponat peccatorem, ut sit ordinata creature? CAPUT VI.—Nisi Deus anterioribus saeculis servaret sua patientia peccatores, unde nascerentur hodie [1383] tot fideles? Alii mali servantur, ut boni inde nascantur. Boni gratia Dei: nam tota damnata est massa peccati. Quid diabolo nequius? et de illius nequitia quanta bona

fecit Deus? Non funderetur pro salute nostra sanguis Redemptoris, nisi per nequitiam desertoris. Lege Evangelium, et vide quid sibi scriptum est: lmmiút diabolus in cor ludae, ut traderet Christum (lo 13,2). Malus diabolus, malus ludas: qualis organarius, tale organum. Usus est ergo male diabolus suo vase: usus est ambobus Dominus bene. Conati sunt ergo ad nostram perniciem: Deus hoc verteré dignitus est ad nostram salutem. 5. Traditio Christi et a luda et a Deo.—Tradidit ludas Christum, et damnatus est. ludas tradidit, et damnatur: tradidit Filium Pater, et glorificatur. Tradidit, inquam, ludas magistrum, et damnatur: tradidit se ipse Filius, et laudatur. Quomodo ludas tradidit Christum, omnes novimus: exspectatis fortassis audire quomodo Pater tradidit Filium. Et hoc nostis: sed commemorabo, ut recordemini. Audi Apostolum dicentem from Deo Patre: Qui proprio Filio non pepercit, sed pro nobis omnibus tradidit ittum (Rom 8:32). Audi et de Filio: Qui me, inquit, dilexit, et tradidit semetipsum pro me (Gal 2,20). Duos iam vide traditores: Patrem Filii traditorem. Filium sui ipsius traditorem, sed utrumque salvatorem, quia utrumque creatorem. ludas ergo quid fecit? Quid enim boni fecit? Bonum de illo factum est, non ipse bonum fecit. Ñeque enim ait ludas: Tradam Christum, ut liberetur genus humanum. In luda tradidit avaritia;

He was paid nothing but for what he did, not for what God made from him. 6. Why have we said this? Because the evil one also has his place in this world. And the Lord certainly knows who his own are and what he is going to do with those who are not his. But you, if you pass by, if you trample earthly things, if your answer that your heart is lifted up is not in vain, 3 as you pass you will seek the place of the wicked and you will not find it. But in that future life, what place will there be for the wicked? Will we then still have the need to exercise with the evil ones? Will gold need to be purified through straw? The whole world is the crucible of the goldsmith. In him are the righteous as if they were gold; there the wicked are like straw; there the tribulation like fire; there God in the condition of a goldsmith. The pious praise God: the gold shines; the wicked blasphemes against God: the chaff smokes. In the same tribulation, as in the same fire, the gold is purified, the straw destroyed; but the goldsmith God is praised for both. 7. I will say it, dearly beloved, exhorting you and myself. Let us, with the help of the Lord, pass above carnal thoughts, lift up our hearts and think of the future life: when your heart is in it, you will have passed. Where is the wicked? Certainly not there. Here it was necessary; There you will look for him, but you will not find his place. Therefore, brothers, when you see, you who live by faith, you in Deo, mercy. Non redditum est Iudae nisi quod fecit, non quod de illo Deus fecit. CAPOT VII.—6. Impío locus hic inter iustos, non in altera vita. Quare ista diximus? Quia est in hoc saeculo impio locus: et prorsus novit Dominus qui sunt eius (2 Tim 2:19); et novit quid pro ipsis faciat, de illis qui non sunt eius. Sed tu si transieris, si terrena calaveris, si non frustrating sursum cor te habere responderes; Transeundo quaeres locum impii, et non invenies. In illa enim vita future quis locus impii? Numquid adhuc opus habemus exerceri malis? Numquid necesse habet aurum adhuc purgari per paleam? Totus enim mundus fornax aurificis. Ibi iusti tanquam aurum: ibi impii tanquam palea. Ibi tribulatio sicut ignis: ibi Deus sicut aurifex. Pius Deum laudat, aurum rutilat; impius Deum blasphemat, palea fumart. Ad unam tribulationem, tanquam ad unum ignem, ule purgatur, ille vastatur; sed Deus aurifex in utroque laudatur. CAPUT VIII.—7.

De saeculari felicítate impiorum ne perturbentur pz'i.—Dicam, carissimi, exhortans vos et me ipsum. Cogitationes carnales in adiutorio Domini transeamus, sursum cor habeamus, de vita Futura cogitemus; ubi cum fuerit cor tuum, transisti. Ubi est impius? Non ibi erit. Hic necessarius erat: ibi quaeres eum, et non invenies locum eius. Quando ergo videtis, fratres, qui ex fide vivitis, quorum cor rectum est,

whose heart is right, you who hope for the same true and everlasting happiness; When you see that men rejoice and rejoice in this false and deceptive happiness, if you are pious, feel compassion; If you are healthy, cry. Thus, he whose feet wavered reproaches himself for having begun to accuse God, despite being already there, although it would be better to say that he was almost there, since he was barely there. He did not deny that God knows everything, but he hesitated as if his feet were wavering. What is hesitating? Dude. What did he say when he reproached himself for not having a straight heart? Why have my feet wavered? Because I was envious, he said, of sinners, seeing their peace. When I saw rich wicked people, I was envious, and I told myself that justice had been a loss for me and that I had uselessly justified my heart and washed my hands among the innocent. Even in doubt, this is how I began to know: Thus, he said, I began to know: this tiring task is before me. Big and tiring task to resolve this question. It really is tiring. One is bad, and he does well; The other is good, and things go badly for him, and God is the judge of both. Consequently, we must conclude that a just judge gives good to the bad and evil to the good. This tiring task is before me. But how long will it last? Until he enters the sanctuary of God and notices the end. Theme: Temporary life, eternal life; do not harm the evil ones; be at peace with everyone. Location: Hippo. Date: August 10, feast of San Lorenzo. Around the year 400. 1. Today is the solemn feast of the blessed martyr Lorenzo. The readings heard fit perfectly with the solemnity. We have heard, sung and received the evangelical reading with great attention. Let us, therefore, follow in the footsteps of the martyrs, imitating them so that the celebration of their festivals is not useless. Who ignores the merits of the aforementioned martyr? Who prayed to him without getting what he asked for? For how many weak men he obtained with his merits even the temporary benefits that he disdained! Benefits that were granted to them not so that they would remain in their weakness, but so that, from the granting of these earthly favors, the love would arise that would lead them to desire better ones. Often, fathers give their children small, worthless toys so that they do not cry if they do not receive them. However, dearly beloved, since there are two lives, one before death and one after, both had and have their lovers. What need is there to describe what this short life is like? We have all experienced how full it is of afflictions and lamentations; how it is surrounded by temptations and overflowing with fears, burned by passions and subjected to the unexpected; how adversity causes him pain, and prosperity fear; The gains make her jump for joy and the losses torment her. And even in the very joy of profits he trembles at the fear of losing what he has acquired and that because of this they will begin to go after him, which did not happen before the acquisition. Misfortune is true and happiness is false. The humble desires to ascend and the elevated fears to descend. Who does not envy those who have; He who has despises he who has not. Who will explain in words the ugliness so great and so visible in this life? And yet, this ugliness has such lovers that I wish we could find some, even if they were very few, who loved the eternal life that never ends, as they love this one, which runs out so quickly, and that, if

lengthens, it is to renew day by day the fear that it will end at every moment. What should I do? How should I act? What can I say? With what stinging threats, with what ardent exhortations will we move the hard, lazy and frozen hearts through the ice of earthly astonishment so that they may once and for all shake off the drowsiness of the world and be inflamed with the love of the eternal? What, I repeat, should I do? What can I say? It occurs to me meanwhile that the same daily events are warning me and suggesting what I have to tell you. Pass, if possible, from the love of this temporal life to the love of the eternal, the one that the martyrs loved, who despised this temporal one. I beg you, I beseech you, I exhort you, not only you, but also myself, to love eternal life. Although she deserves greater love, I only ask that we love her as her lovers love temporal life, not as the holy martyrs loved her, since they did not love her at all or very little and easily put eternal life before her. Therefore, you, few as you are, listen to these few words, because I cannot say much either with this heat and body fatigue. Lorenzo was a deacon who followed the apostles, since he came after them. When the persecution, predicted to the Christians in the gospel we have just heard, was burning with vehemence in Rome and elsewhere, they demanded the goods of the Church from the archdeacon. It is said that he responded: "Let vehicles accompany me to bring the riches of the Church in them." Greed opened its jaws, but wisdom knew what to do. The order immediately came: as many vehicles as he ordered, so many showed up. And the more the requests, the greater was the hope of loot conceived in the heart. He filled the vehicles with poor people and returned with them. To the question: "What does this mean?" he replied: These are the riches of the Church. The pursuer, disappointed, resorted to the flames; but Lorenzo was not cold enough to fear the flames; The first was almost burning with anger, but the second was more with love. What else? A grill was brought and he was roasted. And it is said that, after being burned on one side, he endured the torments with such serenity that what we have just heard in the gospel was fulfilled in him: With your patience you will possess your souls. Then, burned by the flames, but calm thanks to his patience, he said: «It is already cooked; "All that's left is for you to turn me around and eat me."

This was his martyrdom, this was the glory with which he was crowned. His favors in Rome are so well known that it is impossible to list them. He is one of whom Christ said: Whoever loses his soul for my sake will gain it. He saved her thanks to his faith, thanks to his contempt for the world and thanks to martyrdom. What will not be his glory in the presence of God, if the praise he receives from men is so great? 2. Let us follow in his footsteps with faith, and let us also follow him in contempt of the world. Heavenly rewards are not only promised to martyrs, but also to those who follow Christ with complete faith and perfect love. These will be honored among the martyrs. This is what the Truth promises when it says: Everyone who leaves home, or fields, or parents, or brothers, or wife, or children will receive seven times more in this life and eternal life in the future century. What can man do more glorious than to sell his possessions and buy Christ, to offer God an exceedingly pleasing gift: the uncontaminated strength of a soul and the unalloyed praise of devotion; accompany Christ when he comes to take revenge on his enemies; sit by his side when he occupies his throne to judge; to be a joint heir with Christ, equal to the angels and to rejoice in the possession of the celestial kingdom with the patriarchs, the apostles and the prophets? What persecution can overcome, what torments can overcome those thoughts? A resilient, strong, stable soul, founded on religious considerations, stands firm against all terrors.

This is what Christus said: Qui perdiderit animam suam propter me, salvabít eam (ib., 9,24). Salvavit eam per fidem, salvavit per contemptum mundi, salvavit per martyrium. Quanta est gloria eius apud Deum, dum tanta est laus eius apud homines? 2. Martyrum merces Christum sequentibus parata.—Sequamur vestigía eius fide, sequamur et contemptu mundi. Non solum martyribus praemia promittuntur caelestia, sed etiam integra fide et perfection caritate Christum sequentibus. Nam Inter martyres honoratus est, ipsa veritate pollicente, ac dicente: Nemo est qui relinquat domum, aut agrum, aut parenles, aut fratres, aut uxorem, aut filios, et non recipiat septies tantum in isto tempore, in saeculo autemfutura vitam aeternam habebit (Mt 19,29). Quid est gloriosius homini, quam sua vendeé, et Christum emere, offerre Deo acceptissimum munus, incorruptam virtutem mentís, incolumen laudem devotionis; Christum comitari, cum vinore coeperit vindictam de inimicis receptaras; lateri eius assistere, cum sederit iudicaturus; coheredem Christi fieri, Angelis adaequari, cum Patriarchis, cum Apostolis, cum Prophetis, caelestis regni possessione laetari? Has cogitationes quae persecutio potest vincere, quae possible storm will overcome? Dura, fortis, et stabilis religiosis meditationibus fundata mens, et adversus

of the devil and against the threats of the world. Faith in future goods, certain and well-founded, gives it strength. Persecution closes its eyes, but the sky opens. The antichrist threatens, but Christ defends. Death is suffered, but immortality follows. The dead man is deprived of the world; but, returned to life, paradise is shown to him. Temporary life is extinguished, but eternal life is restored. What an honor and what security to leave here with joy, to leave radiant with glory in the midst of hardships and anguish; momentarily close the eyes, with which one saw men and the world, and instantly open the others, with which one sees God, on a happy journey! How fast! You suddenly disappear from earth to find yourself in the celestial realms. It is advisable to embrace these ideas with your mind and heart and meditate on them day and night. If persecution finds the soldier of God in these dispositions, virtue, ready for combat, cannot be defeated. And, if called by God before arriving at combat, the faith prepared for martyrdom will receive, without loss of time, the reward at the hands of the divine judge. In times of persecution the militia is crowned; in times of peace, constancy'. omnes Zabuli terrores et mines mundi animus immobilis perstat, quem [1395] futurerum fides certa et solida corroborat. Clauduntur oculi in persecutionibus; sed patet caelum. Minatur Antichristus; sed tuetur Christus. Mors infertur; sed immortalitas sequitur. Deceased mundus eripitur; sed restituto paradisus exhibitiontur. Vita temporalis exstinguitur; eternal thirst reparatur. Quanta est dignitas et quanta securitas exire hinc laetum, exire inter pressuras et annguishes gloriosum; claudere in momento oculos, quibus nomines videbantur et mundus; aperire eos statim, ut Deus videatur, etiam congratulator migrando! How fast! Terris suddenly retraheris, ut regnis caelestibus reponaris. Haec oportet mente et cogitatione complecti, haec die ac nocte meditari. Theme: Follow Christ, especially in love. Location: Unknown. Date: August 10, feast of San Lorenzo. In the year 417 or later. 1. The Roman Church commends to us today the day of the triumph of the blessed Lorenzo; day when he trampled the roars of the world, despised its flattery, and in both things defeated his pursuer, the devil. All Rome is witness to how glorious and distinguished is the crown of the martyr Lorenzo, what the multitude of his virtues and what the variety of his flowers. In that same Church he held the office of deacon, as you often hear. There he administered the sacred blood of Christ and there he shed his own for the name of Christ. He had wisely approached the table of the powerful, a table of which the Proverbs of Solomon now spoke to us, where it is written: If you sit down to dine at the table of the powerful, look and notice what is offered to you, and thus stretch out your hand, knowing that it is appropriate for you to prepare similar things. Quam gloriosa enim, et quanta virtutum multitudine, quasi florum varietate, distincta Laurentii martyris sit corona, universal testis est Roma. In ipsa enim Ecclesia, sicut solctis audire, diaconi gerebat officium. Ibi sacrum Christi sanguinem ministravit: ibi pro Christi nomine suum sanguinem fudit. Ad mensam potentis prudent accesserat. Ad illam mensam, de qua nobis moda Snlomonis proverbia loquebantur, ubi scriptum est: Si separis cenare ad mensam potentis, cognoscens intellege quae apponuntur tibí; et sic extcnde manum tuam, sciens quoniam similia te oportet praeparare (Prov 23,1.2). Huius cenae mysterium beatus apostolus Ioannes evidentor exposuit, they say: Sicut Christus pro nobis animam suam posuit, sic et nos

scrub it for our brothers. This, brothers, Saint Lawrence understood well; He understood it and did it. In fact, he prepared things similar to those taken at that table. He loved Christ in his life and imitated him in his death. 2. Let us also imitate him, brothers, if we truly love. We cannot return any fruit of love better than the imitation of his example, since Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we can follow in his footsteps. In this phrase, the apostle Peter gives the impression of having seen that Christ suffered only for those who follow in his footsteps and that Christ's passion benefits only those who follow him. The holy martyrs followed him until the shedding of his blood, until they imitated him in his passion; The martyrs followed him, but not alone. The bridge did not collapse after they passed over, nor did the fountain dry up after they drank. What else is the hope of the faithful saints who bear the yoke of marriage under the conjugal alliance, with chastity and concord, or of those who tame the pleasures of the flesh in the continence of widowhood, or of those who, setting the summit of holiness higher and flourishing in new virginity, followed the lamb wherever it went? What hope, I repeat, is left to them; What hope is left for us, if only those who shed their blood for him follow Christ? Must Mother Church lose her children, whom she engendered with greater fertility the greater the tranquility she enjoyed in time of peace? Must you beg for persecution to come

and the test to lose them? Not at all, brothers. How can he ask for persecution who day after day shouts: Do not lead us into temptation? That garden of the Lord, brothers, has—and I repeat it once and three times—not only the roses of the martyrs, but also the lilies of virgins, the ivy of marriage and the violets of widows. In no way, dearly beloved, should any class of men lose hope in their vocation: Christ suffered for all. In all truth it is written of him: Who wills that all men be saved and come to the knowledge of the truth. 3. Let us see, then, how Christ should be followed, regardless of the shedding of blood and the test that is the passion. Speaking of Christ himself, the Apostle says: Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider it a plunder to be equal with God—sublime majesty!—but emptied himself by taking the form of a servant, made in the likeness of men and found to be like a man in outward appearance. What humility! Christ humbled himself: you have, oh Christian!, something to cling to. Christ became obedient, why are you proud? To what extent did Christ become obedient? Until the Word was incarnated, until he participated in human mortality, until he was tempted three times, until he was the object of the mockery of the Jewish people, until he was spit on and chained, slapped and scourged; and if this is not enough, until death. And if there is still

bemus animas pro fratribus I will put (1 lo 3,16). Intellexit hoc, fratres, sanctus Laurentius; intellexit, ac fecit; et prorsus qualia sumpsit in illa mensa, talia praeparavit. Atnavit Christum in vita sua, imitatus est eum in morte sua. CAPUT II.—2. Christum sequi omnes debenmus.—Et nos ergo, fratres, si veraciter amamus, imitemur. Non enim meliorem reddere poterimus dilectionis [13%] fructum, quam imitationis exemplum; Christus enim pro nobis passus est, relinquens nobis exemplum, ut sequamur vestigia eius (1 Pet 2:21). In hac sententia vidisse videtur apostolus Petrus, quod pro his tantum passus est Christus, qui sequuntur vestigia eius, ñeque prosit quidquam Christi passio, nisi illis qui sequuntur vestigia eius. Secuti sunt eum martyres sancti, usque ad effusionem cruoris, usque ad similarityinem passionis: secuti sunt martyres, sed non soli. Non enim postquam illi transierunt, pons incisus est; aut postquam ipsi biberunt, fons ipse siceatus est. Quae est enim spes fidelium bonorum, qui vel sub foedere coniugali iugum mattimonii caste et concorditer ducunt, vel sub continentia viduali domant carnis illecebtas, vel etiam sanctitatis apicem celsius engentes et in nova virginitate florentes sequuntur agnum quocumque ierit? Quae istis, inquam, quae nobis omnibus spes est, si non sequuntur Christum, nisi qui pro ipso sanguinem fundunt? Perditura est ergo filios suos, quos tanta fecundius, quanto securius tempore pacjs

enixa est mater Ecclesia? Quos ne perdat, oranda est persecutio, oranda tentatio? Absit, brothers. Quomodo enim potest orare persecutionem, qui quotidie clamat, Ne nos inferas in temptationem (Mt 6,13)? CAPUT III.—Habet, habet, fratres, habet hortus ille dominicus, non solum rosas martyrum, sed et lilia virginum, et coniugatorum hederás, violasque viduarum. Prorsus, dilectissimi, nullum genus hominum de sua vocatione desperet; pro omnibus passus est Christus. Veraciter de illo scriptum est: Qui vult omnes homines salvas fieri, et in agnitionem veritatis vinore (1 Tim 2,4). 3. In quibus licet Christum sequi, praeter martyrium. Humilitas ipsius sectanda. Vindicta exemplo Christi, non expetenda. Praesentia contemnenda.—Intellegamus ergo praeter effusionem cruoris, praeter periculum passionis, quomodo Christum debeat sequi Christianus. Apostolus dicit, loquens of Domino Christo: Qui eum in forma Dei esset, non rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis Deo. What a maiestas! Sed semetipsum exinanivit, formam serví accipiens, in similarityinem hominum factus, et habitu inventus ut homo. How humble! Humiliavit se Christus: habes, christiane, quod teneas. Christus factus est oboediens: quid superbis? Quousque factus est oboediens Christus? Usque ad incarnationem Verbi, usque ad participationem mortalitatis humanoe, usque nd trinam diaboli temptationem, usque ad irrisionem populi Iudaeorum, usque ad sputa et liga, usque ad alapas et flagella; if parum est, usque ad mortem; et si adhuc aliquid etiam de genere mortis addendum, mortem
Follow Christ, especially in love

than adding the type of death: death on a cross. Such is our example of humility, medicine for our pride. Why do you swell, oh man! Why do you spread yourself, dead skin? Foul pus, why do you swell? You gasp, you lament, you suffocate, because I don't know who insulted you. On what basis do you claim revenge? Why does her thirst burn your jaws, to the point that you only give up going after her when you have taken revenge on the one who hurt you? If you are a Christian, behold your king; May Christ be avenged first, since he who suffered so many evils for you has not yet been avenged, even though his majesty is such that he could have suffered nothing or could have taken revenge instantly. But in him the measure of his power was also the measure of his patience, since he suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we follow in his footsteps. Without a doubt, you are seeing, dearly beloved, that there are many ways to follow Christ, even leaving aside the shedding of blood, chains and prisons, whippings and hooks. Once this humility had passed and death had been defeated, Christ ascended to heaven: let us follow him. Let us listen to the Apostle, who says: If you have risen with Christ, taste the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; Seek the things above, not those of the earth. Vomit whatever is delightful the world of temporal things has inoculated you; Even though he bellows harshness and terrible things, despise him. Whoever behaves like this, do not doubt that he is associated with

the footprints of Christ, until we can say, with reason, in the company of the apostle Paul: Our life is in heaven. 4. But virtue can only be undefeated if charity is not feigned. The one who pours charity into our hearts is the one who gives us true virtue. Why was it that the blessed Lorenzo did not fear the fire applied externally but because the flame of charity burned within? Thus, my brothers, the glorious martyr did not fear the atrocious flames of fire in his body, because the most violent desire for heavenly joys burned in his soul. Compared to the heat inside his chest, the outside flame of the pursuers was cold. How would I have endured the pricks of so many pains if I had not loved the joys of eternal rewards? Finally, when would I have despised this life if I had not loved a better one? And who can harm you, says the apostle Peter; Who can harm you if you are lovers of good? Even if the persecutor inflicts some evil on you, do not fail in the love of good. If you truly love good with all your heart, you will endure any evil with patience and serenity of mind. What harm did the torments inflicted on him by his persecutors do to the blessed Lorenzo? With the same tortures they made him more resplendent, and for us they turned this date of his precious death into a day of celebration.

Theme: Christ's confusion in the face of death. Place: Carthage, in Cipriano's mensa. Date: August 10, feast of San Lorenzo. In the year 413? 1. Your faith - recognizes the grain that fell from heaven and, dead, multiplied. Your faith, I repeat, recognizes that grain, because it lives in your soul. What Christ said about himself, no Christian questions. Certainly, with that one dead and multiplied, many other grains were scattered over the earth. One of them is the blessed Lorenzo, whose sowing we celebrate today. How abundant harvest sprang from those grains scattered throughout the entire globe of the earth! We are seeing it, it fills us with joy; we ourselves are, if by his grace we belong to his barn. Well, not all the harvest goes to the barn. The same rain, beneficial and nutritious, feeds the wheat and the chaff. They will by no means be gathered together into the barn, although they grow together in the sheepfold and are threshed together on the threshing floor. Now is the time to choose. 1. Granum morte multiplicatum.—Agnoscit fides vestra granum, quod in terram cecidit, et mortuum multiplicatum est. Agnoscit, inquam, hoc granum fides vestra, quia ipsum habitat in mente vestra. Hoc enim quod de se ipso dixerit Cbristus, nullus ambigit Christianus. Sed plan illo mortuo grano et muí [1398] tiplicato, tumba grana sunt sparsa in terram: ex quibus est et beatus Laurentius, cuius seminationem hodie celebramus. De illis autem granis sparsis toto orbe terrarum, quanta pullulaverit seges videmus, gaudemus, sumus: si tamen et nos per illius gratiam ad horreum pertinemus. Ñeque enim ad horreum pertinet quidquid in segete est. Eadem quippe pluvia utilis et nutritoria, et triticum pascit et paleam. Absit ut simul utrumque in hórreo recondatur; quamvis simul utrumque in agro nutriatur, et simul utrumque in area trituretur. Nunc tempus electindi est. Antequam veniat ventilatio, fiat morum sepa-

time to winnow. As on the threshing floor, the grain is separated and cleaned before the last winnowing. 2. Listen to me, holy grains, because I do not doubt that there are some here; Well, if I doubted it, not even I would be a grain. Listen to me, I repeat; Better yet, listen to the first grain through my mouth. Do not love your lives in this century. Stop loving them, if you love them, to safeguard them by not loving them, because by not loving them you love them more. Whoever loves his life in this world will lose it. The grain speaks; The grain that fell to the ground and died to multiply speaks; Listen to him, because he doesn't lie. What he taught he fulfilled himself; He instructed us with his precepts and went ahead with his example. Christ did not love his life in this world; He came precisely to lose it, to give it up for us and to recover it whenever he wanted. But he was man and also God. Christ, in fact, consists of the Word, the soul and the flesh; He is God and true man; but a sinless man, to take away the sin of the world. Because of his power he was greater, until he was allowed to say truthfully: I have power to give up my life and power to take it back again; No one takes it from me, but it is I myself who gives it and recovers it again. Since his power was so great, why did he say: Now my soul is troubled? Why does the God-man feel troubled if not because in him is the image of our weakness? I have power to give up my soul and power to get it back again. When you hear this from the mouth of Christ, ratio: sicut inarea, granum adhuc mundatione discernitur, nondum ventilabro ultimo separatur. 2. Anima hic non amanda. Cbristus propinquante morte turbatur, quia nos in se transfigurad—Audite me, grana sancta, quae hic esse non dubito; nam si doubto, nec ipse granum ero; audite, inquam, me; immo audite primum granum per me. Non ametis in hoc saeculo animas vestras: nolite amare, si amatis; ut non loving servetis; quia non amarando plus amatis. Qui amat in hoc saeculo animam suam, perdet eam (lo 12,25). Granum loquitur, granum quod in terram cecidit, et mortificatum est ut multiplicaretur, loquitur; audit, quia non mentitur. Quod admonuit, ipse fecit: instruxit praecepto, praecessit exemplo. Non amavit Christus in hoc saeculo animam suam; ideo come, ut hic perseret eam, pro nobisponeret eam, et cum vellet resumeret eam.

He speaks in his own name; When his soul feels disturbed by the imminence of death, it is him, but in you. In fact, the Church would not be his body if he were not also in us. 3. Focus your attention on Christ: I have power to give up my life and power to take it back again; Nobody takes it away from me. I fell asleep. Thus it says in the psalm: I fell asleep. As if to say: Why do they roar? Why do they jump for joy? Why do the Jews jump for joy as if they had done something? I fell asleep. I, he said; I who have to give my life, when I gave it I fell asleep, and sleep took over me. But since he had the power to recover it again, he added: And I got up. But, giving glory to the Father, he said: Because the Lord received me. When you hear these words: Because the Lord received me, the idea should not cross your minds that Christ himself has not resurrected his body. The Father resurrected him and he resurrected himself. How can we prove that he resurrected himself? Remember what he said to the Jews: Destroy this temple, and I will raise it up in three days. Notice, then, that Christ was born of the Virgin not out of natural necessity, but because he wanted to; He died because he wanted to and in the way he wanted. For his own good, he used bad men, without their realizing it; For our happiness, he put the furious and insane people at the service of his power and among those who killed him he saw those who were going to live with him. still seeing them

possessed by madness in the midst of that crazy people, he said: Father, forgive them, because they do not know what they do. «I, he said, I, as a doctor that I am, take their pulse and from the stake I see their ailments; I'm hanging and I touch them; I die and I give life to you; I shed my blood, and from it I make the medicine of health for my enemies. In a moment of fury they pour it out; then they believe and drink it. 4. Thus, then, Christ himself, our Lord and Savior, head of the Church, born of the Father without a mother; The same, I repeat, Jesus Christ, our Lord and Savior, as far as he is concerned, gave up his life by his own power and by his own power recovered it. Properly, what was said does not fall within this power: My soul is troubled. Proof of which would be that all disturbance had not yet gone away in him and sadness still clouded the devotion of his soul. Their members could be in danger of despair if when death approached they felt that they were losing their calm by not wanting to end this miserable life and being lazy to begin the one that never ends; So, so that despair would not break them, he turned his gaze to those weak members; and those not too strong members welcomed us into

Topic: Commentary on Mt 23,29-39. Place: Cartago, in the Restituta basilica. Date: August 10, feast of San Lorenzo. In the year 401. 1. The tiredness of the audience is demanding the suspension of the sermon; but, in view of the honor we owe to the martyr, I have to pronounce it. So, with the help of the Lord, I will try to moderate myself so that it is neither burdensome for anyone nor too brief, but rather responds to your needs. The most solemn day has shone for Rome, where it is celebrated with a large influx of people. We too, although absent in the body, present in the spirit, are associated with our brothers in a single body under a single head. In fact, the memory of his merits is not only linked to the place where the tomb of his body is located; veneration is due to him everywhere; His flesh rests in one place, but his conquering spirit is with him everywhere. In other words, the blessed Lorenzo was young in body, but a grave man in spirit, greatly enhanced by the freshness of his age and the unfading crown. He was a deacon, inferior to the bishop in office, but equal to the apostle in crown. The solemnity of all the blessed martyrs has been instituted in the Church so that those who did not see them suffer may remember them in the feast and be drawn to imitation by faith. In fact, perhaps its memory would be erased from the hearts of men if it were not repeated in the annual cycle. Not all martyrs can have their fervent solemnities, even if there were no shortage of martyrs for each day, since in the entire course of the year there cannot be found a single day in which martyrs have not been crowned in various places. But, if the most solemn celebrations were continuous, they would cause boredom, while the intervals renew affection. Let us limit ourselves to listening to what we have been commanded and set our eyes on what we have been promised. Let us prepare our hearts in the solemnity of any martyr so that we do not separate ourselves from his imitation. 2. The Lord spoke in the gospel to the Jews and said to them: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, who build tombs for the prophets and say: "If we had lived in the times of our fathers, we would not have given our consent to the death of the prophets." In this way you give a clear testimony that you are children of those who killed the prophets, and you will fulfill the measure of your fathers. In fact, by saying: If we had lived in the times of our fathers, we would not have given our consent to the death of the prophets, they confirmed that they were their children. We, however, if we stay on the right path, do not call our fathers those who killed the prophets, but those who were killed by their fathers. Because if one can degenerate through customs, in the same way one can become a son through them. Thus, we, brothers, were called children of Abraham, without knowing him personally and without bringing carnal descendants from him. How then are we his children? Not in the flesh, but in faith. For Abraham believed God, and it was considered righteousness to him. If, then, Abraham was righteous in believing, all who after him imitated Abraham's faith became his children. The Jews, born of him according to the flesh, degenerated; We, born of foreign people, achieve by imitating them what they lost by their

degeneration. Far be it from us to think that Abraham is their father, even though they descend from his flesh! Their parents were those they themselves confessed they were. If we had lived, they said, in the time of our fathers, we would not have given our consent to the death of the prophets. How do you say you wouldn't have agreed to those you call your parents? If they were parents, you are their child; If you are his son, you had to nod. If, on the other hand, you were going to dissent, you would not be his son; and, if you were not their son, they would not be parents. In this way, the Lord showed them that they would have done the same as the others did, since they called them their fathers. Truly, he said, you bear witness to yourselves that you are children of those who killed the prophets, since you called them your fathers. You too will fill the measure of your fathers. 4. But we do good works like those we are told to do every day, they are the fruit of necessity. What is better, more beautiful and more worthy of praise for a Christian than to share his bread with the hungry, to welcome the needy homeless into his home, to see someone naked and clothe him, to see another dead and bury him, to see people who litigate and make peace, to see someone sick and visit him or heal him? These are all works worthy of praise. Look and see that they are all the result of necessity. You distribute your bread, because you see someone who is hungry; If no one was hungry, who would you share your bread with? Eliminate the need that engenders the other's misery, and your mercy will cease to be useful. But, nevertheless, through these works that necessity has engendered, we arrive, as one arrives with a ship to the homeland, to that life where there will be no need. He who has to remain in his homeland, never leaving it again, no longer needs the ship; but it was the ship, which he would no longer need, that took him there. When you have reached there, the things mentioned above will no longer exist; but, if they are not done here, you cannot get there. Be generous, then, in the good works necessary to be happy, enjoying that eternity where all needs die, because death itself, mother of all needs, will die. For it is fitting that this corruptible be clothed with incorruption and that this mortal be clothed with immortality. Then it will be said to death: Where, O death, is your victory? Where is your eagle, oh death?

Every lack drags us to death and every sustenance tears us from it. That is why the body is subject to change, so that it can be said that some deaths are thrown out with others. Everything that is resorted to, but cannot be counted on for a long time, is something like the beginning of a death. Now consider this life. If you use something that you cannot count on for a long time and in which, if you stay for a long time, you die, you see there an incipient death; and yet, if you do not use it, the other death is not expelled. For example: someone does not eat; If you eat and assimilate what you eat, you recover. When he does not eat, he uses fasting to ward off the death that excess would cause; If you do not accept stopping eating and fasting, you will not escape death. And, in turn, if he wants to persevere in the fast he undertook to ward off the death that excess would cause, he must fear the other death: that of hunger. In the same way that he accepted fasting to avoid death from excess, so he must accept food to avoid death from starvation. If you persevere in any of those things that you lay your hands on, you will faint. You were tired of walking; If you continue walking, you will faint from exhaustion and die. Therefore, in order not to faint while walking, you rest by sitting down; But if you continue sitting, you will die from that. A deep sleep had invaded you;

you have to wake up to not die; but once awakened, you will die if you do not go back to sleep. Present me something that will serve as a remedy to expel an evil and with which you feel so calm that you want to persevere in it; Whatever it is, you have to fear it. Thus, the fight against death is fought with that mobility and mutability of fainting and remedies. But when this corruptible has put on incorruption and this mortal has put on immortality, it will be said to death: Where, O death, is your strife? Where is your sting, O death? Know, oh Christian, that whatever you suffer is nothing compared to what you will receive. It is certainty that faith provides us: it never departs from your heart. You cannot understand or see what you will be; What will it be like, then, that which not even the one who is going to receive it can understand? We will be what we will be, but we cannot understand what we will be. It overcomes our weakness, it surpasses all our thinking, it exceeds our understanding; but we will be that. Dearly beloved, says John, we will be children of God; Obviously, we already are by adoption, by faith, by the pledge we have. We have received as a pledge, brothers, the Holy Spirit. How can someone who has left us such a garment deceive? We are children of God, he said, and it has not yet been revealed what we will be; We know that when he appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is. He said that it has not yet manifested itself, but he did not say what it is that has not yet manifested itself. What we will be has not yet been manifested. If he had said: "We will be this and we will be like this," who would he have told if he had said it? I don't dare say who, but to whom I would have said it. And perhaps he could have said it, because he is the one who rested on the breast of the Lord and at that banquet drank the wisdom of the breast of the Lord. Full of that wisdom, he belched: In the beginning there was the Word. This, then, is what he said: We know that when what we will be is revealed, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is. Similar to who? CAPOT I.—1. Martyrum gloria insipientibus abscondita. Malitia pro poena.—Sicut audivimus, et canto respondimus: Pretiosa est mors sanctorum Domini, sed in conspectu eius (Ps 115,15), non in conspectu insipientium. Visi sunt enim oculis insipientium morí, et aestimata est malitia etitus illorum, Malitia in latino sermone non eam significationero

habere solet, quam habet in ea lingua qua Scriptura locuta est. Malitia enim in latina lingua dici solet, qua mali sunt nomines; illa autem lingua malitia dicitur etiam malum, quod patiuntur homines. Malitia ergo isto loco poena intellegitur. Hoc fraque dixit-. Visi sunt oculis insipientium morí, et aestimata est poena exitus illorum: illi autem sunt in pace. Et si coram hominibus storm passi sunt, haec est malitia: spes eorum, inquit, immortalitate plena est; et in paucis vexati, in multis bene disposentur (Wis 3,2-5). Non enim condignae sunt passiones huius temporis adfuturam gloriam, quae revelabitur in nobis (Rom 8:18). Sed doñee revealetur abscondita est. Et quoniam abscondita est, ideo visi sunt oculis insipientium morí. Sed numquid quia abscondita est, etiam Deo abscondita est, apud quem pretiosa est? Ideo pretiosa est in conspectu Domini mors sanctorum eius. Huic igitur abscondito sacramento oculos fidei debenmus, ut quod non videmus, credamus, et mala iniuste perpessi fortiter toleremus. In this way, whoever does not abandon the path does not fall into them. We have the solemn and faithful promise of our Lord Jesus Christ, who says: I am the way, the truth and the life. 3. Every man, whoever he is, wants to be happy. There is no one who does not desire it or who does not desire it above other things; Furthermore, everyone who desires anything else, desires it with an eye toward that. Men are carried away by various desires; one ambitions this, another that. Within the human race there are different lifestyles. And, within that multitude of lifestyles, each one chooses and takes control of one thing; However, whatever lifestyle is chosen, there is no one who does not want a happy life. Therefore, a happy life is a possession common to all; but the di-

vision of opinions begins with where one goes to it, how one tends towards it and by what path one arrives at it. For this same reason, I do not know if we can find a happy life if we look for it on earth; not because what we are looking for is bad, but because we do not look for it in the right place. Some say: "Happy are the men at arms." The other denies it, who says in turn: "Happy are those who cultivate the field." This is also denied by a third, who adds: "Happy are those who live in the forum in the midst of popular glory, defend causes, and with their words decide on the life and death of men." This is denied by another, and says: "Happy, yes, but the judges, who have the power to hear 3 and sentence." Another, denying the above, says: "Happy are the sailors, who know many regions and acquire great fortunes." You see, dearly beloved, that within this great multitude of lifestyles there is not a single thing that pleases everyone. But the happy life, yes. What does it mean that everyone likes a happy life, when not everyone likes just any life? 4. Let us, then, if we can, give a definition of the happy life to which everyone responds: "This is what I want." CAPUT III.—Diversis cupiditatibus homines rapiuntur, et alius cupit hoc, alius illud: diverse genera sunt vivirdi, in genere humano; et in multitudine generum vivirdi alius aliud elegit et capessit: nemo est tamen quocumque genere vitae elect, qui non beatam vitam cupiat. Blessed Martyrs of the persecution of Valerian in the year 258. Prudentius in the Peristephanon (XIII 70-87) tells us about the torture and the origin of the name of Masa Candida, that is, Masa Blanca: they preferred to end up in a pit full of quicklime rather than sacrifice to the gods. The poet says: «The whiteness of the lime surrounds their bodies, the whiteness of holiness transports their souls to heaven. From then on they deserved to be called Masa Candida.» The historicity of Prudencio's account is doubtful, at least in the details. The place of his martyrdom is also doubtful; while Prudentius places him in Carthage, Augustine places him in Utica (serm.311,10). The commentary on Psalm 144 was preached by Augustine in the basilica dedicated to these martyrs.? As can be seen, it diverges from Prudencio's interpretation. See the previous note.

It is about hearing judicial cases; In other words, to judge,
The truly happy life

want and not everyone is able to? Let's investigate, then. If you are asked if you want to live, does it make the same impression as if you were asked if you want to be a soldier? Regarding the second question, some would say yes, and others, perhaps most, no. If, on the other hand, you ask if you want to live, I think that no one will say no. In fact, everyone has it by nature to want to live and not want to die. In the same way, if I ask someone if they want to be healthy, I think that there will be no one who will tell me no; Nobody wants to experience pain. Health is, certainly, a precious asset for the rich and, perhaps, the only one for the poor. For what good is opulence to the rich, if he lacks health, which is the heritage of the poor? How eagerly would the rich man exchange his silver bed for the poor man's hair shirt if the disease went away with the bed! In these two things: life and health, I see that everyone agrees with me. Is there the same agreement regarding the military, or agriculture, or navigation? Everyone agrees on wanting life and health. But once a man is alive and healthy, does he seek nothing more? Well understood, perhaps you should not look for anything else. Where there is perfect life and perfect health, if something more is sought, what can it be but a corrupted desire? 5. The wicked will have life in the midst of their torments. For the time will come, as the gospel says, when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice; and those who have done good will come out to the resurrection of life, and, on the other hand,

those who did wrong, for the resurrection of judgment. Therefore, the first will go to receive the prize; the seconds, the torment; but some and others will live, without any being able to die. Those who live in the prize embrace a very sweet life; On the other hand, those who live in the midst of torment would wish, if possible, to put an end to that life, but no one will kill them to remove the torment. But pay attention to what the Scripture says, distinguishing: it did not deign to call that life. He did not want to call life what happens between torture, torment and eternal fire, so that the very word "life" indicates praise, not sadness; so that, wherever you hear about life, you never think of torment. In fact, living perpetually among torments is not life at all, but eternal death. The Scriptures call it the second death, which comes after this first, which we all owe to our human condition. It is called death, second death, but no one dies there. Better and more accurate would have been to say that no one lives there. Living, then, in the midst of pain is not living. And how do we prove that Scripture speaks this way? Look how; with the text that I mentioned shortly before: They will hear, he said, his voice, and those who did good will come out for the resurrection of life. He did not say: "Of the happy life", but: for the resurrection of life. The single word "life" carries with it happiness; Well, if it were not so, it would not be said to God: Because in you is the source of life. Nor was it said here: "For in you is the source of life."

omnes, et non habent omnes? Quaeramus ergo. Si cui dicatur, Vis Vivere? numquid sic audit, quomodo si diceretur, Vis militare? In illa enim interrogatione, quod est, Vis militare? aliqui mihi dicerent, Voló: et forte plures, Nolo. Yes autem dicam. See I will live? fucking nemo est qui dicat, Nolo. Omnes enim natura habent insitum, vivere olde, mori nolle. item si di[1402]cam, Vis sanus esse? puto nemo est qui dicat, Nolo: nemo enim vult doleré. Sanitas etiam in divite pretiosa, certe in paupere est sola. Sed quid prodest opulentia diviti, si sanitas non sit ibi, quae patrimonium est pauperi? Valde vellet dives lectum argenteum cum pauperis mutare cilice, si posset aegritudo migrare cum lecto. Ecce ad duo is consensit mihi omnium sensus, vitam et sanitatem. Numquid omnium sensus consensit ad militiam? numquid omnium ad agriculturem? numquid omnium ad navigationem? Omnium ad vitam et sanitatem. CAPOT V.—Cum ergo est homo vivus et sanus, nihilne plus quaerit? Si sapiat, forte nihil plus deben quaerere. Ubi enim est perfection vita et perfection sanitas, si quaeritur amplius, quid erit nisi vitiosa cupiditas? 5. Vita in doloribus non proprie vita. Vita non censenda, nisi quae beata.—Habebunt vitam in cruciationibus impii. Veniet enim hora, sicut Evangelium loquitur, quando omnes qui sunt in monumentis, audient vocem eius: et provenent qui bene egerunt, in resurrectionem vitae; who

vero male egerunt, in resurrectionem iudicii (lo 5,28-29). Ergo illi ad praemium, illi ad tormentum; et utrique vivunt, nec aliquis eorum mori potest. Illi qui vivunt in praemio, amplectuntur dulcissimam vitam: qui autem vivunt in tormento, cupiunt, si fieri possit, finiré talem vitam; et nemo eis dat interitum, ut nemo auferat cruciatum. Sed vide Scripturam loquentem et discernentem: non est dignita talem vitam vocare vitam. In cruciatibus, in tormentis, in ignibus sempiternis noluit appellare vitam: ut ipsum nomen vitae laudis sit, non maeroris; ut ubicumque audis vitam, storm non cogites. Nam in tormentis esse semper, aeterna mors est, non aliqua vita. Ipsam vocant Scripturae mortem secundam (cf. Rev 2:11; 20:6-14), post hanc primam, quam omnes humanoe condicioni debenmus. Et mors secunda, et mors vocatur, et nemo ibi moritur. Satius et melius dixerim, nemo ibi vivit. In doloribus enim vivere, non est vivere. Et unde probamus sic locutam Scripturam? Ecce unde; ex hoc testimony, quod moda commemoravi: Audient enim vocem eius, inquit, et provenent qui bene egerunt, in resurrectionem vitae. Non dixit: Beatae vitae; thirst, in resurrectionem vitae (lo 5,28-29). CAPUT VI.—Solum vitae nomen trahit beatitudem. Nisi enim consequentem haberet beatitudinem nomen vitae, non diceretur Deo, Quoniam apud te est fons vitae (Ps 35,10). Non enim et ibi dictum est, Quoniam
The truly happy life

happy." He didn't add "happy"; He only said life, so that you understand it happily. Since, if it is unhappy, it is no longer life. 6. Here is another testimony, in addition to the two mentioned. It was said in effect: Those who did good, for the resurrection of life; and also: In you is the source of life. Nowhere has it been added: "happy", but it is not understood that there is life if it is not happy, since what is not happy is not life. Listen to another one, taken again from the gospel. It is about that rich man who did not want to abandon what he owned, and who was outraged at having to lose his property, which he would necessarily have to leave behind when he died. I think that, in the midst of enjoying such great opulence of goods, although earthly, he felt challenged by the fear of death and in a certain way his heart said to him: "You enjoy your goods, but you do not know when the fever will visit you. You accumulate, acquire, buy, save and enjoy. They will demand your soul; What you have acquired, who will it be for? Frequently pricked by these thoughts, like stings of fear, as far as we can understand, he approached the Lord and said to Him: Good Master, what must I do to obtain eternal life? He was afraid of dying, and he was forced to do so. I had no escape to avoid it. Cornered by the need to die and the desire to live, he approached the Lord and said: Good Master, what must I do to obtain eternal life? Among other things, to mention only what concerns our case, he heard the following: If you want to come to life, keep

the commandments. This is what I had promised to try. Not even the one who asked said: What must I do to achieve a happy life? He spoke only of eternal life. Not wanting to die, he sought the life that has no end. And, as I said, does the life of the wicked have an end in the midst of torment? But he does not call this life. He knew that it is not life that passes in the midst of pain and torment; I was not unaware that it is more accurate to speak of death. That is why he sought eternal life; so that, when you hear about life, you have no doubt that you will be happy. Nor did the Lord answer him: "If you want to reach a happy life, keep the commandments," but he also mentioned only life, saying: If you want to reach life, keep the commandments. Thus, the life that passes between torments is not life; there is no life other than that which is happy; and it cannot be happy if it is not eternal. This is the reason why that rich man, aware that he was challenged day by day by the fear of death, sought eternal life; Well, in his view, he already had a happy life. He was, in fact, rich, he enjoyed health, and I think he said to himself: "I don't want any more, as long as this continues forever." He had pleasures apparently worthy of being loved, because they satisfied his foolish passions. The Lord corrected him—if he understood it—by simply pronouncing the word “life.” He did not say to him: "If you want to reach eternal life," which he was looking for, as if he already possessed a happy life; nor: "If you want to reach a happy life," knowing that, if it is miserable, it is not even life; but: If you want

apud te est fons beatae vitae. Non addidit, beatae; tantummodo dixit, vitae, ut tu intellegas beatae. Quare? Quia si miserae, iam nec vitae. 6. Idem ostenditur ex alio Scripturae loco. Vita beata non. est, nisi aeterna sit.—Ecce aliud testimonium. Iam diximus duo. Dictum est enim: Qui bene egerunt, in resurrectionen vitae; item dictum est: Apud te est fons vitae. Le 12,20) Hac cogitatione, quantum intellegitur, cum velut quibusdam timoris stimulis saepe compungeretur, accessit ad Dominum, et ait illi: Magister bone, quid faciam, ut vitam aeternam consequar?
