CAPUT VIL—Audivit Inter cetera, ut potius dicamus quod ad rem praesentem pertinet: Si vis vinore ad vitam, serva mandala (Mt 19:17). Hoc est quod me dixeram probaturum. Nec ille qui interrogavit, dixit: Quid faciam, ut vitam consequar beatam; sed tantummodo vitam dixit aeternam. Nolendo mori, quaesivit vitam quae non habet finem. Et numquid non, sicut dixi, etiam in tormentis impiorum vita non habet finem? Sed hanc ille non vocabat vitam. Quae esset in doloribus et cruciatibus, vitam non esse sciebat; mortem potius appellandam esse noverat. Ideo vitam aeternam quaerebat: ut ubi vita auditur, de beatitude non dubitetur. Et Dominus ad illum non dixit: Yes vis vinore ad vitam beatam, serva mandata; sed etiam ipse solam vitam nominavit, et ait: Si vis vinore ad vitam, serva mandata. Ergo illa vita in tormentis non est vita; et illa vita sola est, quae beata: nec beata esse potest, nisi fuerit aeterna. Propterea dives ille sciens se interpellari quotidie timore mortis, vitam aeternam quaerebat. Nam vitam beatam, sicut ei videbatur, iam habebat. Erat enim dives et sanus, et credo quia dicebat sibi: Nihil flew amplius, si possit esse perpetuum. Habebat enim quasi amabiles voluptates, quia satiabat stultas cupiditates. Proinde Dominus uno eum nomine vitae, si ille intellexit, correxit. Non ait: Si vis vinore ad vitam aeternam, quam ille quaerebat, quasi iam habens beatam; nec ait: Si vis come ad vitam beatam; sciens quia si misera est, nec vita diceda est; sed ait: Yes vu

come to life, keep the commandments. Therefore, there is no life other than eternal and happy, since, if it is not eternal, it is not happy either, and if eternity includes torments, it is not life either. 7. What is this, brothers? When asked if you want to live, you all answer yes, and the same when asked if you want to be healthy. But health and life, faced with the fear that it will cease to exist, is no longer life. Living forever turns into always fearing. If you are always afraid, you are always tormented. And if the torment is eternal, where is eternal life? We admit with complete certainty that life is not happy if it is not eternal; Furthermore, only eternal life is happy, since, if it is not eternal, if satiety is not perpetual, without a doubt, it is neither happy nor life. We note that everyone agrees on this. We find that this is certainly the case, but on the level of ideas, not yet on that of possession. Such is the possession that everyone seeks; There is no one who does not look for it. Be it good, be it bad, he searches for it; but the good one with confidence; the bad one, shamelessly. Why do you seek good, you evil? Doesn't your very request already show you how dishonest you are in wanting good while being evil? Aren't you looking for something else? So, if you seek the highest good, that is, life, be good to reach the good. If you want to achieve life, keep the commandments. Once we have reached life—what need do I have to add “eternal” or “happy”?—just life, since that is life: I will pour ai vitam; ibi is eternal, ibi blessed; Si vis vinore ad vitam, serva maniata. Ergo vita, quae aeterna et beata; quia si non aeterna, nec beata; si autem aeterna in poenis, nec vita. CAPUT VIII.—7. Vita vera est, quae aeterna et beata. Ai beatam vitam, necessaria certituio aeternitatis.—Quid est, fratres? Cum quaererem utrum velletis vivere, omnes responderbatis velle vos; utrum velletis sani esse, omnes responderbatis velle vos. Be sanitas et vita si timetur ne finiatur, iam non est vita. Non est enim semper vivere, sed semper timere. If semper timere, semper cruciari. Si cruciatus sempiternus, ubi vita aeterna? Tenemus certe non esse beatam, nisi vitam aeternam; immo non esse beatam, nisi vitam: [1404] quia si non aeterna, et si non cum satietate perpetua, procul dubio nec beata, nec vita. Invenimus, omnes consentiunt. Invenimus plane in cogitatione, nondum in possessione. Haec est possessio quam omnes quaerunt: nemo est qui non quaerat.

Malus sit, bonus sit, ipsam quaerit; sed bonus fidenter, malus impudenter. Quid quaeris bonum, male? Nonne tibi respondert ipsa postulatio tua, quam sis improbus, cum quaeris bonum malus? Nonne rem quaeris alienam? Si ergo summum bonum quaeris, hoc est, vitam; bonus this, ut ad bonum pervenias. Si vis come ai vitam, serva maniata. Cum autem pervenerimus ad vitam, quid addam aeternam? quid addam beatam? semel vitam, quia ipsa est vita, quae et aeterna et beata; cum pervenerimus ad vitam, certum
The truly happy life

the one that is eternal and happy—; Once we have arrived in life, we will be sure to always remain in it. If we have to find ourselves in it with the uncertainty of whether it will last forever, there will also be fear there. And if there is fear, there will be torment; not of the flesh, but, what is worse, of the heart. Where there is torture, how can there be talk of happiness? We will therefore have the assurance that we will remain forever in that life, knowing no end, since we will find ourselves in that kingdom of which it is said: And his kingdom will have no end. And when showing the glory of the saints of God, whose death is precious in his presence, Wisdom says at the end of the reading heard: And their Lord will reign forever. We will find ourselves, therefore, in a great and eternal kingdom; great and eternal precisely because it is just. 8. There no one deceives and no one is deceived. There is no reason to suspect evil of your brother there. In fact, most of the evils of the human race come from nothing more than false suspicions. You think that a man who perhaps loves you hates you, and out of a perverse suspicion you become your best friend's worst enemy. What can he do who you don't trust and who can't show you your heart? He turns to you and says, "I love you." But since he could tell you this while lying - he who lies says the same words as he who speaks the truth -, not believing it, you hated him. For this reason, whoever told you: Love your enemies, wanted to put you on your guard against this future penobis erit in ea nos semper. Nam si erimus ibi, et utrum ibi semper futuri simus, incerti erimus; etiam ibi erit timor. Et si erit timor, cruciatus erit, non carnis, sed, quod peius est, cordis. Ubi autem cruciatus, quae beatitudo? Erit ergo nobis certum quia in illa vita semper erimus, et eam finiré non poterimus: quia in illius regno erimus, de quo dictum est: Et regni eius non erit finis (Luke 1:33). CAPUT IX.—Et gloriam sanctorum Deí, quorum mors est pretiosa in conspectu eius, cum Sapientia demonstraret, ait, sicut in fine lectionis audistis: Et regnabit eorum Dominus in perpetuum (Wis 3,8). Erimus ergo in regno magno et sempiterno; et ideo magno et sempiterno, quia iusto. 8. A felicítate regni Dei procul suspiciones falsee, quae hic sunt origo malorum.—Nemo fallit ibi, nemo fallitur: non est illic ut male suspiceris de fratre tuo. Pleraque enim mala generis humani non aliunde oriuntur, nisi de suspicionibus falsis.

Credis de nomine quod oderit te, qui forte amat te; et per pravam suspicionem fis inimicissimus amicissimo. Quid faciat, cui non credis, et cor suum tibi demonstrare non valet? Loquitur tibi you say: I love you. Sed quia posset tibi hoc dicere et mentians (ea sunt enim verba mentientis, quae vera dicetis), non credendo adhuc odisti. Ideo securum te faceré voluit ab eo sin, qui tibi dixit: Diligite inimicos ves tros (Mt 5,44). Christiane, dilige et inimicos tuos, ne unsuspectus

fallen Christian, love even your enemies, lest, unsuspecting, you hate even your friends. In this life, in fact, we cannot see our hearts until the Lord comes and illuminates the deepest part of darkness; then he will manifest the thoughts of the heart, and everyone will receive his praise from God. 9. Therefore, if a man of complete trust, or a prophet, or God were to tell us in the way he wanted and through whom he wanted: “Live in peace; "You will abound in all things, none of you will die, none of you will be sick, none of you will experience any illness." If he were to say: "I have made death disappear from the human race, I do not want anyone to die," upon receiving such assurance, we would exult with joy and seek nothing more. That's how it really seems to us. If we heard words like those, we would immediately want something else to be added: that each other's hearts could be seen and that there be no envy, so that our seeing would not be based on human suspicion, but on divine truth; so as not to worry about whether my friend or my neighbor hates me, whether he wants me badly, and with that concern cause more harm than suffer it. We would certainly look for that; we would seek the certainty of life and the mutual knowledge of our hearts. You have already noticed what I call life; I will not repeat it, lest, instead of making it clearer, I make it darker. Thus, we would like the truth to be added to life, to mutually know our hearts and not feel deceived by our suspicions; to be sure that we will never abandon that perpetual life. Add truth to life, and you will have a happy life. In oderis et amicos. Corda ergo nostra in hac vita videre non possumus, doñee veniat Dominus, et illuminet abscondita tenebrarum, et manifestabit cogitationes coráis; et tune laus erlt unicuique a Deo (1 Cor 4,5). CAPUT X.—9. Vitae, ut sit beata, adesse debent veritas et amicorum^ cognitio sine metu deceptionis.—Ergo si quís nobis moda diceret, cui procul dubio crederemus, si Propheta diceret, si Deus quomodo vellet, et per quem vellet, diceret: Vivite securi, omnia vobis abundabunt, nemo vestrum morietur, nemo aegrotabit, nemo dolebit; abstuli mortem de genere humano, nolo quisquam moriatur, si diceret; quasi securi facti exsultaremus, et nihil amplius requireremus. Sic nobis videtur omnino.

Si hoc audiremus, continuo vellemus et hoc nobis addi, ut corda invicem videremus, nec invideremus; ut non humano [1405] suspicione, sed divina veritate videremus: ne essem sollicitus de amico meo, de vicino meo, ne me odisset, ne mihi malum vellet, et ipsa sollicitudine prius malum facerem, quam paterer. Quaereremus hoc sine dubio, quaereremus certam vitam, et invicem cognitionem cordium nostrorum. Iam enim intellegitis quam dicam vitam; ne saepius commendando obtundam potius quam instruam. Ergo vitae vellemus addi veritatem, ut corda nostra invicem nosceremus, ne nostris suspicionibus falleremur: ut de ipsa vita perpetua,
The truly happy life

Indeed, no one wants to be deceived, just as no one wants to die. Present me a man who wants to be deceived. There are many who want to deceive, but no one who wants to be deceived. Agree with yourself. If you don't want to be deceived, don't deceive; Don't do what you don't want to suffer. If you want to come to life where you do not suffer deception, live now without deception. Do you want to come to life where you will not suffer deception? Who doesn't want it? If you delight in reward, do not disdain the work that deserves it. Spend your life now without deceiving, and you will come to the life where you will not be deceived. To the truthful the truth will be given as a reward and to the one who lives well in time will be rewarded with eternity. 10. Therefore, we all, brothers, want life and truth. But where to get there, where to go? Although we do not yet possess it, thanks to the mind and reason, we already know by faith and see the goal to which we are heading: we tend towards life and truth. One thing and another is Christ. Are you looking for where to go? I am the way, he said. Are you looking for where to go? And the truth and life. This is what the martyrs loved and why they despised present and temporary goods. Do not be surprised by its strength: love defeated pain. Let us therefore celebrate the 4th solemnity of the Candida Mass with candid conscience and let us not fear the roughness of the path if we want to reach such great good: let us follow the footsteps of the martyrs and set our sights on the heads of the martyrs and our own. Who has made us the proquod ab ea non caderemus certi essemus. Adde vitae veritatem, et invenís vitam beatam. Nemo enim vult failedi, quomodo non vult mori. Da mihi hominem qui falli velit. Qui fallere velint, quam multi inveniuntur; who felli velit, nemo. Composes tecum. Non vis falli, noli fallere; quod pati non vis, noli faceré. Vis come ad vitam ubi non fallaris, age moda vitam ubi non fallas. Vis comere ad vitam, ubi non fallaris? quis nolit? Delectat merces; non dedigneris opus, cuius merces est. Topic: Endure the Lord. Place: Carthage. Date: August 18, feast of the martyrs of the Mass Candida. In the years 405-411.

Today we celebrate the solemn day of the blessed and numerous martyrs of the Candida Mass. Blessed, because poor in spirit; blessed, because humble; blessed, because they cried; blessed, because they hungered and thirsted for righteousness; blessed, because merciful; blessed, because pure in heart; blessed, because they suffered persecution not in vain, not for an evil cause, but for justice. For a martyr is not made by the punishment, but by the cause. He who has prudently chosen his cause suffers the penalty calmly, so that, if he suffers anything, it is for justice, lest he have to suffer here, and then go from these tribulations to others much less bearable. His soul was patient with the Lord; endured the Lord; He was in no hurry to receive the award. This is enduring the Lord: receiving him when he wants to give it to you. He will certainly give it to you, for neither the truth deceives, nor will the omnipotent lack

As if you asked where this delight should come from, he added: Because in you is the source of life. Here is the life that does not die, here is the health that does not get sick. For the health of man is in vain. Among human things, there is certainly nothing more valuable than health; and yet it is vain. How then are the others to be considered? What are the riches, the delights, the power of man, if the health of man is vain? Therefore, brothers, let us desire that health, let us ask for it with all our vows, let us try to achieve it with customs. Let us seek her by believing in her, hoping in her and loving her. This one, however, if you want to give it to us, let's be grateful. pilgrims enjoy this way on the road, what will be their joy in the homeland! The martyrs fought in this life, fighting they walked, and walking they did not anchor themselves. Indeed, those who love walk, because one does not run towards God with steps, but with affection. Our path itself seeks the walkers. There are three kinds of men he detests: those who stand still, those who turn back, and those who go off the path. May our walk be free and protected, with God's help, from these three types of evil. Another thing is that, while we are walkers, some go slower and others faster; some and others, however, walk. Those who stop must be encouraged, those who turn back must be made to return, and those who stray from the path must be brought back to it; The slow ones have to be motivated and the fast ones imitated. He who does not advance remains stopped on the road; who, perhaps, abandons a better purpose to return to what he had left behind because it was worse, has turned back; He who abandons the faith has strayed from the path. Let's worry about the slow ones, but from the position of the fastest ones; In any case, let us find ourselves among those who walk. 2. Who is the one who does not advance? Who thinks he is wise; who says: "What I am is enough for me"; who does not pay attention to the one who said: Forgetting what is behind and in tension towards what is before, in my intention I pursue the palm of the supreme vocation of God in Christ Jesus. He said he was running, that he was chasing something; He did not stand still, he did not look back; and far be it from us to think that whoever taught it, who

I kept it and showed it! So that we would imitate his speed, he said: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ. I think, dearly beloved brothers, that you are on the path with me. If I am slow, overtake me; I will not be envious of you; I'm looking for who to follow. If, on the other hand, you think I'm going faster, run with me. One is the goal that we all rush to reach, both the slowest and the fastest. This is what the Apostle himself said: Forgetting what is behind and in tension towards what is before, in my intention I pursue only one thing: the palm of the supreme vocation of God in Christ Jesus. The core of the phrase is this: I pursue only one thing. To get to this, what did you say before? Brothers, I don't think I have reached it. Here is the one who does not stand still: the one who does not believe he has achieved it; Here is the one who does not want to be a pilgrim: the one who does not stay on the road, the one who will enjoy the homeland. Me, he said. Who is that "I"? I, who worked harder than all of them. However, when he said: I worked harder than all of them, he did not express the "I." I don't think I have reached it. The “I” is okay when it refers to something humble, not something of pride. As for me, he said, I don't think I've reached it. That's him. But when he said: I worked harder than all of them, he continues: but not I, but the grace of God with me. Does not the grace of God reach her? Rightly, then, he said there: I. Not achieving it is the result of our weakness; achieving it is the result of the help of divine grace, not of human weakness. Who is there, then, to show us?

The perfect wayfarer marches well, walks well and stays on the path; but, nevertheless, he is still a wayfarer, he has not yet reached the goal. Well, in fact, if you walk, and you walk along the path, you are heading somewhere and you are trying to get somewhere. The Apostle had not yet reached the goal he was striving to reach. And he exhorts the perfect to realize that they are not yet perfect and to recognize their imperfection. He is a perfect wayfarer who knows that he has not yet arrived at the place where he is going and knows how far he has traveled and how much he still has left. Let us, then, who are perfect, recognize that we are not yet perfect,

so as not to remain imperfect. What am I saying, brothers? Isn't the martyr Cuadrado perfect? 'What is more perfect than a square? Its sides are equal, everywhere it is identical; In whatever way it is put, it is always standing, never fallen. Oh beautiful name, indicator of a figure and sign of a future thing! It was already called Cuadrado and had not yet been crowned. The temptation that was going to make him square had not yet come, and yet, when he was called by that name, it was indicated to whom he had been predestined before the creation of the world; In it the name and the fulfillment are combined. Paria sunt latera, undique aequalis est forma; quacumque verterit, statio est, non ruina. O nomen pulchrum, demonstrans figuram, et indicas remfuturam! Iam Quadratus et antea vocabatur, et nondum coronabatur: nondum in temptatione apparuerat, per quam esset ille quadratus; et tamen, quando vocabatur, praenuntiabatur praedestinatus ante mundi constitutionem, et, ut hoc vocaretur, hoc in illo compatitur, ut impleretur; et tamen ambulabat, et tamen adhuc in via erat; et, quamdiu erat in hoc corpore, totum timebatur, et ne remaneret, et ne retro rediret, et ne exorbitaret. The same Apostle said: I am going to tell you something speaking humanly in attention to the weakness of your flesh: as you gave your members to the service of impurity for iniquity, now lend them to the service of justice for sanctification. The exhortation seems great. Each one should measure himself with these words of the Apostle: let no one pass his hand in flattery; use a faithful scale and tell yourself the truth. Why do you expect to hear it from my lips? Tell yourself. I have tried to put a mirror in which everyone can look at themselves. I am not the clarity of the mirror, which shows the face to whoever looks in it. I am referring now to your inner faces, which I can reach by hearing, but I cannot see. I put the mirror in front of you: let everyone look at themselves and tell themselves what they are like. Consider the words of the Apostle that I mentioned as if they were the mirror. I am going to tell you something, speaking humanly, in attention to the weakness of your flesh: as you gave your members to the service of impurity for iniquity, now lend them to the service of justice for sanctification. What does it mean like this? Do this as you did that. When you gave your members as weapons of iniquity to sin for impurity, that delighted you. No? I ask you; Pay attention and respond. Did it delight you? I hear your response, even if you remain silent; Indeed, you would not have done it if it had not delighted you. Therefore, as you gave your members

at the service of impurity for iniquity and you did it with delight, so justice will someday delight you. God tells you: «I don't want you to do it out of fear; "Were you doing the other thing out of fear?" Thus he said, thus: As you gave your members to the service of impurity for iniquity, so now lend them to the service of righteousness for sanctification. You run to justice out of fear, while you ran to impurity out of love. What is more beautiful than justice? Tell me, I beg you. It is worthy of being loved, at least, as is impurity. When you ran towards impurity, you went despite the prohibition; you offended your father, and you ran; You were willing to be disinherited so as not to separate yourself from their evil. What can you say? Justice demands from you what impurity obtained from you. You heard the gospel: I did not come to bring peace to the earth, but the sword. He said he was going to separate the children from the parents. Set your gaze, then, on that sword. Do you perhaps want to serve God and your father forbids it? When you loved impurity, you ran after it even if your father forbade you. Now justice prohibits you from continuing to love her; Here too you found your father's prohibition. Bring out your freedom, as then your passion. Then you were willing to be disinherited in order not to separate yourself from that impurity; Do it now too so as not to separate yourself from the beauty of justice. It is a great and fair thing. Who is there who dares to say: "Impurity is more deserving of love than justice"? Meanwhile, justice presents you with a

adversas peccatum certastis (Hebr 12:4). Quando tolerat, quando sustinet mundum saevientem, qui spernere non potest blandientem? 4. Ait idem apostolus: Humanum dico propter (884) infirmitatem carnis vestrae: sicut exhibituistis memhra vestra deserviré inmunditiae ad iniquitatem, sic nunc exhíbete membra vestra deserviré iustitiae in sanctificationem (Rom 6,19). Magnum est valde, quod videtur hortatus. Metiatur se unusquisque in his verbis apostoli: non adulatorie pálpense; appendat se, et dicat sibi verum. What do you expect me to hear? Ipse sibi dicat. Ego disposui speculum proposere, ubi se qui que attendat. Non sum ego speculi fulgor, qui faciem suam intuenti renuntiet. Facies enim illas dico modo, quas habemus intus: ipsas per aurem convenire possum, videre non possum. Sneculum sane propono: attendat se unusquisque, et renuntiet sibi. Ipsa verba apostoli, quae comme [94] moravi, in vicem speculi aceipite. Humanum dico propter infirmitatem carnis vestrae: sicut exhibituistis membra vestra deserviré inmunditiae ad iniquitatem, sic nunc exhíbete membra vestra deserviré iustitiae in sanctificationem. What is it, sic? Sicut íllud, ita et istud. When you exhibited membra tua arma iniquitatis sin ad inmunditiam, delectabat te? I interrogate: attend, respond. Delectabat te? Audio respondertem, etiam tacentem: non enim faceres, nisi delectaren Sicut ergo exhibituisti membra tua deserviré immunditiae ad iniquita-

tem, et cum delectatione ista fecisti, ita delectet te aliquando iustitia. Nolo timore facías, dicit tibí deus: numquid enim íllud timore faciebas? Sic, inquit, sic. Sicut exhibituistis membra vestra deserviré inmunditiae ad iniquitatem, sic nunc exhíbete membra vestra deserviré iustitiae ad sanctificationem. Ad iustitiam timore compelleris: ad inmunditiam amore currebas. Quid pulchrius iustitia, pray you? Dignified is vel sic amari, quomodo amata is filthy. Quando currebas ad inmunditiam, prohibebaris, et ibas: patrem offendebas, et currebas: paratus eras exheredan, et ab illius pravitate non separan. What dicturus is it? Hoc a te exigit iustitia, quod de te habuit inmunditia. Audistis evangelium: Non veni pacem mittere in terram, sed Radium (Mt 10,34). Dixit se separaturum filios a parentibus (cf. ib., 35). Ergo attende illam machaeram. Forte vis deo serveré, et pater prohibet? Quando immunditiam diligebas, etiam patre prohibin te currebas: moda te prohibet iustitia amatorem suum; invenisti et hic patrem prohibentem. Exere libertatem tuam, qui exeruisti tune cupiditatem tuam. Paratus eras tune exheredan, et ab illius inmunditiae pravitate non separan: paratus esto exheredan, et a iustitiae pulchritudine non separan. Magnum est, sed iustum est. Quis est qui audeat dicere, Sed plus debuit amari inmunditia, quam iustitia? Interim iustitia gradum tibi facit. Certe, inquit, dissimilis sum: certe plurimum distat Inter illius
Commentary on Rom 9:19

step. «In truth, he says, I am nothing like impurity; In truth, the distance is great between the darkness of that impurity and my light, between that evil and my beauty, between their decorum and mine; Without a doubt, the distance is immense. In the meantime, I'll give you a step. That's how I want it, although I should be more demanding, much more; all the more so the greater the distance that separates us. But I say something in the human way; I differentiate the divine. Why do I differentiate the divine? I speak to you in a human way in attention to the weakness of your flesh. I ask you this way because I am still condescending to your weakness. Therefore, as you gave your members to the service of impurity for iniquity, so now you must do much more; but at least walk like this; Get at least this far. But go from there. For now, I speak to you in a human way; But as I told you the other thing, so I also tell you this." 5. Was Cuadrado like that? Certainly not so; It was much more and much more worthily. Look at that impurity, and see how much more piety and charity, the beauty of justice and the sweetness of sanctification, demand of you. What more does he require of you? Listen to it. The lover of impurity does not want his actions to be known; He fears being condemned for it, he fears prison, he fears the judge and the executioner. He desires the honesty of another's wife and deceives her husband; seek the darkness; He fears nothing as much as a witness, he fears the judge; He fears that it will be known, because he fears being punished for it. Now, what the beauty of justice demands more, and which the Apostle deferred for the moment when he said: I speak in a human way in attention to the weakness of your flesh, hear it from the mouth of the

Lord: What I say to you in darkness, that is, in what is hidden, say it in the light, and what you hear in the ear, preach it on the roofs. Does the adulterer perhaps announce his clumsiness from the roof? But why does he not only not announce it on the roofs, but rather seeks to hide under the roof? Why did the Lord say that? Because since impure love got there, it fears being discovered and punished. On the other hand, the lovers of that invisible beauty; the lovers of that beauty where the most beautiful of the children of men is found; Why are lovers of that beauty not afraid to preach on the rooftops what they heard in their ears? Find out why he fears: he fears that it will be known and that he will be punished. Find out why this one does not fear: the Lord Himself added it next. After having said: What I say to you in darkness, say it in the light, and what you hear in the ear, preach it on the housetops, he said: Do not fear those who kill the body. To say in the light what you hear in the darkness and to preach on the housetops what you hear in the ear, do not fear those who kill the body. The adulterer fears those who kill the body; Well, when you lose your body, you lose your pleasure factory. He who lives from the body fears losing his body. Everything he desires is the work of the body. That is why pleasure is not enough for him; burns with passion until reaching filthy bodily delight 2. But you, man of God, if you have interior eyes with which to see the beauty of charity, with which to see the beauty of piety; if you have eyes

inmunditiae tenebras et luzern meam, inter illam pravitatem et pulchritudínem meam, inter íllius decus et decus meum; certe plurimum disstat. Interim gradum pono. Sic flew: nam plus debeno, plus omnino debeno; quantum disto, tantum debeno. Sed humanum dico, divinum differo. [95] Quare divinum differo? Humanum dico propter (885) infirmitatem camis vestrae. Ideo sic, quia parco adhuc infirmitati. Ideo, sicut exhibituistis membra vestra deserviré inmunditiae ad iniquitatem, sic nunc plus quidem debentis, sed saltem sic ambulate, ad hoc pervenite. Sed et hinc transite. Interim humanum dico: sed, sicut illud, ita et hoc. 5. Numquid Quadratus sic? Non plañe sic, sed plus, et digne plus. Attendite enim illas inmunditias, et videte quid de vobis plus exigat pietas et caritas, et iustitiae pulchritudo, et sanctificationis dulcedo: quid de vobis plus exigat, attendite. Amator inmunditiae facta sua mala sciri non vult: timet ne inde damnetur, timet inde carcerem, timet iudicem, timet carnificem. Uxoris alienae pudicitiam appetit, maritum fallit: tenebras quaerit, conscium perhorrescit, iudicem metuit; timet sciri, quia timet inde puniri. Iam vero illud quod sibi exigit plus pulchritudo iustitiae, quod interim distulit apostolus, cum diceret, humanum dico propter

infirmitatem camis vestrae, audi hoc a domino: Quod dico vobis in tenebris, hoc est, in occulto, dicite in luz, et quod in aure auditis, super tecta praedicate (Mt 10,27). Numquid praedicat super tectum adulter flagitium suum? Sed quare ille non solum non praedicat super tectum, sed quaerit occultari tecto? quare hoc ille? Quia tune usque potuit amor munditiae: timet enim detegi, timet puniri. Hi vero amatores illius invisibilis pulchritudinis, amatores illius decoris, ubi est ille speciosus forma prae filiis hominum (Ps 44,3); amadores ergo illius pulchritudinis, unde non timent praedicare super tecta, quod in aure audierunt? Quaere unde timeat ille: ne cognoscatur et puniatur. Quaere unde iste non timeat: ipse dominus secutus adiunxit. Cum enim dixisset, quae dico vobis in tenebris, dicite in lumine, et quod in aure auditis, super tecta praedicate: Nolite, inquit, timere eos qui corpus occidunt (Mt 10,28). Ut quae auditis in tenebris in lumine dicatis, ut quod in aure auditis super tecta praedicetis, nolite timere eos qui corpus occidunt. Timeat adulter eos qui corpus occidunt: cum enim adulter ille perdiderit corpus, voluptatum perdit officinam. Ule timeat I will lose corpus, qui vivit ex corpore; totum enim, quod concupiscit, per corpus operatur: ideo in illo voluptas non sufficit; [96] inardescit cupiditate, quoadusque perveniat ad corporis inmundissimam voluptatem. Your autem, homo dei, if you have oculos
Commentary on Rom 9:19

In your heart, see what you are going to use to enjoy your beloved, because to enjoy her you do not need the members of the body. The lover of sordid pleasure fears losing his body; Instead, peace on earth to men of good will. 6. How far you are from this love, oh Christian! May you reach that human level and do good with delight, like sin before! In fact, if you do good with delight, if you believe in Christ with delight, if you enjoy wisdom with delight to the extent of your ability, if you listen to and fulfill its precept with delight, that human level adjusted to your weakness begins to exist in you. You have already begun to have a good gift, but you have not yet reached the perfection of Square. But, like I said, if you got there, keep going; There's still a way to go, don't stop. You still have something to do: do not fear or hide your good works out of fear. Those who rebuke you and shoot you, what do they say to you? «Here is a great apostle! Your feet are already hanging from the sky; where do you come from? And you are afraid to answer: "From the church," lest they reply: "Aren't you ashamed, bearded man, to go where widows and old women go?" Because you don't hear such things, you are afraid to say, "I was in church." How can you stand the persecutor, you who feel panic at a simple insult? It is true that we are in times of peace. They are the ones who should blush. The many who arrived are ashamed and the few who remained are not ashamed. Those who arrived, where did they arrive? Those who stayed,

where did they stay? Those came to the light of peace; These were left in the darkness of confusion. Are you not ashamed to be ashamed of what is worthy of glorification? Are they not ashamed of their foolishness, and are you ashamed of something glorious? And where is what you heard: Draw near to him and you will be enlightened, and your faces will not blush? 7. I have said this, my brothers, because I know and it pains me greatly that the tongues of the few pagans who do not mistreat, but only insult, are feared, and that the spirits of those who want to believe are inhibited, since they do not find the rest that comes with being invited by a Christian. What else? What should I say? You see that any pagan is exacerbated so that he does not become a Christian, and you, who are one, remain silent and even consider it a triumph that they condescend to you, that is, that they do not insult you. When they intimidate him, you say in your heart: “Thank God; "He has said nothing to me." You flee not with your body, but with your soul. You stand still there and flee; You fear that that cursing tongue will turn against you and you do not come to the aid of him whom you must win for Christ. You don't help him, you keep quiet; As I said, you flee not with your body, but with your soul; you are a mercenary; You see the wolf coming and you run away. And what more do I have to say? We all just heard it. May the Lord instill terror in us; If it is to be loved, it must be feared. He said: Whoever is ashamed of me before men. And see when he said that: when the world did not yet believe, but rather roared. Whoever is ashamed of me in front of me

cordis, unde videas pulchritudinem caritatis, unde videas pulchritudinem pietatis; si habes oculos cordis, vide unde fruaris amata tua: ut enim ea fruaris, non membra corporis quaeris. Timeat perimi corpus amator sordidae voluptatis, sed pax in tena in hominibus bonae voluntatis (Lk 2:14). 6. Quam longe es ab hoc amore, o christiane! Utinam usque ad illud humanum pervenias, et cum delectatione benefacias, sicut ante cum delectatione (886) peccabas: si enim cum delectatione bene facis, si cum delectatione in Christum credis, si cum delectatione sapientia eius pro tua capacítate perfruaris, si cum delectatione praeceptum audis et facis, coepit in te esse illud humanum propter infirmitatem tuam. Iam coepisti habere bonum datum, sed needum implesti Quadratum. Sed, sicut dixi, si pervenisti, agree; adhuc via est, noli remanere. Est adhuc quod facias: noli timere, et abscondere facta tua bona timendo. Reprehensors, exagitatores, quid tibi dicunt? Magnus your apostolus! de cáelo tibi pendent pedes: unde venis? Et times dicere, De ecclesia, ne dicatur tibi: Non te podert, barbate, iré quo eunt viduae et aniculae? Ne auditas, sometimes dicere, In ecclesia fue. Quomodo ierres persecutorem, qui horrescis insultatorem? Et certe tempus est pacis. lili erubescere debuerunt: erubescunt tam multi, qui accesserunt, et non erubescunt tam pauci, qui remanserunt. Et hi accesserunt: quo? lili autem remanserunt: ubi?

Accesserunt hi ad luzem pacis; remanserunt illi in tenebris confusionis. Non erubescitis gloríada erubescere? Non erubescunt illi pudenda: et vos erubescitis glorianda? Et ubi est, quod audistis: Accedite ad eum et illuminamini, et vultus vestri non erubescent? (Ps 33,6) [97] 7. Haec dixi, fratres mei, quoniam scio, et plurimum doleo, timeri linguas paucorum paganorum, non saevientium, sed tantum insultantium, et teneri vivos credere volentium, cum non acquiescunt in exhortationibus christianorum. Et quid plura? aut quid ego dícturus sum? Vides exagitari nescio quem paganum, ne fiat christianus, et tu christianus taces: pro magno habes quia tibi parcit, id est, quia tibi non insultat. Quando illum deterret, dicis in corde tuo: Deo gratias! nihil mihi dixit. Fugis, non flesh, sed mind. Ibi stas, et fugis: sometimes ne in te lingua maledica convertatur, et non subvenís ei, quem deben Christo lucrifacere. Non subvenís, taces: ut dixi, non carne sed mente fugis, mercenarius es: vides lupum venientem, et fugis (cf. lo 10,12). Et quid plus ego dicturus sum? Audivimus omnes mode. Dominus terreat: qui amandus est, ipse metuendus. Qui me, inquit, confusus fuerit coram hominibus. Et videte quando ista dicebat: quando mundus non credebat, Sed fremebat — qui me confusus fuerit coram hominibus, confundatn

of men, I will be ashamed of him before my Father who is in heaven; But whoever confesses me before men, I will also confess him before my Father who is in heaven. Do you want Christ to deny you or recognize you? When you find that Christ denies you, the one who insulted you will be far away. The time will come to fulfill what was promised; Will he who kept so many promises appear to be a liar only when it comes to the day of judgment? Let them live in their infidelity—better, let them also lack their infidelity—; but present yourselves before them as models in the confession of faith, not in being defeated by silence. In fact, if they find Christians who defend the weak, brave to proclaim their faith, free to confess it, prudent in teaching it and charitable in instructing others, they will remain silent, believe me; They won't have anything to say. They would say nothing but meaningless words; They would be a clanging cymbal. What ceased to exist in their temples remained in their mouths. eum coram patre meo qui in caelis est: qui autem me confessus fuerit coram hominibus, confitebor illum et ego coram patre meo qui in caelis est (Mt 10,33.32). You see Chtisto negati, do you still see Christo confiden? Longe habebis insultatorem, quando tui Christum inveneris negatorem. Veniet quod pollicetur: qui tanta exhibituit, de solo die iudicii fallax invenietur? absit. Habeant illi perfidiam suam, immo vero et ipsi cateant perfidia sua; sed proponite vos illis ad confessionem imitandos, non ad silentium superandos. lili enim, si invenerint christianos fortiores infirmorum defenders assertione fidei, libértate confitendi, prudentia docendi, caritate instruendi, silebunt, credite: quod enim dicant, (887) non habent. Vox inanis est, cymbalum tinniens (cf. 1 Cor 13:1): quod destitit in templis ipsorum, remansit in ore ipsorum.

Topic: Commentary on Mt 16:25. Place: Carthage, in Cyprian's mensa. Date: August 21, feast of San Cuadrado. In the years 396 or 397. 1. We have heard how the evangelical trumpet sounds that exhorts the martyrs to the combat in which they will conquer the world: Whoever wants to save his soul will lose it; whoever loses it for me will find it. By saving her he loses her, by losing her he finds her. What does this mean if not that there is a health of the soul according to this world and another according to God? At the moment of temptation with which the martyrs were tested, presenting them with the alternative between the denial of Christ and the test of death, those who wanted to save their souls according to the world denied Christ, and lost them; On the other hand, those who lost them according to the world, confessed Christ, and found them. To whom could they trust their soul more safely than to their creator? Who can preserve what already existed but he who could create what did not exist? Learning and teaching this
[PLS 2,694] (MA 1,646) SERMO SANCTI AUGUSTINI EPISCOPI AD MENSAM CYPRIANI DE SANCTO QUADRATO (II)

1. Evangelical tuba exhortans martyres ad certamen, quo vincerent mundum, quomodo increpuerit audimus: qui animam suam vult salvam faceré perdet eam; nam qui perdiderit eam propter me, (647) inveniet illam (Mt 16,25). Saving lost, losing inveniet. Quid est hoc, nisi quia est quaedam salus animae secundum hoc saeculum, et est alia salus animae secundum deum? In article ergo temptationis, qua probad sunt martyres, ita ut alterutrum eis proposeretur, aut Christi negatio, aut mortis temptatio, procul dubio qui voluerunt salvas faceré animas suas secundum saeculum, negaverunt Christum, et perdiderunt eas; qui autem secundum saeculum perdiderunt animas suas, confessi sunt Christum, et invenerunt eas. Cui enim tutius commendatur anima, quam suo creatori? Quis potest conservere quod erat, nisi qui potuit faceré quod non erat? Mensa is the altar erected in honor of a martyr (see serm.310,2) and, by extension, the basilica. This is the Ager Sixti basilica, where the body of Saint Cyprian was buried. In it Augustine preached sermons 8, 13, 49, 114, 131, 154,
313 A (= DENIS 14), 313 B (= DENIS 15),

Cuadrado - he was, in fact, a bishop -, whose solemn feast we celebrate today, confessed Christ with all his people, clergy and laity. He sent ahead the flock that was pasturing. The Candidate Mass, whose solemnity we celebrated four days ago, was the people of God entrusted to his government. What a great plastered wall ruled this Square! And all those souls and the wall formed with them still did not see the Church that we contemplate; They did not see it yet, but they built it with the stones that were themselves; When they died they ran like living stones to their frame. Now we see the Church extended throughout the entire world; then it was great in a few, and now widespread and diffused among many. We also see that what was predicted by the prophets is fulfilled, who had anticipated what we now see as the future. But to make this a reality, when they were few, great strength was necessary. With their passage they widened the narrow road; They passed over the rough edges and preceded us. His followers were those who in those times endured various tribulations for the name of Christ. Blessed are they losing their souls! Or fortunate losses! Thus they throw, thus those who sow lose. Who doubts that, in every field, what is sown is thrown and covered with earth? But how great is the hope of the harvest that precedes that of the sower! Nor does anyone see the harvest when it is sown; everything is left in the hand of God, it is entrusted to the Hoc discens et docens iste Quadratus — erat enim episcopus — cuius sollemnitatem hodie celebramus, cum tota plebe sua, clericis et laicis, confessus est Christum. Praemisit gregem, quem pascebat: post quadriduum Quadratus secutus est. Massa enim Candida, cuius ante quadriduum sollemnitas celebrata est, plebs etat dei, gubernatiotú huius [695] credita. Quam magnum parietem signinarium regebat iste Quadratus! Et illae tot animae, et ex tot animabus, nondum videbant ecclesiam, quam videmus: nondum videbant, et de se ipsis eam construebant, atque in eius conpagem dying lapides vivi currebant. Et ecce videmus ecclesiam toto terrarum orbe diffusam, tune in paucis magnam, never in multis latam atque diffusam; et cernimus impleri praedicta prophetarum, quae praecesserunt future omnia quae videmus. Be, ut hoc ieront, quando paucitas erat, fortitudo magna erat. Angustam viam transeundo dilataverunt, et áspera duna tracing transierunt, praecesserunt nos.

Secuti sunt hos, quicumque illis temporibus pro nomine Christi tribulationes various pertulerunt. O beati losing your souls! or felicia detrimental! Sic proiciunt, sic perdunt, qui seminant. Quis enim dubitet, in omni seminatione ea, quae seminantur, proici, obrui? Be quanta spes messis est, quam praecedit seminantis! Et quando seminatur, messem nemo videt: totum
Bishop of Utica. See nt.l to serm.306 B.
Commentary on Mt 16:25

land. The earth preserves it, fertilizes it, multiplies it; but by the work of him who made heaven and earth. 2. The name of this martyr invites us to say something about the holy square. The holy Noah had an ark made of square wood. Why were they chosen to be square? What was meant by this but that no one can knock down a square? Whichever way you leave it, it gains stability. Destroy yourself by turning it over; get tired trying to knock it down; once you have knocked it down, you will find it as it was before the knockdown. Any position suits you. They showed them the damage they were going to suffer; The confessors of Christ were dispossessed of all their property: Cuadrado remained standing. He was threatened with exile and the loss of his carnal homeland: thinking about his spiritual homeland, Cuadrado continued standing. They inflicted torture and cruel torture on him: thinking of the great torments of hell, Cuadrado continued standing. They promised him great rewards in the world if he denied Christ: thinking of the celestial crown, Cuadrado continued standing. 3. This is how the Christian should be; but to be like this he must invoke Christ. Let him be the one who squares, who rules, who does not allow the one who falls to fall. It was not said in vain: The righteous man falls seven times and gets up again. We should not refer what has been said to the fall into some serious sin. The one who was innocent falls seriously and becomes a murderer; He who was chaste falls and becomes an adulterer. It is not to these falls that what was said refers: The just falls seven deo creditur, terrae committitur. Servat terra, fecundat terra, multiplyt terra: sed illo agent, a quo factum est caelum et terra. (648) 2. Nomen huius martyris admonet nos de sancta quadratura aliquid dicere. Sanctus Noe de lignis quadratis arcam iussus est fabricare. Quid electum est in quadratura, quid praesignatum est, nisi quoniam quadratum stantem deicere nullus potest? Quacumque enim degeris, stabit. Contere you coming back, work saying; et deiciendo sic invenies, quem deiecisti, quomodo stabat antequam deiceretur. Locate statio illi collocata est. Proposita sunt damna, ablatae sunt res confitentium Christum: stetit Quadratus. Proposita sunt exilia, et amissio patriae carnalis: cogitata patria spiritali stetit Quadratus. Inpacta storm saevique cruciatus: cogitatis tantis gehennae doloribus stetit Quadratus. Promissa ingenua praemia saecularia, ut negeretur Christus: cogitata caelesti corona stetit Quadratus. 3.

Talis debent esse christianus: sed, ut sit talis, invokendus est Christus. Ipse quadret, ipse regat, ipse cadentem cadere non permittat. Non enim frustration dictum est: septies cadit iustus, et resurgit (Prov 24:16). Non ad casus alicuius gravis peccati debenmus referre, quod dictum est. Cadit enim graviter, qui innocens et fit homicida; cadit, qui castus erat et fit adulter. Non de talibus casibus dictum [696] est, septies cadit iustus
Commentary on Mt 16:25

times and rises, but to falls in tribulations. Falling is equivalent to being humiliated. No matter how many times the righteous are humiliated, they always rise up. Square is anyone who remains standing even if he is turned around. The seven times equal the whole; With that perfect number it indicates how many times 3 falls. "Seven" is equivalent to "how many times", just like in this phrase: I will praise you seven times a day. His praise is always in my mouth. And so that you can see that this is the meaning of the phrase: The righteous man falls seven times and rises again, let us examine the context: what the Holy Scripture said before and what it added after those words. This way the meaning will appear clear. What does Scripture say where this phrase appears? Do not lead the wicked to the pastures of the righteous nor let yourself be seduced by the fullness of the belly. And it continues: The righteous man falls seven times and gets up again; the wicked, however, will be weakened in their evils. The words that follow the phrase begin to illuminate it: The righteous man falls seven times and gets up; the wicked, however, will be weakened in their evils. Therefore, he who falls seven times and rises is not weakened by evils. This is falling and rising: being humbled and not weakening. 4. What then does the above mean: Do not lead the wicked to the pastures of the righteous nor let yourself be seduced by the fullness of the belly? I am going to say what I can, as the Lord deigns to grant me; Whoever knocks loudest will find something better. Behold, dearly beloved, I am preaching to you the word of God;

You all hear it, you all delight and enjoy it, but not all of you fulfill it. Such are the pastures on which the soul of the righteous feeds; but the soul of the wicked is also fed there. The righteous and the wicked hear it together; both say once the sermon is over: "We are satisfied." But you distinguish those who eat healthily from those who eat it too; He acquires plenty in his belly, but not solidity for his mind. Distinguish, then: Do not lead the wicked to the pasture of the righteous, that is, do not compare him with the pasture of the righteous. "Don't take it," that is, don't compare it. One and the other feed in different ways. Don't think they are the same; do not put him next to the righteous. If you hear that he also has the Scriptures: do not be seduced by the fullness of the belly. Do not lead the wicked to the pastures of the righteous, for he also feeds joyfully therein; Don't let yourself be seduced by the fullness of your belly, since it has everything. Let temptation be the one who asks and shows how each one has been fed. See that I show you the pastures of the righteous: Seven times he falls and rises; and now those of the wicked: the wicked, on the other hand, is weakened in his evils. The righteous are fed: like a square stone, it will stand no matter how you place it. The wicked is fed: like a round stone, he finds no stability in any position.

et resurget; sed dictum est hoc de casibus tribulationum. Cadere quippe humiliari est. Quantumque fuerit humiliatus iustus, resurgit. Quadratus ille est, qui vertitur, et stat. Et quod ait, septies pro universitate posit, perfect number insinuans, quotienscumque ceciderit. Septies, quotienscumque; sicuti est septies in die laudabo te (Ps 118,164). Semper laus eius in ore meo (Ps 33,2). Et ut noveritis istum esse sensum in his verbis, septies cadit iustus et resurgit, circumstantia videamus, quid supra dixerit sancta scriptura, et quid post haec verba subiecerit: ibi sensus evidens apparebit. Quid ergo ait scriptura, ubi posita est this sententia? Noli applicare impium ad pascua iusti, ñeque seducaris saturitate ventris (Prov 4,15). Et sequitur septies enim cadit iustus, et resurget; impii autem (649) infirmabuntur in malis (Prov 24:16). Iam de consequentibus verbis post hanc sententiam coepit ista elucere sententia: septies cadet iustus et resurget, impii autem infirmabuntur in malis. Ergo qui cadit septies et resurget, non infirmatur in malis; et hoc est ipsum cadere et resurgere, humiliari et non infirman. 4. Quid est ergo, quod superius dictum est, noli applicare impium ad pascua iusti, ñeque seducaris saturitate ventris? Beatus apostolus adhibuit testimonium de scripturis in quo nobis gloriam martyrum commendauit. Propter quod scriptum est, inquit: Credidi, propter quod locutus sum et nos credimus, propter quod et loquimur (2 Cor 4:13). Si enim tantummodo credidissent et non loquerentur, non paterentur. Credendo itaque adprehenderunt uitam et loqueado inuenerunt mortem, sed mortem in qua corpus corruptibile seminaretur et incorruptio meteretur. Istum sensum, id est, quod credimus propter quod et loquimur, alio loco, diem apostolus sic explicauit: Corde creditur ad iustitiam, ore confessio fit ad salutem (Rom 10,10).

Here someone may ask: "How is it that one confesses for one's health, if the martyrs died precisely when they confessed?" It is clear that confession does not lead to health. Have you forgotten: Help us in tribulation, and the health of men will be in vain? Without a doubt, they confessed with their mouths to obtain health, but the health of the faithful, that of Christians, not that which is common to men and donkeys. This same health common to man and beasts, who grants it but the creator of everything? From whom we have received being, we have also received the power to be healthy. The faithful know well that God is the creator not only of man, but also of beasts. For this very reason, Lord, you will make men and donkeys healthy, according to the abundance of your mercy, O God! As you are God and creator of men, the abundance of your mercy went so far as to give health to the donkeys. What do men have more than this: But the sons of men will wait in the shadow of your wings? What will they expect but another health, not temporary, but eternal? Other health will be possessed; Another is what is expected, and that is why the martyrs remained very firm in their faith, since they despised what they had to receive what they expected. There is health and health; They knew one and believed in the other; one they saw, another they did not see. What faith, beloved, what faith! Despise what you see; What you believe will come. From here some distinction begins to be drawn in-

between men and the son of man. All the sons of men are men. How are not all men sons of men? Because Adam and Eve were men, but not children of men. In which of these two categories did Christ the Lord prefer to be? It was fitting that He who made man should become man for man and do what he had made, so that what was made would not perish. He could certainly form his flesh from wherever he wanted, being true man and true flesh; In fact, to form the first man he did not look for a father or mother. To make the first man he did not look for human semen. But the time came for the one who had made man to become man. He did not just want to be a man, which was possible if he had wanted to, but he preferred to be the son of man. And how vehemently, how consistently he insists that he is the son of man! When you read the holy gospels, notice and consider how many more times he says he is the son of man than the Son of God. Indeed, the majesty of God did not need to be highly praised; On the other hand, the humility of the Exalted had to be instilled more assiduously. Among the many other occasions in which the Lord Jesus testifies that he is the son of man, it is worth remembering, above all, that when he says to his disciples: Who do men say that I, the son of man, am? Who do they say you are but the son of man? But there are many children of men who are similar by race, but unequal by their virtues or personal situations. So ask: Who do people say I am? He was told that some said it was Elias, others that Jere.

We are closer to that goal today than yesterday, tomorrow than today, and someday that will arrive for which the when was always unknown. Let us live attentively, because we do not know when we are going to die. We don't know when and we don't know how close what we call "sometime" is. For this reason, the blessed martyrs, when the moment of temptation arrived and of choosing between staying with this temporary life, accepting the uncertainty of "when" or clinging to the one that will be possessed forever - why are you surprised, my brothers? -, as they had faith, they weighed the two possibilities and chose; They won, because they chose the best; They chose him because they loved him; And where did it come from to love him if not from being loved themselves? Oh blessed ones! Oh glorious ones! Oh brave ones! Oh magnificent and happy! Oh dedication to God! Oh men, squares everywhere! What you despised is a good, but temporary. What you chose is an eternal and incorruptible good. No wonder you stood firm in your confession; anyone

eum dicerent Heliam, alii Hieremiam, alii Iohannem baptistam uel unum ex prophetis, tamquam filium hominis unum ex magnis hominibus. Sed hoc nomines quibus et pecoribus communis est salus. Vos autem, inquit, quem me esse dicitis? (Mt 16:15) quasi illi non essent nomines. Ait ille: hoc et hoc me dicunt homines pertinent ad hominem. Commendat Christus suam humilitatem. Confitetur Petrus Christi maiestatem. Sic decebat, sic oportebat. Audi Petre, quid Christus pro te, et tu, dic quis pro te filius hominis. Quem me enim esse dicunt homines filium hominis? Quis est iste qui pro te factus est filius hominis? You are Christus filius dei vivi. Ego, (19) inquit, commendo humilitatem meam, tu agnosce diuinitatem meam. Ego dico quid pro te factus sim, tu dic unde te fecerim. Filii autem hominum pertinent ad filium hominis, ut salutem contemnant hominibus iumentisque communem, sub tegmine alarum tuarum sperabunt. Quid ergo, karissimi, ut salutem istam contemnerent martyres, non est ist salus aliquod bonum? Si bonum <non> esset, quis glorietur quia contemnit quod nullum est bonum? Contemnat

bonum ut ueniat ad melius. Loquimur de salute ista quam nemo quaerens culpandus est. Videmus nihil aliud agere homines, quantum pertinet ad uitae praesentis sustainculum, nisi ut salus ista, <a>ut reparetur si defecerit, aut obtineatur si <de> fuerit. Sed quamdiu — erit huius finis uelis nolis — quamdiu poteris tenere istam salutem qui reuocare non potes extremum diem? Fixa est unicuique aliqua meta novissimi diei. Ad istam metam omnes currunt, nec uolentes currunt, sed impelluntur. Huic metae propinquiores sumus hodie quam heri, eras quam hodie, et quod semper ignoratum est quando, ueniet aliquando. Sollicite ergo uiuamus quia nescimus quando moriamur. Nescimus quando, et [788] nescimus quam prope sic hoc quod diximus "aliquando." Ac per hoc beatissimi martyres, cum uenissent ad artic<ul>um temptationis, ut eis aut uita esset temporalis retinenda incertum «quando» admitiendo, aut illa prendenda quae est sine fine retinenda — Quid miramini fratres mei? — quia fidem habuerunt, appenderunt et elegerunt, uicerunt quia melius elegerunt, elegerunt quia dilexerunt, et ut diligerent unde, nisi quia dilecti sunt, habuerunt? That was the place where the pursuer wanted to throw you, you did not fall. This is to be truly blessed: he made us wonderfully white with his blood. The divine word said it in the Apocalypse: These are those who have come from many and great tribulations, washed their stoles and turned them white. Where did they turn them white? In the blood, not of anyone, but of the lamb. All blood stains red; the blood of the lamb, white. How do you turn it white? Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world. There is nothing strange that they have washed their stoles in blood, since there are things that can be washed in blood, as one author says: "They wash their necks and arms in abundant blood." They wash, yes; but do they turn them white? How could anything not turn white that was washed in that blood of which it was said: This is my blood, which will be shed for many for the forgiveness of sins? quod elegistis. Merit in confessione stetistis: quacumque uos persecutor uertere uoluit, non ruistis. Hoc est esse uere beatum: ille uos miro moda de sanguine candidauit. Diuinus sermo ait in apocalypsi. Topic: Do not swear for fear of perjuring. Location: Unknown. Date: August 29, feast of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist. From the years 414415. 1. The reading of the holy gospel presented before our eyes a cruel spectacle: the head of Saint John on a tray; He, testimony of the cruelty of a beast, beheaded out of hatred for the truth. A young woman dances, her mother feels cruelty overflowing, among the pleasures and lasciviousness of the diners she swears recklessly, and the sworn is impiously fulfilled. What he himself had predicted was realized in John. Of Jesus Christ the Lord had said: It is fitting that he increase and that I decrease. John diminished when he was beheaded and Christ grew up on the cross. The truth bred hate. The reproaches of the holy man of God, who certainly sought the salvation of those to whom he addressed them, could not be endured with a calm spirit. They returned evil for good. What could he talk about if not what he was full of? And what could they answer him if not what they were full of? He sowed wheat, but found thorns. IN DECOLLATIONE BEATI IOANNIS BAPTISTAE, I

CAPOT I.—1. Ioannis Baptistae caedes qua occasione facía.—Cum sanctum Evangelium legeretur, crudele spectaculum ante oculos nostros constitutum est, caput sancti Ioannis in disco, feralis missus crudelitatis, propter odium veritatis. Puella saltat, et saevit mater: et Ínter delicias et lascivias convivantium temeré iuratur, et impie quod iuratur, impletur. Factum est Ioanni quod ipse praedixerat. De Domino enim Iesu Cristo dixerat: Illum oportet crescere, me autem minui (lo 3,30). This minutus is in capite, ille crevit in intersection. Odium peperit veritas. Non potuit aequo animo tolerari, quod homo Dei sanctus monebat: qui utique salutem eorum quaerebat, quos sic monebat. Replyunt illi mala pro bonis. Quid enim ille diceret, nisi quo plenus erat? Et quid illi responderent, nisi quo pleni fuent? Ule triticum seminavit, sed spinas invenit. Saybat regi: Non licet tibi habere uxorem fratris tui (Mark 6,17-28). Vincebat enim
Do not swear for fear of perjuring

his brother, contrary to the law. He liked that woman, but she was not cruel. He had respect for those who told him the truth. But the detestable woman conceived hatred, which, when the time came, had to give birth to it. When she was giving birth to him, she gave birth to her daughter, a dancer daughter. And that king who considered Juan a holy man; who, although he did not obey him, feared him out of respect for God, was filled with sadness when he was asked for the head of John the Baptist on a platter. But, in honor of the oath sworn and the guests, he sent a soldier from his guard and fulfilled what he had sworn. 2. This circumstance, beloved, invites me to speak to you something about the oath, looking at your life and customs. A false oath is no small sin; On the contrary, swearing falsely is such a great sin that the Lord prohibited all swearing to avoid swearing falsely. It says in effect: It was told to you: "You shall not perjure," for you must give an account to the Lord of your oath; But I tell you not to swear in any way, not even by heaven, which is the throne of God; nor for the earth, which is the footstool of his feet; nor with any other oath; not even for your head, since you cannot make a hair white or black. In your mouth there is nothing but "Yes, yes" and "No, no." If something happens from there, it comes from evil. 3. In the Holy Scriptures we notice that the Lord swore when Abraham obeyed him until the immolation of his beloved son. The angel spoke to him from heaven, saying: I swear by

myself, says the Lord, that since you obeyed my voice and did not spare your son dear to me, I will bless you and multiply your offspring like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea; and in your lineage all peoples will be blessed. You can see that Christians fill the entire globe of the earth: this proves that God's oath was true. Likewise, in the psalms it is prophesied of Christ the Lord: The Lord has sworn, and will not repent: "You are a priest forever according to the rite of Melchizedek." Those who know the Scripture know what Melchizedek, priest of the exalted God, offered when he blessed Abraham. It is not necessary for us to remember it, for the sake of the catechumens. But the faithful recognize how what we now see coming true was prophesied. Where does all this come from? Of the oath of the Lord. The Lord has sworn, and will not repent; distinctly from Herod, who regretted having taken the oath. 4. If, then, the Lord swore, why did Christ the Lord forbid his people to swear? I'll tell you why. Swearing truly is not a sin. But since it is a great sin to swear falsely, he who does not swear at all turns away from it. Even he who swears in truth is close to swearing falsely. Therefore, the Lord, who forbade swearing, did not want you to walk on the edge so that it would not happen that in some narrow place your foot would slip and you would fall. "But the Lord swore," he says. He who does not know how to lie swears without fear. Do not worry that the Lord has sworn, because perhaps

regem libido: tenebat apud se prohibitam uxorem fratris suí. Sed eum tamen sic libebat, ut non saeviret. Honorabat eum a quo verum audiebat. Sed mulier detestabilis odium concipiebat, quod aliquando dato tempore pareret. Quando parturiebat, peperit filiam, filiam saltantem. Et rex ille qui sanctum virum habebat íoannem, qui eum propter Dominum timebat, etsi ei non oboediebat, posteaquam ab illo petitum est caput Ioannis in disco, contristatus est. Sed propter iurationem et propter conrecumbentes, misit spiculatorem, et implevit quod iuravit. CAPUT II.—2. luratio omnis prohibita propter periculum jalsae iurationh.—Admonet nos locus iste, earissimi, ut propter vitam et mores vestros aliquid vobis de iuramento tractemus. Falsa iuratio non est leve peccatum: immo tam magnum peccatum est, falsum iurare, ut propter reatum falsee iuratíonis Dominus prohibuerit omnem iurationem. Ait enim: Dictum est, Non periurabis, reddes autem Domino iusiurandum tuum: ego autem dico vobis, non iurare omnino, ñeque per caelum, quia throneus Dei est; ñeque per terram, quia scabellum pedum eius est; ñeque aliud quodcumque iuramentum; ñeque per caput tuum iuraveris; quia non potes faceré capillum album aut nigrum. Sit autem in ore vestro: Est, est; No, no. If quid amplius est, it is bad (Mt 5,35-37). 3. Iuratio a Deo adhibita.—Invenimus autem in Scri[1407]pturis sanctis Dominum iurasse, quando ei usque ad immolationem dilecti filii oboedivit Abraham. Locutus est el angelus de cáelo they say: Per memet-

ipsum iuro, dicit Dominus, quia obaudisti vocem meam, et non pepercisti filio tuo dilecto propter me, benedicens benedicam te, et implebo semen tuum, sicut stellas caeli, et sicut arenam maris; et benedicentur in semine tuo omnes gentes (Gen 22:16-18). Quod videtis totum orbem terrarum Christianos implere, exhibitat verax iuratio Dei. Itemque in Psalmis de Domino Iesu Christo prophetatum est: Iuravit Dominus, et non paenitébit eum: Tu es sacerdos in aeternum secundum ordinem Melchisedech (Ps 109,4). Qui noverunt Scripturas, sciunt quid protulerít Melchisedech sacerdos Dei excelsi, quando benedixit Abraham (cf. Gen 14:18-20). Non oportet ut hoc memoremus, propter catechumenos. Fideles tamen agnoscunt, quemadmodum ante! prophetarum sit, quod moda videmus impleri. Et unde hoc? Quia iuravit Dominus. Et iuravit Dominus, et non paenitebit eum: non quomodo Herodem paenituit quia iuraverat. CAPUT III.—4. Nobis tamen merit prohibita.—Cum ergo Dominus iuraverit, quare Dominus Christus suos iurare prohibuit? I say quare. Non est peccatum, verum iurare. Sed quia grande peccatum est falsum iurare, longe est a peccato falsum iurandi qui omnino non iurat: propinquat falsee iurationi, qui vel verum iurat. Dominus ergo, qui prohibuit iurare, supra ripam te noluit ambulare, ne pes tuus in angusto labatur, et cadas. Be Dominus iuravit, inquit. Securus iurat qui lyingi nescit. Non te moveat quia Dominus iuravit; quia forte non debent iurare nisi Deus.

No one should swear not to be God. What do you do when you swear? You put God as witness. You put him, and he puts himself. But you who are a man and are deceived in many things, often present the truth as a witness to your falsehood. Sometimes, a man perjures, even without meaning to, when he thinks that what he swears is true. It is not a sin as great as that of someone who swears despite knowing that what he swears is false. How much better is he who obeys Christ the Lord and does not swear! He is far away from such a serious sin. 5. I know that this is something very hard for your custom, but it was also hard for me.' The fear of God removed the oath from my mouth. You see that I live among you. Who has heard me swear even once? Didn't he have the habit of swearing all the time? But when I read the gospel, I feared, I fought against my custom, and in the same struggle I invoked the help of the Lord. The Lord granted it to me so that I would not swear again. Nothing is easier for me now than not to swear. I have reminded your charity of this so that you do not say: "Who is capable of this?" Oh! If one fears God and is terrified of perjury, the tongue is restrained, the truth is maintained and the oath disappears. Tu enim quando juras, quid facis? Testem Deum adhibes. Your illum, ipse se ipsum. Be your homo, quia in multis falleris, plerumque adhibes testem veritatem ad tuam falsitatem. Aliquando et nolens homo periurat, cum verum putat esse quod iurat. Non est quidem tantum peccatum, quantum eius qui scit falsum esse, et tamen iurat. How melior, et a peccato isto gravi omnino longe fit, qui audit Dominum Christum, et non iurat? CAPUT IV.—5. Consuetudo iurandi ab Augustino victa,—Scio grave esse consuetudini vestrae; sed et grave Fuit consuetudini nostrae. Timendo Deum abstulimus iurationem de ore nostro. Ecce vobiscum vivimus: quis aliquando audivit iurantes? Numquid non consueveram quotídie iurare? At ubi legi, et timui, luctatus sum contra consuetudinem meam, in ipsa luctatione invokevi Dominum adiutorem. Praestitit mihi Dominus adiutorium non iurandi. Nihil mihi facilius est, quam non iurare. Hoc ideo admonui Caritatem vestram, ne dícatis: Quis potest? Or yes Deus timeatur! or if periuri expavescant! lingua frenatur, veritas tenetur, iuratio tollitur.

Topic: The dangers of the oath. Location: Hippo. Date: August 29, feast of the beheading of Saint John the Baptist.

1. The text that we heard when the gospel was read gives me reason to say the following to your charity: you see that even the miserable Herod felt affection for the holy man and man of God John; But, drunk with the joy and satisfaction that a dancer gave him, he rashly swore and promised to give him whatever the girl he had liked so much asked for. But when he asked for something so cruel and nefarious, he was truly saddened, because he saw how great the crime was going to be. Placed between his oath and the girl's request, where he saw the monstrous crime, he feared falling into perjury, and in order not to offend God by perjuring himself, he offended Him with his cruelty. Someone will tell me: "What should Herod have done then?" If I say that he should not have sworn, who does not realize that he should not have sworn? But the question here is not whether a man should swear, but rather what he who has already sworn the oath should do. This is the big question. He swore recklessly; who ig-

If we say to him: "Forgive Juan, so as not to commit a crime," we are inciting him to perjury. If we say to him: "Do not perjure," we put him in the position to commit a great crime. What need is there to find yourself in such a situation where it is difficult to find a way out? 2. However, after carefully examining the Scriptures, I can think of an example in which I see how a pious and holy man fell into a rash oath, and preferred not to do what he had sworn rather than fulfill his oath by shedding human blood. I will remind your charity. When Saul, full of ingratitude, persecuted the holy David, he went, accompanied by his people, wherever he could so as not to be found or killed by Saul. One day he asked a rich man named Nabal, who was shearing his sheep, for food for himself and his companions. Lacking mercy, he refused to give it to her and, more seriously, responded in bad ways. Saint David swore that he would kill him, since he was armed. It was easy to do and, with anger as an advisor, it even seemed fair. David, unsuspecting, took the oath and set out to fulfill what he had sworn. It came out to

He met Abigail, Nabal's wife, and offered her what she needed and had asked for. She humbly begged him, tamed him and kept him from shedding her husband's blood. He swore recklessly; but, driven by greater piety, he did not fulfill his oath. Therefore, dearly beloved, I return again to exhort you. See that holy David, although angry, did not shed that man's blood; but who can deny that he swore falsely? Of the two sins, he chose the lesser; minor only in comparison to another major. For, considered in itself, false swearing is a great sin. First of all, you must work and fight against your bad, bad, bad and very bad habit, and eliminate the oath from your mouths. 3. But if someone asks you for an oath, as the only way, perhaps, to convince himself that you did not do something that he thinks you have done, and you utter that oath to eliminate the bad suspicion he harbors, you do not sin as much as he, who was the cause, for the Lord Jesus said: In your mouth there is nothing but "Yes, yes"; "No no". oath if the same thought were visible to the eyes of one's neighbor? 4. Write in your hearts what I am going to tell you: «Whoever forces a man to swear, knowing that he will swear falsely, is worse than a murderer. The murderer, in effect, kills the body, he kills the soul; moreover, to two souls: that of the one whom he forced to swear and his own. You know that what you affirm is true and what he says is false, and you force him to swear? Behold, he swears, perjures and perishes; you, what have you found? Better yet, you too perished, because you wanted to be satisfied with his death. 5. I am going to tell you something that I have never spoken to your charity about; something that happened in this town, in this church. There was a certain simple, innocent, good Christian man here, known to many of you or, better yet, to all the inhabitants of Hippo. His name was Tutuslimeno. Which of you, citizens here, does not know Tutuslimeno? He told me what I am going to tell you. I don't know who denied him what he had entrusted to him or what he owed him. Disturbed, he asked him to take an oath. That one swore, this one lost; This one lost, yes, but that one completely perished. This Tutuslimeno, a serious and faithful man, narrated that that same night he appeared before the judge and, with great force and full of terror, he arrived in the presence of a certain man, a very exalted and admirable man, who exercised the presidency, to whom others equally exalted were subject. Full of

Disturbed as he was, he received orders to appear, and they questioned him with these words: "Why did you force the oath of someone who you knew was going to swear falsely?" He answered, "He denied me what was mine." He received in response: "And was it not better that you should lose what you claimed as yours rather than have this man's soul perish because of his false oath?" He ordered that he be whipped while lying on the ground. He was beaten so hard that when he woke up, traces of the blows appeared on his back. After being corrected, he was told: «You are forgiven for your good faith; For the rest, be careful not to do it again." He therefore committed a serious sin and was corrected. But he will commit an even more serious sin whoever, after this my sermon and exhortation, does something similar. Beware of swearing falsely and swearing recklessly. You will guard against these two evils with maximum security if you uproot from yourself the habit of swearing.

Ecce iurat, ecce peierat, ecce perit; your crux invented? Immo et tu peristi, qui de illius morte te satiare voluisti. CAPUT V.—5. Tutuslymeni ob hoc peccatum divina correptione fiagellatus.—Aliquid dicam, quod numquam dixi Caritati vestrae, in hoc populo, quod contigit in hac ecclesia. Fuit hic homo quidam simplex, innocens, bene fidelis, a multis vestris, id est, Hipponensibus, immo ab omnibus cognitus; Tutuslymeni vocatus. Tutuslymeni quis vestrum non novit, qui cives estis? Ab illo audivi quod dico. Nescio quis negavit ei, vel quod commendaverat, vel quod ei debenbatur; et hominis fidei se commisit. Commotus provocavit eum ad iusiurandum. Iuravit ille, iste perdidit: sed isto perdente, ille penitus periit. Dicebat ergo iste Tutuslymeni homo gravis et fidelis, ipsa nocte exhibitum se Fuisse ad iudicem, et eum magno Impetu atque terrore se pervenisse ad praesidentem excelsum quemdam et admira-
