Respondit ille: [1410] Negavit mihi rem meam. Responsum est illi: Et nonne melius erat, ut rem tuam quam demandings to lose, quam animam hominis istius false iuratione perimeres? Prostratus iussus est caedi. Caesus is also graviter, ut in dorso evigilantis vestigia plaguetum apparerent. Sed dictum est illi, postquam emendatus est: Parcitur innocentiae tuae, de cetero cave ne facías. Fecit quidem ille grave peccatum, et emendatus est; sed multo gravius ​​peccatum faciet, qui post istum meum sermonem et istam meam admonitionem et exhortationem tale aliquid fecerit. Cávete a false iuratione, cávete a reckless iuratione. Ab his duobus malis securissime cavebitis, si consuetudinem iurandi a vobis abstuleritis.
Commentary on Psalm 131,17-18

Topic: Commentary on Psalm 131,17-18. Place: Carthage; in the Basilica of Cyprian. Date: September 13, vigil of the feast of San Cipriano. Prior to the year 400. 1. In the house of God, I speak to your charity about what the psalm has indicated to me: who is it that says: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. I will cover his enemies with concussion, but my sanctification will flourish on him; what is that lamp that has prepared his Christ and who are his enemies, whom he covered with confusion with that lamp; what the sanctification; who prepared the lamp for his Christ and what things will flourish upon his Christ. Among all these words, only one thing appears clear and evident: what it says: to my Christ. We must not think of anyone other than Christ, our Lord and Savior. So, scrutinizing, as God grants it to me, the depth of these meanings, I have found out that this is what God the Father says. It is God the Father, that is, the person of God the Father, who speaks through the mouth of the prophet: I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. May the Son of God and the Christ of God

[MA 1,43] (PL 46,846) SERMO HABITUS CARTHAGINE IN MAPPALIBUS, ID EST, IN BASÍLICA BEATI MARTYRIS CYPRIANI, PER VIGILIAM NATALIS EIUS, DE RESPONSORIO PSALMI CENTESIMI TRICESIMI PRIMI: «PARAVI LUCERNAM CHRISTO MEO; INIMICOS EIÜS INDUAM CONFUSIONEM» (PS 131, 17)

1. Loquimur caritati vestrae in domo dei quod praesens psalmus admonuit: quis est qui dicat, paravi luzernam Christo meo. Inimicos eius induam confusionem; super ipsum autem florebit sanclificatio mea (Ps 131,17.18); et quae illa luzern sit, quam paravit Christo suo; et qui sint inimici Christi eius, quos per illam luzernam induit confusionem; et quae sanctificatio eius, qui paravit luzernam Christo suo, quae florebit super Christum eius. In his enim omnibus verbis illud tantum videtur planum et apertum, quod hic ait, Christo meo: non enim aliud intellegendum est, quam Christus dominus et salvator noster. Perscrutantes itaque, quantum largitur deus, altitudinem sensus huius, invenimus hoc deum Patrem dicere. Deus ergo Pater, id est, persona dei Patris per prophetam loquitur: Paravi luzernam Christo meo. Filium autem dei

They are the same person, it is not necessary to expose it to Christians. Having found out, then, who the person speaking is, let us see what is the lamp prepared by God the Father for his Son the Christ. The Lord himself says of John the Baptist: He was the lamp that burned and gave light, and you wanted to enjoy his light for a moment. He called John a lamp, a lamp lit at the source of light to bear witness to the truth. In such blindness and such weakness of the inner eye lay the men who, using the lamp, sought the sun of justice. For if someone had a clean eye of the heart, he would see the sun itself directly and would not look for the lamp as a testimony in his favor. Having said of that lamp: You wanted to enjoy its light for a moment, he added: Vero, I have a greater testimony than Juan's. The lamp, then, has been lit in the night for the weak. And how did you turn it on? The Father says to Christ, his Son, referring to John: Behold, I send my angel before you, who will prepare the way before your face. He prepared a lamp for his Christ. 2. How did he cover his enemies with confusion by means of the lamp? Consider first what I said, namely: that the lamp was lit at the source of the light. John himself attests to it: We, he said, have received of his fullness. John stood out so much for his excellence that he was considered not as the precursor of Christ, but as Christ himself. If the lamp had been extinguished or blackened by the smoke of pride when the Jews came to it to askreumdem esse et Christum dei, it is not exponendum christianis. Invent itaque loquentis persona videamus, quae sit luzern a deo Patre Christo filio praeparata. Dominus ipse dicit of Iohanne baptista: Ule erat luzern ardens et luzens, et vos voluistis exultare ad horam in lumine eius (lo 5,35). Lucernam ergo dixít Iohannem, accensam de fonte luminis, ut testimonium perhiberet veritati. In hac enim caecitate iacebant homines, et in hac oculi interioris infirmitate, ut sol iustitiae per luzernam quaereretur. Nam si quis haberet mundum oculum cordis, eum ipsum prius intueretur, nec ad eius testimonium luzernam quaereret. Cum enim de illa (847) luzern dixisset, Voluistis exultare ad horam in lumine eius, ego autem, inquit, habeo testimonium maius quam Iohannem (ib., 36). Lucerna ergo infirmis in nocte accensa est. Et quomodo illam accendit?

Pater Christo filio suo de Iohanne dicit: Ecce mitto angelum meum [44] ante te, qui praeparabit viam ante faciem tuam (Mt 11,10). Paravit Lucernam Christo suo. 2. How inimicos eius per ipsam luzernam induit confusionem? Ac prius videte quod diximus, de fonte luminis accensam luzernam. Ipse Tohannes testatur: Nos autem, inquit, de plenitudine eius accepimus (lo 1,16). Erat autem Iohannes tanta excellentia praecellens, ut non ante Christum missus, sed ipse Christus putaretur. lile autem, si luzern csset extincta, et nidore superbiae fumida, quando ad eum missum est

him: You, who are you? Are you the Christ, or Elijah, or a project? He would have answered: "I am." He would have found the right moment for his boasting by attributing false honor to the error of men. Would he have had to make an effort to convince them of what those who questioned him were anticipating telling him? But he, as a humble one, was sent to prepare the way for the exalted one; That is why he was a friend of the husband: because he was a servant who recognized the Lord. He said, "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness, 'Make his ways straight.' I am neither the Christ, nor Elijah, nor a prophet." And they: "Who are you then?" What did he answer them? "I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: 'Prepare the way for the Lord.' This had already been predicted by Isaiah; To whom his prophecy referred, see there. You had read this in Isaiah, I said, and perhaps, once you read it, you did not know who it was said about; He said it about me." How he humiliates himself who was exalted so much that he was considered the Christ! See how much he humiliates himself. «I, he said, certainly baptize you in water; but whoever comes after me is older than me. And I could say that he is a little older than me. He says he is older than him. —Tell me, to what extent is it greater? —I am not worthy, he replied, to untie the strap of his shoe.

the greatness of this one who considers himself unworthy of untying the strap of another's shoe? What is the measure of his greatness? Who do we ask? If we ask John himself about his greatness, we will not find it, because he humiliates himself and says nothing about himself, not even what is true, with boasting. From whose mouth can we hear the greatness of John, who is not worthy to untie the thong of the shoe of one who was considered a man? Let us ask the Lord himself and say to him: "Lord, John gave a great testimony of you, and since he stood out so much among men that some considered him the Christ, they asked him who he was, and he answered that he was not the Christ, that another would come, greater than him, and so greater that he was not worthy to untie the strap of his shoes. As a faithful lamp he spoke of the excellence of your light. This is what Juan said about you. Let's see who is the one who said that about you, what is the greatness of the one who humbled himself so much before you confessing that you are much older than him. Who is he? He said what he said about you; Tell us something about him." Listen to what the Lord says about John: Among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist. But what did he say? But whoever is less is greater than him in the kingdom of heaven. He indicates himself; God is not arrogant when he praises his greatness. What does it mean: who is a minor? Who is later in age and older in majesty. Younger than John is Christ the Lord, but in what he did for us, not in what he did to us. He who was born after John hears how the Father says to him: I have begotten you not before John, not before

3. From here you can already deduce the plan by virtue of which John was sent before Christ. You see to what extent he is older and to what extent he confesses that he is: to the point of considering himself unworthy of untying the strap of his shoe. What is a Iudaeis, dictumque illi, tu quis es? You are Christus, a Helias, a prophet? (lo 1,19.21) diceret, Ego sum. Invenerat enim occasionem iactantiae suae, ultro honorem falsum errore hominum deferente. Numquid hoc persuadere laborabat, quod priores dicebant qui interrogabant? Sed missus est humilis ad parandam viam excelso: inde amicus sponsi (cf. lo 3,29), quia servus cognitor domini. Et ait, ego sum vox clamanth in eternal: stop viam Domino, straight facite semitas eius (lo 1,22.23; Mt 3,3). Ego non sum Christus, nec Helias, nec propheta. Et illi: Quis ergo es? Et quid dixit? Ego sum vox clamanth in deserto: Várate viam Domino. Iam enim ista praedixerat Esaias (cf. Is 40:3): de quo autem praedixerit, ibi intellegitur. Legistis, inquit, hoc in Esaia, et forte lectum ignorastis unde sit dictum: ego sum de quo est dictum. Quantum autem se abicit, qui tantum erigebatur, ut Christus putaretur, quantum se abicit, videte. Ego quidem, inquit, baptizo vos en aqua; qui autem post me venit, maior me est. And aliquanto posset me maior dici. Maiorem se illum dícit. Dec, how much longer do we need? Cuius non sum, inquit, dignus corrigiam calciamenti solvere (Luke 3,16). 3. Iam hinc intellegite dispensationem, quare Iohannes ante Christum praemissus est. Videtis, quanto sit minor, quantoque illum fateatur esse maiorem, ut dicat indignum se solvere corrigiam calciamenti eius. Quantus est iste, qui se dicit indignum solvere corrigiam calciamenti

huius? Quantus is? ubi quaerimus? Si ab ipso Iohanne quaeramus, quantus sit Iohannes, non invenimus; humiliat enim se, et nihil [45] de se, vel veraciter, iactanter loquitur. Quantus ergo sit Iohannes, who is not dignus corrigiam calciamenti solvere eius qui homo putabatur, a quo audituri sumus? Ipsum dominum interrogemus, et dicamus ei: Domine, perhibuit de te Iohannes magnum testimonium, et cum eius magna excellentia inter homines appareret, ut Christus esse putaretur, quaesitumque ab eo esset quis esset, dixit non se esse Christum, dixit venturum esse maiorem se, et tanta maiorem, ut non sit dignus correct solvere (848) calciamenti eius. Tamquam luzern fidelis locuta est de excellenti lumine tuo. Hoc de te Iohannes. Videamus quis sit qui de te ista, quantus sit Ule qui se ita humiliavit tibi, teque both amplerem se confessus est. Who is he? Ule de te ista: tu de illo dic nobis aliquid. Audi vocem domini de Iohanne: In natis mulierum nemo exsurrexit maior Iohanne baptista. Sed quid ait? Qui autem minor est, in regno caelorum maior est Alo (Mt 11,11). Se ipsum dicit: non enim arrogans est deus, cum commendat magnitudeinem suam. Quid est, quid minor est? Qui posterior aetate, maior maiestate. Posterior enim natus Iohanne est dominus Christus, sed in eo quod factus est propter nos, non in eo per quod facti sumus. Ule qui post Iohanem natus est audit a Patre: non
Commentary on Psalm 131,17-18

of David nor before Abraham, but before the dawn. If, then, he has condescended in some way to our weakness, so that the day was preceded by the lamp, and what the lamp said about the day was believed, how much more should what the day said about the lamp be believed, namely: that among those born of women there has arisen no one greater than John the Baptist! Therefore, if it is an older man to whom no one was born, who considers himself unworthy to untie the shoe strap of another person, who is this other person whose shoe strap is not worthy of untying that older man than whom there was no other? If John was already such a great man that there could be no one greater than him, whoever is greater than him must be more than a man. If Juan was already such a great man that there was no other greater than him, whoever is greater than him is more than a man. But he who is more than man, became man through man, and rightly the sanctification of the Father flourishes upon him. 4. On him, in fact, the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove. Then the flower of holiness was manifested more fully to John himself in the form of a dove, a form of simplicity and innocence. Thus it was fulfilled: And upon him my sanctification will flourish. I, he said, didn't know him. Vero who sent me to baptize in water told me: "He on whom you see the Holy Spirit descending like a dove and resting on him, that is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit." And I, he said, bear witness to what I saw, that he is the chosen one of God. Who does he bear witness to? Of him upon whom he saw sanctification

of the Father. Where did you see the Holy Spirit descend from? For the Spirit never departed from the Son, nor the Son from the Spirit, nor the Son from the Father, nor the Father from the Son, nor the Spirit from the Son and the Father; but these things are understood with the purified mind differently from how they are manifested to the eyes. The Father is not prior to the Son in time, nor does the Son temporally follow the Father, since there is no time there. The Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God, creator of time. There is no possibility of saying: "The Father is prior, and the Son is posterior." From the moment he is Father, from that moment the Son exists. Find out how long he has been a Father. With thought you transcend the earth, the sky, the angels, the visible things, the invisible things and the entire creation; Then you ask: "Since when did you start being a Father?" This is not how one asks about eternal things. Do not ask since when but rather what has a beginning. Do not ask how long ago he from whom it begins what has begun and who has no beginning from anyone, because he has no beginning at all. As the Father has no beginning, so neither does the Son, but the Son is the splendor of the Father. The radiance of the fire exists from the moment in which the fire exists, and the radiance of the Father, from the moment the Father exists. Since when does the Father exist? Always and forever. Thus, then, also the splendor of the Father exists from always and forever; and yet, since he is his splendor, his Son did not begin with time in being begotten by the Father. Who can see this? File your heart, shake off the dust, wash

before Iohanem, not before David, not before Abraham, sed ante luciferum genui te (Ps 109,3). Si ergo adcommodatum est aliquid infirmitati nostrae, ut diem luzern praecederet, et creditum est lucernae de die, quanto magis credendum est diei de luzern, quia in natis mulierum nemo exsurrexit maior Iohanne baptista? Homo igitur, que nemo maior natus erat, cum dicit se indignum solvere corrigiam calciamenti cuiusdam, quid est ille, cuius non est dignus solvere corrigiam calciamenti homo quo nemo maior erat? Si iam Iohannes tantus homo, ut amplificar non possit esse homo, quicquid illo maius, amplius est quam homo. Si iam Iohannes tantus homo, ut maior illo nullus sit homo, qui maior illo est, amplius est quam homo. Et qui amplius est quam homo, tamen propter hominem homo, merit super eum floret sanctificatio Patris. 4. Super eum enim Spiritus sanctus in specie columbae descendit: flos sanctitatis in specie columbae, in forma simplici atque innocenti tune demonstratus est plenius ipsi Iohanni, ut impleretur, et super ipsum florebit sanctificatio mea. Ego, inquit, non noveram eum: [46] sed qui me misit baptizare in aqua, ipse mihi dixit, super quem videris spiritum descendentem sicut columbam, et manentem super eum, ipse est qui baptizat in Spiritu sancto. Et ego, inquit, quod vidi testimonium perhibeo, quia ipse est electus Dei (lo 1,33.34). De quo testimonium perhibet?

Super quem vidit florere sanctificationem Patris. Unde vidit descendentem Spiritum sanctum? Non enim a Filio aliquando recessit Spiritus, aut aliquando Filius ab Spiritu, aut aliquando Fílius a Patre, aut Pater a Filio, aut Spiritus a Filio et Patre: sed aliter ist intelleguntur mind purgata, aliter oculis demonstrantur. Nullo tempore praecedit Pater Filium, nullo tempore sequitur Filius Patrem: nullo tempore, quia ibi nullum tempus. Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus, creator temporum, unus deus. Ibi ergo non est utdicas, Prior est Pater, posterior Filius: ex quo Pater, ex illo Filius. Quaere, ex quo (849) Pater. Do you overcome cogitatione terram, caelum, angelos, visibilia, invisibilia, universam creaturam, et quaeris, Ex quo coepit Pater? Non sic quaeruntur aetema: noli quaerere ex quo, nisi quod incipit. Noli quaerere ex quo, a quo incipit quicquid coepit, et quod a nullo incipit, quia non incipit. Sicut autem non incipit Pater, non incipit Filius, sed est Filius splendor Patris. Sic splendor ignis, ex quo ignis; et splendor Patris, ex quo Pater. Ex quo autem Pater? Ab aeterno in aeternum. Ergo et splendor Patris ab aeterno in aeternum; et tamen, quia splendor illius, Filius illius, et sic non coepit tempore, ut genitus sit a Patre. Quis hoc videoat? Lima cor, excute pulverem, dilue
Commentary on Psalm 131,17-18

the stain. Let everything that disturbs the inner gaze be cured and healed, and what is said and believed before being seen will appear. 5. Now, brothers, we believe it. What do we believe? That the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit do not precede each other in time. Although the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit do not precede each other in any time, yet I have not been able to name the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit without these names retaining time and being retained by it. The Father is not before, nor the Son after, and yet I have not been able not to say one before and one after and all the syllables occupied their own time, and the second could not sound in my words until the first had passed. He spent time pronouncing my syllables to express what he has no time for. Thus, my brothers, when that Trinity was sensibly manifested to this flesh, the entire Trinity appeared in the river in which John baptized the Lord. Once baptized, he came out of the water, the dove descended and the voice sounded from heaven: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. The Son manifests himself in man; the Spirit, in the dove; the Father, in the voice. Something inseparable has manifested itself separately; Of course, it is the case that one can speak of a thing and not rather of the cause of all things, and that it is possible to speak of a cause. What do we say when we talk about God? We talk about him, and he himself allows it, that he is not as we think of him and he cannot be talked about even in the way we think of him. But behold, in regard to men, brothers, he showed himself to serve

given a dove, and thus it was fulfilled: My sanctification will flourish on him. It will flourish, he told himself; that is, it will be clearly manifested, since there is nothing more resplendent and more visible on a tree than its flower. Ea, we have now reached the last words of the antiphon: See, upon him my sanctification will flourish. Now I remember that I have overlooked who the enemies confused by the lamp are. 6. I have prepared a lamp for my Christ. They are words of the Father referring to his Son. What lamp is it? From John. Ask the Son himself. He was the lamp that burns and shines. I will cover your enemies with confusion. Who but the Jews are the manifest enemies of Christ? Well, he also has hidden enemies. All those who live in evil and impiety are enemies of Christ, even if they cross themselves in his name and even if they call themselves Christians. To whom shall he say: I do not know you; to which they will answer: Lord, have we eaten and drunk in your name and in your name have we done many wonders? What does it mean we have eaten and drunk in your name? They did not consider their own food much, and that is why they said that it belonged to Christ. There is a certain food that is eaten and drunk, and that is Christ; Even enemies eat and drink Christ. The faithful know which immaculate lamb they feed on; and I hope they feed on it without deserving punishment! For, as the Apostle says, everyone who eats and drinks it unworthily, eats and drinks his own condemnation. So they are enemies of Christ

maculam: quicquid interiorem perturbat intuitum curetur et sanetur, et apparebit quod dicitur et creditur, antequam videatur. 5. Mode tamen credimus, fratres. Quid credimus? Patrem et Filium et Spiritum sanctum nullo tempore se praecedere. Cum ergo Pater et Filius et Spiritus sanctus nullo tempore se praecedant, non tamen potui nominare Patrem et Filium et Spiritum sanctum, nisi ista nomina tempora tenerent, et temporibus suis tenerentur. Non est prior Pater et posterior Filius, et tamen ego non potui dicere nisi unum prius et alium posterius, et sua tempora omnes syllabae tenuerunt, et secunda syllaba in verbis meis sonare non potuit nisi cum prima transisset. Peracta sunt tempora in syllabis meis, cum ea dicerem quae non habent tempora. Sic ergo, fratres mei, cum' illa trinitas sensibiliter ostenderetur [47] huic carni, in fluvio apparuit omnis trinitas, ubi baptizatus est dominus a Iohanne. Baptizatus est enim, ascendit a baptismo, descendit columba, et sonuit vox de cáelo: Hic est filius meus dilectus, in quo bene pleasedui (Mt 3,17). Filius in homine, Spiritus in columba, Pater in voce. Res indiscreta discrete monstrata est; si tamen digonda estres, sed potius rerum omnium causa, si tamen causa. Quid enim dicimus, cum de deo dicimus? Et tamen dicimus, et dici se sinit, qui non est velut cogitatur, dici autem non potest nec quo moda cogitatur. Be quantum ad homines, fratres, ecce

per columbam apparuit, et impletum est, super ipsum autem florebit sanctificatio mea. Florebit enim dictum est, clare apparebit: nihil enim in arbore flore clarius, nihil lucidius. Age iam pervenimus ad ultima verba hypopsalmatis, super ipsum autem florebit sanctificatio mea. Remember me praetermisisse qui sint inimici qui confusi sunt per luzernam. 6. Varavi Lucernam Christo meo. Pater dicit from Filio suo. What Lucernam? Iohannem. Interroga ipsum Filium. Ule erat luzern ardens et luzens (lo 5.35). Lnimicos eius induam confusionem. Inimici Christi aperti, qui, nisi Iudaei? Habet enim occultos inimicos Christus. Omnes inique atque impie vivos inimici sunt (850) Christi, et si signentur nomine eius, et si vocentur christiani. Quibus enim dicturus est, non novi vos, et dicunt illi, domine, in nomine tuo manducavimus et bibimus, in nomine tuo virtutes fines fecimus? (Mt 7,23.22; Le 13,25.26). Quid, manducavimus et bibimus in nomine tuo? Non enim escás suas pro magno iactabant, et inde se ad Christum pertinere dicebant. Est esca quaedam quae manducatur et bibitur, et Christus est; et ab inimicis Christus manducatur et bibitur. Norunt fideles agnum inmaculatum quo vescuntur; atque utinam sic vescantur, ut non sint poenae debitores! Sicut enim dicit apostolus, quicumque manducat et bibit indigne, iudicium sibi manducat et bibit (1 Cor 11:29). Ergo inimici Christi sunt, qui malunt
Commentary on Psalm 131,17-18

who prefer to live in evil rather than obey him and who, when they are told that he will come to judge the living and the dead, fear that he will come. If they had been allowed, they would have moved so that he would not have come; But since they couldn't get it, they tried to get him not to return. The Jews already tried to prevent him from returning. The Son was sent to those bad settlers, to the bad tenants, who did not want to deliver the fruit and stoned the servants who were sent to them. Then said the father of the house, the owner of the vineyard, I will send my son; Maybe they have respect, at least, for him. But they thought thus: This is the heir; Come, let us put him to death, and the inheritance will be ours. They could not prevent it from coming from the Father, and they tried to prevent it from returning to him. But for whose good? They saw him as mortal, and as such they despised him; but in his person they could only kill death. In the death of Christ your death died. He, once resurrected, ascended to the Father and will return. Why do you fear? Love, and you will be safe. Do we not ask that his kingdom come? So, brothers, we pray, and are we afraid to be heard? 7. But these, as I had begun to say, are the hidden enemies. After the miracles that the Lord performed, they said to him: Tell us by what power you do these things. They asked him with malicious intent, so that they could accuse him of blasphemy if he confessed his own power. The same thing happened as with the coin case. They wanted to accuse him, and if he affirmed that tribute had to be paid to Caesar, he would have, in a certain way, renounced the Jewish people, his subject and tributary; If, on the contrary, he had said that it did not have to be paid, he would be accused before Caesar's friends and ministers, in that he forbade paying it. But the Lord said to them: "Show me the coin: whose image and inscription is it?" They answered him: "Caesar's." "Then return to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's." Which is equivalent to saying: if Caesar looks for his image in the coin, isn't God going to look for his in man? Thus, here also the accusing enemies spoke evil in the heart and from the heart. I would have said once in my heart if those who spoke thus did not have a double heart; As shortly before, a double heart is mentioned, not a simple one. See, then, the difference. It was said of the servants of God, although they were many, that they had one heart: They had one soul and one heart towards God. Many people have only one heart, while a single deceitful person has two. Thus, then, as they spoke in the heart and from the heart: Tell us by what power you do these things; that is to say: "If you tell us, we honor you, we venerate you and we pray to you." These words seem to come from a heart. But on the other, since it was double,

Praise of Saint Cyprian
Theme: Praise of Saint Cyprian. Place: Cartago, in the San Cipriano mensa. Date: September 14, feast of San Cipriano.

1. Today we celebrate the day of the passion of the blessed martyr Cyprian. In such a pleasant and devout solemnity, your ears and hearts demand from me the proper sermon. Without a doubt, the Church then felt sad, not because harm had been caused to the martyr, but because of the desire to have with her the one who was leaving. He always wanted to have such a good guide and doctor present. But those who had been afflicted by worry about the fight were consoled by the victor's crown. And now, reading and loving what happened then, we remember it not only without sadness, but even with immense joy. We have been granted this day to be one of joy, not fear. And we do not fear him coming as if he were terrifying us, but rather we wait for him to return, because he brings us joy. It gives us satisfaction to remember with joy the complete passion of this most faithful, most courageous and most glorious martyr, now past, but then future for the brothers who, worried, had to face it.
IN NATALI CYPRIANI MARTYRIS, I

CAPUT I.—1. Cypriani passio recolitur.—Sermonem a nobis debitum auribus et cordibus vestris exigit tam grata et religious solemnitas, qua passionem beati Martyris celebramus. Tristis procul dubio tune Ecclesia Fuit, non darnno cadentis, sed desiderio recedentis; semper cupiens videre praesentem tam bonum rectorem atque doctorem. Sed quos afflixerat sollicitudo certaminis, consolata est corona victoris. Et nunc, non solum sine ulla tristitia, verum etiam cum ingenti laetitia cuneta quae tune gesta sunt legendo et diligendo recolimus; dieque isto gaudere iam concessum est, non timere. Ñeque enim eum formidamus terribiliter venientem, sed expectamus hilariter redeuntem. Placet itaque universam illam fidelissimi et fortissimi et gloriosissimi Martyris passionem cum exsultatione remember praeteritam, quam tune fratres cum sollicitudine sustinuerefuturam.

2. First of all he was exiled to Curubis' for confessing faith in Christ; This measure did nothing to harm Saint Cyprian and, on the other hand, was of great use to the city. Where could he be sent where Christ was not, for confessing the one who was exiled? Christ, then, who says: I will be with you always to the end of the world, received his member wherever the fury of the enemy drove him. Oh foolish disbelief of the pursuer! If you are looking for a place of banishment to which to send the Christian, find first, if you can, one from which Christ will be forced to leave. You think that you are expelling this man of God from his homeland to a foreign country, who, in Christ, will be exiled nowhere and, in the flesh, is a pilgrim wherever he is. But he delights to consider and mention now the following moments of his passion after this banishment, thus considered by the enemy, although he did not experience it as such. Once the holy martyr Cyprian, the chosen one of God, returned from the city of Curubis, to which he had been banished by order of the proconsul Aspasius Paternus, he remained in his gardens, waiting day by day for them to come for him, as had been revealed to him 2. 3. What could the fury of the persecutor now roar against a heart always ready and strengthened by a revelation from the Lord? How could he abandon in his passion someone who did not allow him to live worried about the uncertainty of the future? 2. Exsilium ipsius. Reditus ab exsilio.—Primo igitur quod pro fide confessionis Christi in exsilium Curubin missus est, non sancto Cypriano aliquid nocitum, sed multum illi praestitum est civitati. Quo enim ipse mitteretur, ubi ille non esset, propter cuius testimonium mittebatur? Christus ergo qui ait: Ecce ego vobiscum sum omnibus diebus usque ad consummationem saeculi (Mt 28,20), in omni loco membrum suum excipiebat, quocumque furor inimici pellebat. O stulta infidelitas persequentis! Si quaeris exsilium quo Christianus iubeatur I will go; prius, si potes, inveni unde Christus cogatur exíre. De patria sua in alienam te arbitraris excludere hominem Dei, in Christo nusquam exsulem, in carne ubique peregrinum. Sed iamconsidere et commemorare delectat post illud, quod Cyprianus non senserat, sed inimicus putabat exsilium, quid ex ordine passionis ipsius consecutum sit.

Cum enim Cyprianus sanctus martyr electus a Deo de civitate Curubitana, in quam exsilio [1411] praecepto Aspasii Paterni proconsulis missus fuet, regressus esset; in hortis suis manebat; et inde quotidie sperabat vino ad se, sicut ostensum illi erat. Quando enim desereret patientem, quem non est passus praeoecupari nescientem? Iam ergo quod ad eum Place where Saint Cyprian was exiled by order of the proconsul Aspasio Paterno. Praise of Saint Cyprian

So, to carry him to martyrdom, two were sent, who even put him on the cart and placed him in their midst. This, too, was a divine warning for him to remember with joy that he belonged to the body of him who was numbered among the wicked. In fact, Christ was hung on the tree between two thieves, thus giving an example of patience. Cyprian, in turn, carried to martyrdom in a chariot and in the middle of two guards, followed in the footsteps of Christ. 4. What can be said about the fact that, finding himself guarded by guards when the martyrdom was postponed for one day and a crowd of sisters and brothers gathered there to spend the night at the doors, he ordered that the young women be protected? How carefully this must be reflected upon! With how many praises it must be proclaimed! With what praise it should not be praised! Since the death of the body was already close, the pastoral care did not die in his shepherd's soul. The concern to defend the flock of the Lord dominated his soul, sober until his last day of life here. The hand of the cruel executioner, already on the verge of falling, did not shake from his soul his zeal as a most faithful servant. Thus, he thought of being a martyr without forgetting that he was a bishop, worrying more about the account he had to give to the prince of the shepherds for the sheep that had been entrusted to him than about what he would answer about his own faith to the unfaithful proconsul. He certainly loved the one who had said to Peter: Do you love me? Feed my sheep. And he tended his sheep, for which he was preparing to shed his blood, imitating him. He ordered to protect the girls

You come, knowing that he had not only a simple Lord, but also a cunning enemy 3. In this way he armed his virile chest in confession against the lion that roared openly, at the same time that he defended the female sex against the wolf that stalked the flock. 5. Thus, in truth, he who thinks of God as judge, before whom each one must render an account of the life lived here and of the duties that were attached to him, looks for himself; there, as the Apostle testifies, every man must receive in accordance with what he did while in the body, whether good or evil. Look for yourself who, living by faith and making sure that his last day is not a cause for concern, considers each one as the last, and in this way he reaches the last day pleasing God with his customs. It was thus that the blessed Cyprian, most merciful bishop and most faithful martyr, looked for himself, and not as the cunning tongue of the devil, who spoke through the mouth of the impious judge, possessed by him, seemed to exhort him, saying: "Look for yourself." In fact, seeing that his soul remained immovable when he said to him: "The emperors have ordered you to perform the prescribed rites," and that he even answered: "I will not do it," he added these words: "Take care of yourself." That is the perfidious language of the devil; If not from the one who was ignorant of what he said, then from the one who spoke through him. The proconsul, in effect, was an interpreter not so much of the human princes, under whose orders he boasted of being

passioni exhibitendum duo missi sunt, which eum etiam secum in resume levaverunt in medioque posuerunt; et hoc divinae admonitionis Fuit, ut gaudens recoleret ad eius corpus se pertinere, qui inter iniquos deputatus est. Christus namque inter duos latrones ligno suspensus, ad exemplum patientiae praebebatur (cf. Mark 5,17.28). Cyprianus autem inter duos apparitores, ad passionem curru portatus Christi vestigia sequebatur. 4. Cypriani sollicitudo pastorális.—Quid illud quod cum in alium diem dilatus apud custodes esset, atque illuc se multitudo fratrum ac sororum congregans, pro foribus pernoctaret, custodiri puellas praecepit, quanta intentione consideradum? quanta laude praedicandum? How much praeconio commendandum is there? Vicina corporis morte, non moriebatur in animo pastoris vigilantia pastorális; et cura tuendi dominici gregis usque ad extremum vitae huius diem sober mind tenebatur: nec excutiebat ab animo diligentiam fidelissimi dispensatoris, manus iam next cruenti carnificis. Ita se martyrem cogitabat futurum, ut esse non oblivisceretur episcopum: magis curans quam rationem pastorum principi de commissis sibi ovibus redderet, quam quid infideli proconsuli de fide propria respondet. Amabat quippe eum, qui Petro dixerat: Do you love me? Walk oves meas (lo 22.17). Et pascebat oves eius, pro quibus sanguinem fundere illum imitans praeparabat. Custodiri puellas praecepit, sciens non solum

se habere simplicem Dominum, sed etiam versipellem adversarium. Itaque adversus leonem aperte frementem in confessione virile pectus armabat, adversus lupum insidiantem gregi sexum femineum muniebat. CAPOT III.—5. Quomodo sibi consulendum. Dies omnis pro extreme computandus. Proconsulis verba ad Cypnanum, et huius responsum.—Ita veré sibi consultit, qui Deum iudicem cogitat, apud quem causam gestae huius vitae atque ab illo sibi muneris iniuncti quisque dicturus est: ubi omnis homo recipit, sicut testatur Apostolus, quae per corpus gessit, sive bonum, sive malum (2 Cor 5,10). Ita sibi consult, qui ex fide vivirs, et satagens ne ab extreme praeoecupetur die, extremum computat omnem diem, et sic Deo plácitos mores perducit usque ad extremum diem. Ita sibi beatus Cyprianus et episcopus misericordissimus, et martyr fidelissimus, consulebat, non sicut eum lingua subdola diaboli per os possessi a se impii iudicis monere videbatur they say: "Consule tibi." Cum enim eius immobilem mentem videret, quando eí dixit: «Iusserunt te [1412] principes caerimoniari»; responcütque ille: «Non fació»; adiecit et ait: "Consulate tibi." Ipsa est lingua subdola diaboli: etsi non huius qui nesciebat quid loqueretur, illius tamen qui per eum loquebatur. Loquebatur enim proconsul, non tam secundum principes nomines, quorum iussa

subdued, as of the prince of the aerial powers, of whom the Apostle says: Who works in the children of infidelity. Cipriano knew well that it was the devil who spoke through his mouth, although he himself was unaware of it. When he heard what the proconsul told him, namely: "Look for yourself," Cyprian knew well, I repeat, that what flesh and blood said without any malice, the devil said with cunning, and in this way he warned two subjects of the same action: the proconsul with his eyes, the devil with faith. The first did not want Cipriano to die; the second did not want him to be crowned. For this reason, the Saint, in front of him, was calm; in front of this, cautious; He responded to one openly and defeated the other secretly. 6. “Accomplish,” he said, “what you have been commanded to do; "In something so fair there is no room for advice." He had told her: "Look out for yourself." And he got this answer: "In something so fair there is no room for advice." Advice is given or asked for. The proconsul, who did not want to receive them from Cyprian, nevertheless exhorted him to follow his own. But Cipriano responded: «In something so just there is no room for advice. "I do not ask for advice, because there is no indecision in me, since justice itself has removed all doubt from me." The just, in fact, lives in the certainty of faith to die peacefully in the flesh. Many martyrs had preceded Cyprian, who with his very ardent exhortations had encouraged them to defeat the devil. It was right, then, that he who with his truthful word had sent them ahead should follow them without fear in their passion. Therefore,

"In something so fair there is no room for advice." What can we say to this? What should be our joy in this? Having conceived so much joy, what will burst forth from our hearts and our mouths but those last words of the venerable martyr? In fact, after Galerius Maximus 4 read him the written sentence: "We are pleased that Tascius Cyprianus be punished with the death penalty," he responded: "Thank God." Having, then, in this place the memory5 of such a great event, the festivity of such a solemn day and such a salutary example, let us also say with all the fibers of our hearts: "Thanks be to God."

sibimet iniuncta iactabat, quam secundum principan potestatis aeris de quo Apostolus dicit: Qui operatur in filiis diffidentiae (Eph 2,2): quem per huius quoque linguam opera Cyprianus noverat, quod ipse non noverat. Noverat, inquam, Cyprianus, cum a proconsule audiret: «Consule tibi» quod caro et sanguis diceret stolide, hoc diabolum dicere subdole; atque intuebatur in one opere duos; istum oculis, illum fide. Nolebat eum iste mori, nolebat ille coronan; proinde circa istum placidus, circa illum cautus; huic aperte responderbat, illum occulte vincebat. CAPOT IV.—6. Cypriani verba. Sententia in Cyprianum.—"Fac, inquit, quod tibi praeceptum est: in re tam justa mile est consult it." Dixerat quippe ule, "Consule tibi." Ad hoc responsum est, "In re tam iusta nulla est consulted." Consult enim qui consilium vel impertit, vel quaerit. Sed proconsul non a Cypriano consilium accipere volebat, sed eum potius ut a se acciperet, admonebat. At ille, "In re, inquit, tam iusta nulla est consultatio." Non adhuc consulo, quia non adhuc dubito; abstulit enim mihi dubitationem ipsa iustitia. Iustus autem, ut securus moriatur in carne, certus vivit in fide. Praecesserant Cyprianum multi martyres, quos flagrantissimis exhortationibus suis ad vincendum diabolum accenderat; et erat utique iustum ut quos veridicus loquendo prae-

1. May the Holy Spirit deign to tell me what I have to say to you at this moment, since we have to offer the praise of the most glorious martyr Cyprian, whose birthday we celebrate today, as you know. The Church frequently uses this name, miserat, patiendo intrepidus sequeretur: ergo "in re tam iusta nulla est consultatio." Quid ad haec dicamus? quid ad haec exsultemus? Tanta conceptione gaudiorum, in quid erumpat cor nostrum et os nostrum, nisi in ipsam venerabilis Martyris ultimam vocem? Cum enim Galerius Maximus decretum ex libello recitasset: "Tascium Cyprianum gladio animadverti placet." Respondit ille, “Deo gratias.” Habentes igitur de re tanta memoriam praesentis loci, festivitatem solemnissimi diei, propositionem saluberrimi exempli, omnibus medullis nostris dicamus et nos, Deo gratias. SERMO
IN NATALI CYPRIANI MARTYRIS, II

CAPUT I.—-1. Natale Cypriani martyris Africa tota percelebre.—Spiritus sanctus doceat nos in Jiac hora quae oporteat dicere: dicturi enim sumus aliquid de laude Cypriani gloriosissimi martyris, cuius Natalem hodie, sicut nostis, celebramus. Quod nomen sic frequentat Ecclesia, id The proconsul who succeeded Aspasio Paterno, and who summoned him from exile, tried him and sentenced him to death. See nt.l to serm.273.

that is, "births", but indicating with it the precious death of the martyrs. The Church, I repeat, uses it so frequently that even those who do not belong to it speak like it. Without referring only to this city, but to all of Africa and even to the regions on the other side of the sea, not only to Christians, but also to pagans, Jews or heretics, who can be found who does not speak with us about the birth of the martyr Cyprian? What does this mean, brothers? We do not know the date of his birth; but, since today he suffered his passion, today we celebrate his birth. But we wouldn't celebrate that date even if we knew it. On that day, in fact, he contracted original sin, while on this day he conquered all sin. On that day he emerged into this light from his mother's weary bosom, while on this day he departed from the deep bosom of nature to that light that bathes the gaze of the mind with happiness and joy. 2. In life he ruled the Church of Carthage, and when he died he filled it with glory. There he exercised the episcopacy, there he accomplished his martyrdom. In that Jugar where he left his mortal remains, a cruel crowd then gathered to shed the blood of Cyprian out of hatred for Christ; A devout crowd gathers there today, who in honor of the birth of Cyprian drinks the blood of Christ. And in that place the blood of Christ is drunk in honor of the birth of Cyprian, all the more sweetly the more devoutly the blood was shed there est, Natales, ut Natales [1413] vocet pretiosas martyrum mortes. Sic, inquam, hoc nomen frequentat Ecclesia, ut etiam qui non sunt in illa, hoc dicant cum illa. Quis enim hodie, non dicam in hac our civitate, sed plañe per Africam totam transmarinasque regions, non Christianus solum, sed Paganus, aut Iudaeus, aut etiam haereticus poterit inveniri, qui non nobiscum dicat Natalem martyris Cypriani? Quid est hoc, brothers? When natus sit,ignomus; et quia hodie passus est, Natalem eius hodie celebramus. Sed illum diem non celebraremus, etsi nossemus. Illo enim die traxit origínale peccatum: isto autem die vicit omne peccatum. Illo die ex fastidioso matris uterus istam processit in luzem, quae oculos carnis illecebrat; isto autem die ex occultissimo naturae sinu illam discessit ad luzem, quae visum mentís congratulator et blessed illustrat. CAPUT II.—2. Carthaginiensis Ecclesia Cypriani episcopatu et martyrio nobilitata.

Mensa Cypriani apud Carthaginem.—Carthaginiensem Ecclesiam vivos gubernavit, moriens honoravit. Ibi episcopatum gessit, ibi martyrium consummavit. In eo quippe loco, ubi posit carnis exuvias, saeva tune multitudo convenerat, quae propter odium Christi sanguinem funderet Cypriani: ibi hodie venerans multitudo concurrit, quae propter Natalem Cypriani bibit sanguinem Christi. Et both dulcius in illo loco propter Natalem Cypriani sanguis bibitur Christi, quanto devotius ibi propter nomen Christi sanguis fusus est Cypriani. Denique, sicut nostis,
Saint Cyprian, glory of Carthage...

of Cipriano. Finally, as those of you who have been to Carthage know, a table of God has been built in that same place, which, however, is called Cyprian's table; not because he had ever eaten there, but because he was immolated there and because with his own immolation he prepared this table, on which he neither gives nor is given in food, but rather a sacrifice is offered to God, to whom he offered himself. But why is that table that belongs to God called Cyprian's table? This is the reason: if now she finds herself surrounded by obsequious faithful, Cipriano saw himself surrounded by persecutors right there; where he now receives the honor of the prayers of friends, there Cyprian was trampled by the fury of his enemies; To finish, where she was lifted up, there he was brought down. Sing to God, proclaim a psalm to the name of him who rises above the sunset: he was the one who has done all this for the martyr. 3. But, Carthage having had its chair and having its memory, what reason would we have to celebrate its birth, if the death of its saints were not precious in the presence of the Lord? His voice was heard throughout the whole earth, and his words were heard in the ends of the earth. He taught faithfully what he himself was going to do, and did with strength what he had taught. Living holy, he came to a precious death, and dying unjustly, to a glorious life. And he got the name of martyr's triumph because he fought until blood was shed in the fight for the truth. quicumque Carthaginem nostis, in eodem loco mensa Deo constructa est; et tamen mensa dicitur Cypriani, non quia ibi est unquam Cyprianus epulatus, sed quia ibi est immolatus, et quia ipsa immolatione sua paravit hanc mensam, non in qua pascat sive pascatur, sed in qua sacrificium Deo, cui et ipse oblatus est, offeratur. Sed ut mensa illa, quae Dei est, etiam Cypriani vocetur, haec causa est; quia ut illa moda cingatur ab obsequentibus, ibi Cyprianus cingebatur a persequentibus: ubi nunc illa ab amicis orantibus honoratur, ibi Cyprianus ab inimicis frementibus calcabatur: postremo ubi illa erecta est, ibi prostratus est. Cántate Deo, psalmum dicite nomini eius: qui ascendit super occasum (Ps 67,5), ipse fecit ista super occisum. CAPUT III.—3. Cypriani mors pretiosa.—Sed cum Carthago habuerit cathedram eius, Carthago habeat memoriam eius; unde nos celebraremus Natalitia eius, nisi esset pretiosa in conspectu"Dominimors sanctorum eius (Ps 115,15)?

In omnem terram exiit sonus eius, et in fines orbis terrae verba eius (cf. Ps 18:5). Docuit fideliter quod facturus erat, fecit fortiter quod docuerat. Ad pretiosam mortem iuste vivir, ad gloriosam vero vitam iniuste dying pervenit; Atque adeptus est triumphale martyris nomen, quia perduxit usque ad sanguinem pro veritate certamen.

He not only preached to be heard, but also wrote what can be read; He reached some places through foreign languages, and others through his letters; He was known in many regions; partly, because of the celebrity of his most courageous passion, and partly, because of the very gentle sweetness of his writings. 1. The passion of the blessed martyr Cyprian has made today a day of celebration for us; The fame of his victory has gathered us with devotion in this place. But the celebration of the martyrs' festival should consist of imitating their virtues. It is an easy thing to honor a martyr; the great thing is to imitate CAPUT IV.—4. Cypránus et passione et scriptis suis per orbem clarus.—Verum quia non solum dixit quae audirentur, sed scripsit etiam quae legerentur, et ad alia loca per alienas linguas, ad alia vero per suas [1414] litteras venit, et innotuit regionibus multis, partim per famem fortissimae passionis, partim per dulcedinem suavissimae lectionis: álacres celebremus hunc diem, et ita omnes unanimiter supplicemus, ut in Ecclesia maiore communem patrem audire et videre mereaniur; habituri et de sermone eius gaudium, et de passionis eius gloria profectum, per Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum. IN NATALI CYPRIANI MARTYRIS, III

CAPUT I.—1. Solemnitates martyrum celebrandae imitatione virtutum. Mundi blandientis errors et saevientis terrores sapientia et patientia surpass.—Istum nobis festum diem passio beatissimi Cypriani martyris fecit, cuius nos victoriae celebritas in istum locum devotissimos congregavit. Sed celebratio solemnitatis martyrum, imitatio debent esse virtutum. Facile est honorem martyris celebrate; magnum est fidetn atque patien-

your faith and patience. Let us do the one so that we desire the other; Let's celebrate in such a way the first thing we love, especially the second. What do we praise in the faith of the martyr? Who fought for the truth until death, and that is why he won. He despised the flattery of the world and did not yield to its cruelty; Consequently, he presented himself as a victor before God. Errors and terrors abound in this world; The blessed martyr overcame errors with wisdom and terrors with patience. His was a great feat: following the lamb, he defeated the lion. The cruelty of the pursuer was like the roar of a lion; but, looking at the lamb above, he trampled the lion below; to the lamb who destroyed death with his death, who hung on the tree, who shed his blood and redeemed the world. 2. The first apostles, blessed rams of the holy flock, saw the Lord Jesus himself hanging on the cross, they mourned his death, they were afraid of his resurrection, they loved him made powerful and they themselves shed their own blood for the blood they saw. Think, brothers, what it means for men to be sent around the world to preach that a dead man was resurrected and ascended to heaven, and for this preaching they have suffered everything the madness of the world has inflicted on them: privations, banishments, chains, torments, fire, beasts, crosses and deaths. And they suffered this for I don't know what? Was Peter, my brothers, dying for his glory or preaching for himself? One died so that another could be honored; One gave himself to death so that another tiam martyris could imitate. Hoc sic agamus, ut illud optemus: hoc sic celebremus, ut illud potius diligamus. Quid laudamus in fide martyris? Quia usque ad mortem pro veritate certavit, et ideo vicit. Blandientem mundum contempsit, saevienti non cessit: ideo victor ad Deum accessit. Abundant in isto saeculo errors et terrores: beatissimus Martyr, errors sapientia, terrores patientia surplus. Magnum est quod fecit: secutus agnum, leonem vicit. Quando persecutor saeviebat, leo fremebat: sed quia agnus sursum attendebatur, leo deorsum calcabatur: qui morte mortem destruxit, ligno pependit, sanguinem fudit, mundum redemit. CAPUT II.—2. Apostoli de Domino quae ipsi viderant confitendo mortui.—Primi beati Apostoli arietes gregis sancti, ipsum Dominum Iesum viderunt pendentem, doluerunt morientem, expaverunt resurgentem, amaverunt potentam, et ipsi sanguinem fuderunt pro eo quod viderunt.

Cogitate yourself, fratres, quale Fuit mitti nomines per orbem terrarum, praedicare hominem mortuum resurrexisse, in caelum ascendisse; et pro ista praedicatione perpeti omnia quae insaniens mundus inferret, damna, exsilia, links, storm, flammas, beasts, crosses, deaths. Hoc pro nescio quo? Numquid enim, fratres mei, Petrus pro sua gloria moriebatur, aut se ipsum praedicabat? Alius moriebatur, ut alius honoraretur; alius occidebatur, ut alius coleretur. Numquid hoc faceret, nisi flagrantia caritatis,

was adored. Would I do this, perhaps, if the fragrance of charity and the consciousness of truth were not at the root? They had seen what they announced; Indeed, when would they be willing to die for something they had not seen? They were forced to deny what they had seen, but they did not deny it: they preached the death of someone they knew was alive. They knew why they despised life; They knew for what happiness they endured temporary unhappiness, for what rewards they despised these evils. Their faith does not allow itself to be placed in the balance with the entire world. They had heard: What good is it for a man to gain the whole world if in return he suffers detriment to his soul? The charms of the world did not delay their rapid career, nor the passing goods of those who emigrated to another place; Whatever this happiness may be and however dazzling it may be, it must be left here, it cannot be transferred to the other life; The time will come when those now alive will also have to leave it here. 3. Therefore despise the world, Christians; despise the world, I repeat over and over again. The martyrs despised him, the apostles despised him, the blessed Cyprian despised him, whose memory we celebrate today. You want to be rich, feel full of honors and be healthy; everything was despised by him in whose memory you have gathered. Why, I beg you to tell me, why do you love so much that which was despised by him whom you so venerate? the one whom, without a doubt, you would not honor if he had not despised him? Why do I find you in love with things despised by him whom you worship? With all certainty: if he had loved them, you would not worship him

today. Don't love them either, because he didn't close the door after he entered. You too despise them and enter after him. It is clear where you have to do it: Christ is the door. The door opened for you as its side was pierced by a spear. Remember what came from there and choose where to enter. From the side of the Lord, pierced with a spear when he hung dead from the tree, water and blood flowed: the one is your purification, the other your redemption. 4. Love and do not love; love some things and don't love others. There are, in fact, things whose love is beneficial and things whose love is a hindrance. Do not love what is a hindrance to you if you do not want to encounter torment. What you love about the land is a hindrance; It is viscous for the wings of the spirit, that is, of the virtues, with which we fly to God. Do you want to not be hunted and you love viscose? By being captured sweetly, have you not been captured? The greater the delight it causes, the greater the strangulation it produces. This is what I say: you praise, acclaim and love him. The answer does not come to you from me, but from wisdom: "I want lives, not words." Praise wisdom with life, not with words, agreeing with it. 5. The Lord says in the gospel: We have sung to you, and you have not danced. How could I say this if I hadn't read it? He who is vain laughs at me, but he who has authority supports me. If I had not anticipated whose words those words are,

of conscientia veritatis? Viderant quod dicebant: nam quando pro ea re morerentur, quam non viderant? Quod viderant, denegare debenbant. Non negaverunt; praedicaverunt mortuum, quem sciebant vivum. Sciebant pro qua vita contemnerent vitam; sciebant pro qua felicítate ferrent transitoriam infelicitatem, pro quibus praemiis is damna contemnerent. Fides eorum cum toto mundo non appenderetur. Audierant: Quid prodest homini, si totum mundum lucretur, animae autem suae detrimentum patiatur? (Mt 16,26). Non re[415]tardavit illecebra saeculi festinantes, transitara migrants, quantumlibet et quomodo libet fulgens congratulations hic dimittenda, ad alliam vitam non transferenda, aliquando hic et a vivirtibus relinquenda. CAPUT III.—3. Contemptum mundi martyres exemplo docent.—Contemnite ergo saeculum, Christiani; contemnite saeculum, contemnite. Contempserunt martyres, contempserunt Apostoli, contempsit beatus Cyprianus, cuius hodie memoriam celebramus. Divites esse vultis, honorati esse vultis, sani esse vultis: totum ille contempsit, ad cuius memoriam convenistis. Quid, obsecro, tantum amatis, quod contempsit quem sic honoratis? quem, si ista non contempsisset, non utique sic honoraretis. Quare te invenio earum rerum amatorem, quarum veneraris contempto-

rem? Certe illum, si haec amaret, non venerareris. Et tu noli amare: non enim intravit, et ostium contra te clausit. Contemne et tu; et intra post illum. Patet qua intres: Cbristus est ianua. Et tibi est ostium apertum, quando est latus eius lancea perforatum. Quid inde manavit recolé; et choose qua possis intrare. De latere Domini pendentis et mororientis in ligno, posteaquam est lancea perforatum, aqua sanguisque profluxit (cf. lo 19,34). In one is mundatio tua, in altero redemptio tua. CAPUT IV.—4. Rerum terrenarum amor viscus animae.—Amate, et nolite amare: ad aliquid amate, et ad aliquid amare nolite. Est enim quod ad profectum ametur, et est quod ad impedimentum ametur. Noli amare impedimentum, si non vis invenire tormentum. Quod amas in terra, impedimentum est: viscum est pennarum spiritualium, hoc est virtutum, quibus volatur ad Deum. Capi non vis, et viscum amas? Numquid ideo non caperis, qui dulciter caperis? Quanto magis delectat, mucho fortius strangulat. Haec dico: et laudatis, et clamatis, et amatis. Respondet tibi, non ego, sed sapientia: Mores flew, non voices. Sapientiam lauda living; not ringing, be ringing. CAPUT V.—5. Cantica profana et saltationes pulsae de ecclesia, ubi sepultus Cyprianus.—Dominus dicit in Gospel: Cantavimus vobis, et non saltastis (Mt 11:17). Quando hoc ego dicerem, si non legerem? Irridet me vanitas, sed iuvat auctoritas. Si non praemisissem quis hoc

Who among you could have endured my saying: We have sung to you, and you have not danced? Do we have to dance in this place, even if we have to sing the psalm? Some time ago, not many years ago, the insolence of the dancers had penetrated even this place. Even in this very place where the body of a martyr lies so holy, as many of a certain age remember; such a holy place, I repeat, was invaded by the pestilence and insolence of the dancers. During the entire night, nefarious things were sung here and people danced to the beat of the songs. But when it pleased the Lord, using my holy brother, your bishop, from the moment the holy vigils began to be celebrated here, that pestilence that had offered a certain resistance, then gave way to his zeal and was ashamed before his wisdom. 6. By the benevolence of God, such things no longer take place here, since we do not celebrate games in honor of demons, an occasion in which all this usually happens to the delight of those who are honest, who with their filth tend to deprave their worshipers; rather, the sanctity and solemnity of the martyrs is celebrated here. There is no dancing here; but, even though there is no dancing, the words of the gospel are read: We have sung to you, and you have not danced. They are reproached, recriminated and accused for not having danced. Far be it from us to return to that insolence! Listen to how wisdom wants us to understand it. Sing who keeps

da; He who fulfills what is commanded dances. What is dancing but adjusting the movement of the limbs to the music? What is our song? I'm not going to say it, lest it be something of mine. I'm better off being an administrator than an actor. I recite our song: Do not love the world or the things of the world; If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father does not dwell in him, since all that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world. But the world passes away, and so does its lust; Whoever, however, fulfills the will of God, remains eternal, just as God also remains eternal. 7. What a song, my brothers! You listened to the singer, let us listen to the dancers: do with the good ordering of customs what the dancers do with the movement of their limbs. Do it like this within yourself: let the customs adjust to the music. Tear out evil desires and plant charity. How long this tree produces is a good thing. The former cannot engender anything good, the latter nothing evil. I proclaim it, you praise it, but no one changes. But no, what I just said is not true: the fishermen changed, later even many senators changed, Cipriano changed, in whose memory2 we meet today. He himself left writing and testified what his life was like in another time, how evil, impious, deserving of being disapproved and reproved.

Intus hoc agite: mores consonent. Cupiditas exstirpetur, caritas plantetur. De ista arbore quidquid exit, bonum est. Cupiditas nihil boni potest generare: caritas nihil mali. He adjusted to the rhythm of the good song and the new song; He adjusted, he loved it, he persevered, he fought and he won. 8. You often say: "Times are difficult, times are hard, times abound in misery." Live well, and you will change times with your good life; times will change and you will have nothing to complain about. Indeed, my brothers, what are times? The extension and succession of centuries. The sun rises; After twelve hours, it is on the opposite side of the world. The next day he goes out again in the morning, to set himself again. List how many times the same thing happens: that's what the times are. Who did the sunrise hurt? Who was harmed by its installation? Consequently, time has not harmed anyone. The damaged ones are the men; Those who harm are also men. Oh great pain! They are men who are damaged, the dispossessed, the oppressed. By whom? Not by lions, not by snakes or scorpions, but by men. Those who suffer harm lament it; If it were possible, would they not do the same thing that they reproach others for? We will come to know the man who murmurs at the moment when it is possible for him to do the same thing against what he murmured. I praise him, I will praise him again if he stops doing what he reproached.

sin and did not sin; who did not march after gold. It is the gold that must follow you, not you the gold. Gold is a good thing, because God did not create anything bad. Don't be bad, and the gold will be good. Behold, between a good man and a bad man I put gold. Suppose the bad guy appropriates it; the poor are oppressed; the judges, corrupt; Laws are violated and social life is disturbed. Why all this? Because it was the bad guy who appropriated the gold. Suppose the good takes it: the poor are fed, the naked are clothed, the oppressed are liberated, and the captives are redeemed. How many good things gold produces in the hands of the good and how many evils in the hands of the evil one! Why then do you say, sometimes full of bad humor: "Oh, if gold did not exist!"? Don't love gold. If you are bad, you go after him; If you are good, he will go after you. What does it mean he's after you? That you govern him, not he you; that you possess him, and not he you. 10. Let us return, then, to the words of Holy Scripture: Who did not march after gold. Who could sin and did not sin. Who is this, and shall we praise him? Who is this or who is there here? There are many who hear it; but are there any here? Far be it from me to lose hope that anyone will be found here; better, not some, but some. Far be it from me to distrust the era of such a great family man. He who sees the threshing floor from afar thinks that there is only straw in it; but whoever knows how to look, also finds grain. Where does it bother you to see so much?

Tempora mala non faciunt nisi homines mali.—Et dicitis: Molesta tempora, gravia tempora, misera tempora sunt. Vivite bene, et mutatis tempora Vivite bene: tempora mutatis, et non habetis unde murmuretis. Quid sunt enim tempora, fratres mei? Spatia et volumina saeculorum. Ortus est sol, peractis horis duodecim ex alia roundi parte occidit; alia die mane ortus iterum octdit; numera quoties: ipsa sunt tempora. Quem laesit solis ortus? quem laesit occasus solis? Ergo neminem laesit tempus. Qui laeduntur, homines sunt; a quibus laeduntur, homines sunt. O great pain! homines laeduntur, homines spoliantur, homines opprimuntur. Whoa? non a leonibus, non a colubris, non a scorpionibus; thirst ab hominibus. Dolent qui laeduntur. Si [1417] possint, non faciunt ipsi quod reprehendunt? 1. Most holy and solemn day, the most well-known and famous ornament of this Church, the one that has shone for our joy today. The blessed Cyprian has made it resplendent for us with the glory of his passion. No language, not even his own, would be enough to sing the praises of one who was as respected as a bishop and venerated as a martyr. Therefore, in this my sermon that I feel the duty to preach to you, you must approve the affection of my will before demanding the effect of my faculties. In this way, a holy praiser who felt incapable of praising God, for which no prayer or thought is sufficient, says: Please, Lord, please you what comes willingly from my mouth. I also say that; May that also be my wish, para devotionemque vestram, ut istum diem honeste ac sobrie peragamus, et hoc exhibitamus diei, quo Cyprianus beatissimus passus est, quod amavit ut pateretur.

Far be it from us to believe with childish imagination that God is armed with material weapons. The condition of the weapons with which he is equipped and with which he usually helps his soldiers is confessed by those who have received his help when, exclaiming and thanking him, they say to him: Lord, you have crowned us with the shield of good will. The double-edged sword of God, a sword that the Body of Christ that is the Church asks to be drawn and wielded against those who persecute Him, can be understood in those words in which the Savior himself says to his body: I ​​did not come to

bring peace to the earth, but the sword. With that spiritual sword he separated from his martyrs, longing for the heavenly joys, the earthly affections, fatally soft, which would have forced them to return from heaven to earth if the sword of Christ had not cut them off. But there is another very clear sword of God: the soul of the righteous in the hand of God, of which it is said in the psalm: Deliver my soul from the wicked; your sword, from your enemies from your hand. First he said: my soul, and then he repeated: your sword; First he said: of the wicked, and then he repeated it with these words: of the enemies of your hand. 5. He unsheathed this sword, scattering his martyrs everywhere and wielded it against those who persecuted the Church, so that, as they did not bow before the words of the preachers, they would break before the vigor of those who died. God, in fact, makes his resistant weapons against his enemies: those he makes his friends. So, then, that sword of God, the soul of the blessed Cyprian, resplendent with charity, sharpened by truth, wielded and made to vibrate by the power of God that fought, how many battles did it not fight! How many legions of opponents he did not defeat with his reasoning! How many enemies he wounded! How many adversaries he knocked down! How numerous were the enemies in whose hearts he put to death the same enmities, his enemies, and turned them into friends, through the buttonholes God was going to fight more assiduously against others! Change your shows too; The Church shows your mind others that are more respectable and venerable. The passion of the blessed Cyprian was now read; We heard it with our ears, but we were contemplating it with our minds; We saw their struggle, and, in a way, we feared for those who were in danger, but we hoped for God's help. Finally, do you want to know quickly what difference there is between our shows and those in the theater? We, to the extent that our mind is healthy, wish to imitate the martyrs whose spectacle we attend; We, I repeat, wish to imitate the holy martyrs whose struggle we witness. Honest spectator: you are crazy if, when you are a spectator in a theater, you dare to imitate your favorite actor. I contemplate Cipriano and I love Cipriano. If he makes you angry, curse me and tell me: "Be like him." I contemplate it, I delight in it and, as far as possible, I embrace it with the arms of my mind; I see him fight and rejoice in his victory. Be angry, as I said, and tell me: "Be like him." Don't be angry if I tell you: "Be like him." But I'll save you, I won't say it; Recognize who your friend is and change your shows to mine. Can he who contemplates it be honest? Cease the greed of the buyer, and venal clumsiness will cease to exist. By contemplating what is infamous, you are supporting it. Why do you contribute to the existence of what you yourself accuse? I am amazed if the infamy of your favorite does not reach you. But let us suppose that you, spectator of passions and buyer of clumsy pleasures, are not affected by such infamy, that your honesty remains intact, if that is possible. Will I dare to ban the shows? I dare to do it, of course I dare; This place and who put me in it gives me value. The holy martyr could endure the cruelty of the pagans, shall I not dare to instruct the Christians who listen to me? If he despised open anger, will I fear the insults that are done to me in secret? I will say it certainly: let the hearts of the listeners argue with me if I say something false. Quid a te propter dignitatem de [69] curia removisti, et propter voluptatem tibi «In Rome, the profession of actor was exercised by foreigners, slaves and freedmen, who, like all people who had to live by selling their ingenuity or their work, were considered dishonored... Theatrical actors and other representatives of shows lacked active and passive voting in elections, and the sphere of private rights was also greatly limited, as deduces from the Digest: neither the comedian nor his children can be related to senatorial families; If the wife of a senator artem ludicram faceré coeperit (begins to work as an actress), he must throw her out of the house. For women, comic art was legally equated with prostitution and judicial condemnation... And not only that, but a senator could not visit or receive a visit from a comedian, and even for a gentleman (social class) it was difficult to talk to an actor on the street. For this reason, the actors were usually freedmen, slaves or foreigners, which made it difficult for this group of people to achieve social dignity" (J. GUILLEN, Urbs Roma. Vida y customs de los Romanos. II. La vida Pública [Salamanca 1978] p.406-407). Read also The City of God II 27. In imperial times, commoners used to be called the mass of citizens who did not belong to either the senatorial order or that of knights (equestrian).

The Church of the Martyrs
Topic: The Church of the Martyrs. Place: Carthage, in Cipriano's mensa. Date: September 14, feast of San Cipriano. Before the year 400.

1. We have sung the psalm: Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us up as a prey to his teeth. It is the gratitude due to the gifts of God. Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us up as prey to his teeth. It is, certainly, the cry of gratitude, and deserved gratitude. But when will man be able to thank God for all his gifts? I do not know if when the blessed martyr shed his sacred blood in this place there were as many people here enraged against him as the crowd that now praises him. I repeat it again - because it pleases me to see that the people come with devotion to the house of the Lord built in this place and also to compare the times -; I say again and repeat, and as far as I can I urge your devotion, that I do not know if, when the blessed martyr shed his sacred blood in this place, there were as many angry people here as the crowd that now praises him. Even if there was, the Lord was blessed, who did not give us up as

prey to its teeth. When they killed him, they believed they had conquered him; but they were defeated by those who died and rejoiced in it. No wonder they were angry if they were defeated. Because the persecutors did not want to kill, but rather devour, that is, integrate them into their body. They were pagans, they were impious and worshipers of demons and idols; That's what they wanted us to be when they wanted to devour us. Look at what we do with food when we eat it. Si ergo illi occidere voluerunt, isti occisi sunt: ​​fecerunt quod voluerunt illi, passi sunt isti; quomodo benedictus Dominus, who does not dedit us in venationem dentibus eorum? Qualis gratulatio est, benedictus Dominus, qui non dedit (867) nos in venationem dentibus eorum? Quia persecutors non occidere, sed devorare voluerunt, id est, in corpus suum transferre. Pagani werent, impii weret, daemonum et idolorum cultres weret: hoc nos faceré volebant, quandore devorare cupiebant. Intendite, quid cibo faciamus, quando manducamus. po? The body of the wicked existed: they devoured those who consented to wickedness; Without a doubt, they integrated into his body. On the other hand, the martyrs, although they urged them to deny Christ and worship an idol, persistently resisted, disdained the idol, confessed Christ and did not consent to pass into his body. Say, say, say with glory, with happiness and with truth: Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us up as prey to his teeth. Their networks are infidelity, impiety and the denial of Christ. The nets have been laid. You're hearing the hunters. If you want to protect yourself from them, despise those who scare you. You know what hunters do. They spread the nets in one place and from another they scare away the wild animals that they trap in them. You fear evil; Where does fear take you? The place you flee to is worse. Behold, the holy martyrs, seeing where the hunters had spread their nets—if the persecutor threatened death it was so that they would deny the savior—had to suffer; but for that very reason they were not caught. What rich booty, what abundant game, impious Babylon would have had to feed on if Bishop Cyprian had denied the Lord! With what a banquet, with what extraordinary hunting, impious Babylon would have been fed if Bishop Cyprian, the doctor of the Gentiles, who frustrated the idols, betrayed the demons, conquered the pagans, confirmed the Christians, and inflamed the martyrs, had denied the Lord! If, then, such a great and famous man had denied the Lord, what a prey to rejoice

to wicked Babylon! Blessed be the Lord, who did not give us up as prey to his teeth. Although they were angry against them, persecuted, tormented, imprisoned, chained, beaten, set on fire and handed over to wild beasts, since he did not deny Christ, the confessor of the Lord was crowned. They lost their cruelty, the martyrs found glory. The Church of the Martyrs

sheared You too have teeth, oh holy Jerusalem, city of God, Church of Christ!; You also have teeth. It is said to you in the Song of Songs: Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep coming up from the wash, which always give birth to twins, and among which there is none barren. Good, good for not having feared the teeth of Babylon. \The teeth of Babylon were the secular powers; teeth of Babylon were the doctors of illicit rites. You have not been given over to those teeth. Recognize yours; You do what they tried to do. Look at yourself: you have teeth too. Your teeth are like a flock of shorn sheep. What does sheared mean? Who have laid down their worldly burdens. What does sheared mean? Who have laid down their wool like the weight of worldly burdens. Your teeth were those of whom it is written in the Acts of the Apostles that they sold all their things and deposited the price of them at the feet of the apostles so that it could be distributed to each one according to his need. You received the wool from your traversed sheep. That flock came up from the bath of holy baptism. They all gave birth, since they fulfilled the two precepts. You remember, you remember; As educated people, you have acclaimed when I mentioned the two precepts: I have not said they are evil, and yet I have received the proof by the cry of your heart. You have recognized them. I'm going to say it for those who attend church more occasionally. Says the Lord, the most true teacher, the prince of martyrs: You shall love the Lord your God

with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind, and you will love your neighbor as yourself. In these two commandments the entire law and the prophets are summarized. Your teeth expired precisely because you gave birth to these twins. To you who have such teeth it is said; To you, oh Church!, it is said to you in the figure of the blessed Peter: Arise, kill and eat; Get up. That was told to Peter - when a tray containing all the peoples, symbolized in animals, came down from heaven; it was said to hungry Peter, that is, to the eager Church; 'Get up, why are you hungry?; Get up, you have food ready. You have teeth, kill and eat. Kill what they are and make them what you are; put to death what they are and make them what you are. You heard well; having such teeth, you have killed well, you have eaten well. You have attracted to you the very judges whom you have not feared; You disdained those who mistreated you and made them honor you. What was promised to your Lord was fulfilled: And all the kings of the earth will worship him and all the peoples will serve him. 4. The persecutors did not attest to this when they showed their cruelty. How many persecutors saw the blessed Cyprian shed his blood, bend his knees, lend his neck to the executioner in this place! There is no need to doubt it, we have to believe it.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, in whom we have our hope of eternal salvation, being God, became man, so that man, separated from God, would not consider himself left and abandoned in that distance. In chapter 12 of the Life of Augustine, Saint Posidius narrates how, due to an error on the part of the guide, the Saint avoided the ambushes that had been laid for him. It goes like this: «More than once, armed circumceliones, they prepared ambushes for the servant of God Augustine, when, at the request of his diocesans, he made the pastoral visit – and this was very frequent – ​​in order to instruct and strengthen the Catholics in the faith. Once, led by a subcenturion, their stratagem failed, for it happened that, when they were waiting for him on the road, assisted by divine Providence, the driver got lost, and by another route the bishop arrived with his entourage at the place where they were going, this error, later known, being a cause for freeing themselves from the impious hands of their persecutors. "They thanked God for having escaped unscathed, because those hitmen did not spare either laymen or priests, as is evident from the public records."

8. Therefore, my brothers, I pray to your charity that you have your heart prepared and firm in God.
