If you want to know where it is, ask the first reading you heard: If death prematurely takes possession of the righteous, he will find himself at rest. For whom or where can there be rest in this world, if everything is full of tribulations and, when tribulations subside, temptations appear everywhere? We must fear this world, whether it threatens or flatters. Fear God, and rather despise the world, the better to guard against it. Therefore, if we want to find ourselves at rest when death overtakes us, let us be fair. 2. Someone may say: "It's too much for me." Let us pay attention to what is written: If death prematurely takes possession of the righteous, he will be at rest. As we try to figure out who is righteous, we are terrified by the psalm: Every man is a liar. Topic: Dedication, that is, our own sanctification. Location: Unknown. Date: Feast of the dedication of a church. 1. The festival that brings us together is the dedication of this house of prayer. This is, in fact, the house of our prayers, since the house of God is ourselves. If we are the house of God, we are built in this world to be dedicated to the end of the world. Every building, better yet, every building, requires work; dedication calls for joy. What happened here when this building was built, happens now when the faithful gather in Christ. Believing is equivalent, in a certain way, to removing the beams and stones from the forests and mountains; Being catechized, baptized and formed is equated to the task of carving, polishing and adjusting by the hands of carpenters and craftsmen. However, they only build the house of God when they adjust to each other through charity. If you are viin domino confidamus, viam tentationis evadamus, vitam felicitatis habeamus. SERMO
IN DEDICATIONE ECCLESIAE, I

CAPUT I.—1. Aedificatio et dedicatio domus Dei in nobis. Mandatum novum canticum novum.—Celebritas huius congregationis, dedicatio est domus orationis. Domus ergo nostrarum orationum ista est, domus Dei nos ipsi. Si domus Dei nos ipsi, nos in hoc saeculo aedificamur, ut in fine saeculi dedicemur. Aedificium, immo aedificatio habet laborem, dedication exsultationem. Quod hic fiebat, quando ista emergebant, hoc fit modo cum congregantur credentes in Christum. Credendo enim quasi de silvis et montibus ligna et lapides praeciduntur: cum vero catechizantut, baptizantur, formantur, tanquam inter [1472] manus fabrorum et opificum dolantur, collineantur, complanantur. Verumtamen domum Domini non faciunt, nisi quando caritate compaginantur. Our love has other motivations, more than love, it is hate. He who loves evil, what does he hate? Maybe your neighbor? Be frightened: you hate your soul. You have heard that God loved us; and it is true that he loved us; and, if we look at what we were like when he loved us, we will blush with shame. But, if that does not happen, it is because, by loving us as we were, he made us different from what we were. We are ashamed to remember our past and filled with joy in what we hope for the future. Why, then, be ashamed of what we were and not rather trust that in hope we have been saved? Furthermore, we have heard: Draw near to him, and you will be enlightened and your faces will not blush. If the power goes out, you fall into confusion again. Come close to him and you will be enlightened. He is light, and we, without him, darkness. If you turn away from the light, you will remain in darkness; but, if you approach it, you will give light; but not yours, for you were once darkness, says the Apostle to the faithful who were previously unfaithful: You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. If then you are light in the Lord, without the Lord you are darkness. Therefore, if you are light in the Lord and darkness without him, draw near to him and you will be illuminated.

CAPUT II.—2. Amandus Deus propter ipsum, et proximus propter Deum.—Amemus, gratis amemus: Deum enim amamus, quo nihil melius invenimus. Ipsum amemus propter ipsum, et nos in ipso, tamen propter ipsum. lile enim veraciter amat amicum, qui Deum amat in amico, aut

quia est in illo, aut ut sit in illo. Haec est vera dilectio: propter aliud si nos diligimus, odimus potius quam diligimus. Qui enim amat iniquitatem: quid odit? forte vicinum suum, forte vicinum suam? Expavescat, odit animam suam (Ps 10:6). Odium animae, amor nequitiae. Ergo contra odium nequitiae, amor animae. Qui diligitis Dominum, odio habete malum (Ps 96,10). Bonus est Deus, malum est quod amas, et te ipsum malum amas: quomodo amas Deum, cum adhuc amas quod odit Deus? Audisti enim quia Deus dilexit nos (cf. 1lo 4,10): et verum est, dilexit nos; et quales dilexerit, si attendamus, erubescimus. Sed ideo non erubescimus, quia diligendo tales, fecit esse non tales. Erubescimus remembrancee praeteritorum, gaudemus spe Futurum. Quare enim iam erubescamus quod Fuimus, et non potius confidamus quia spe salvi facti sumus? 3. Pay attention to the dedication psalm we just sang, to the building that rises from its ruins. You tore my jacket: this belongs to the ruins. What corresponds to the building? And you girded me with joy. The cry of dedication: So that my glory sings to you and does not feel sorrow. Who is speaking? Recognize him by his words. If I try to expose it, it is a dark thing. Therefore I will repeat his words, so that you may instantly recognize the speaker and love him. Who could say: Lord, you freed my soul from hell? What soul has already been delivered from hell but that of whom it was said elsewhere: Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell? It is about dedication and it sings of liberation; The song of dedication of the house is sung with joy and it is said, I will exalt you, Lord, because you welcomed me and did not make my enemies happy because of me. Look at the Jewish enemies, who thought they had killed Christ, defeated him as an enemy and caused him to perish as a mortal man like the rest. He rose again on the third day, and this is his cry: I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me. Notice the Apostle, who says: Therefore God exalted him and gave him a name above every name. And you did not make my enemies happy because of me. They, indeed, rejoiced at the death of Christ; but, once resurrected, promoted and announced, some repented. When it was preached and announced by the perseverance of the apostles, some repented and were converted, while others were hardened and

they confused; No one, however, rejoiced at his death. Now, when the churches are full, are we to think that the Jews find joy in it? Churches are built, dedicated, filled, how can they rejoice? Not only do they not rejoice, but they even feel confused and the cry of joy is fulfilled: I will exalt you, Lord, because you have received me and did not rejoice my enemies because of me. You did not rejoice them at my expense; If they give credit to me, you will rejoice in me. 4. In order not to get lost in many words, let's come to what we have sung before. How does Christ say: You tore my coat and girded me with joy? His sack was the likeness of sinful flesh. Don't think it's vile because I say: my bag; inside it was your price. You broke my jacket. He did it through the Jews, without their knowledge, to redeem those who knew it and confuse those who denied it. They ignore, in effect, the good that they caused us with their evil actions. The sack was hung up, and the wicked man seemed to be filled with joy. The pursuer tore the sack with his spear, and the redeemer poured out our price. Quid ergo ad aedificium? Et accinxisti me laetitia. Vox dedicationis, Ut cantet tibí gloría mea, et non compungar. Quis est qui loquitur? In verbis eius agnoscite. If I expose obscurum est. Ergo verba eius dicam, continuo agnoscetis loquentem, ut ametis alloquentem. Quis est qui dicere potuit, Domine, eruisti ab inferís animam meam? (Ps 29,12.13.4) Cuius anima iam ab inferís eruta est, nisí de qua dictum est alio loco: Non derelinques animam meam in inferno (Ps 15,10)? Proponitur dedicatio, et cantatur liberatio: iubilatur canticum dedicationis domus, et dicitur: Exaltaba te, Domine, quoniam suscepisti me, et non iucundasti inimicos meos super me (Ps 29,2). Attendite Iudaeos inimicos, qui se putabant occidisse Christum, vicisse quasi inimicum, perdidisse quasi hominem ceteris similem atque mortalem. Resurrexit tertia die, et haec vox eius: Exaltabo te, Domine, quoniam suscepisti me. Attendite Apostolum dicentem: Propter quod eum Deus exaltavit, et dedit illi nomen quod est super omne nomen (Phil 2,9). Et non iucundasti inimicos meos super me. Ipsi quidem in Christi morte iucundabantur, sed in eius resurrectione, ascensione, praedicatione aliqui compungebantur. In eius ergo praedicatione et per Apostolorum constantiam diffamatione aliqui compungebantur et convertebantur, aliqui obdurabantur et confundebantur; nulli tamen iucun-

Prophetia de Christo capite, nobis eius membris aplata.—Dicat ergo caput nostrum, dicat caput pro corpore occisum, pro corpore dedicatum; dicat, audiamus: Conscidisti saccum meum, et accinxisti me laetitia (Ps 29,2), id est, conscidisti mortalitatem meam, et accinxisti me immortalitate et incorruptione. Ut cantet tibí gloria mea, et non compungar (ib., 13). What is it, non compungar? Iam contra me non ferat lanceam persecutor, ut compungar: Christus enim resurgens a mortuis iam non moritur, mors illi ultra non dominabitur: quod enim mortuus est, peccato mortuus est semel; quod autem vivit, vivit Deo. Ita et nos, inquit, existimemus nos mortuos esse peccato, vivere autem Deo, in Christo Iesu Domino nostro (Rom 6,9-11). Ergo in illo cantamus, in illo dedicati sumus. Quo enim caput praecessit, et membra secutura speramus. Spe enim facti sumus: spes autem quae videtur, non est spes; quod enim videt quis quid sperat? Si autem quod non videmus speramus,

per patientiam exspectamus (ib., 8,24-25), per patientiam aedificamur. Forte autem est illic et vox nostra, si bene attendamus, si diligenter intueamur, si oculum acutum geramus; non quemadmodum solent corporum caeci amatores: si ergo spiritualem oculum intendamus, in ipsis vocibus Domini nostri Iesu Christi et nos ipsos invenimus. Non enim frustration dixit Apostolus: Scientes quia vetus homo noster simul crucifixus est cum illo, ut evacuetur Corpus peccati, ut ultra non serviamus peccato (ib., 6,6). Agnosce ibi vocem tuam: Ut cantet ubi gloria mea, et non compungar (Ps 29,13). Modo enim cum istas corporis mortalis sarcinas baiulamus, non deest unde compungamur. Nam si cor non compungitur, quare pectus tunditur? Cum ergo venerit etiam nostri corporis dedication, quae praecessit in Domini exemplo, tune non compungemur. sleeping; Christ was hanging dead when the other thing happened. Sleep and death are related; the same one side and the other side: the Lord was wounded in the place of sins. these works of love come from. Theme: We are God's construction. Location: Unknown. Date: Feast of the dedication of a church.

1. The faith that carries the eye of piety in its heart sees how the good works of the faithful done with their temporal and earthly goods are deposited in the heavenly treasuries. Which is why, when he sees with the eyes of the flesh these buildings that are built to gather together the community of pious men, he inwardly praises what he sees on the outside, and the visible light gives him something to enjoy the invisible truth. But faith is not dedicated to looking at the beauty of the elements of this enclosure, but rather at the great beauty of the inner man, of which cum factum est: mortuus pendebat iste, cum factum est. Cognata duo sunt somnus et mors, latus et latus [1475] compunctus est Dominus in loco peccatorum. Sed de illo latere facta est Eva, quae nos peccando mortificadoret; de isto autem latere facta est Ecclesia, quee giving birth to us will vivify.
IN DEDICATIONE ECCLESIAE,

2. Therefore, as this visible building has been built to bring us together bodily, in the same way we build the building that we ourselves are to God, who is to dilectionis. Retribuet ergo Dominus fidelibus suis tam pie, tam hilariter, tam devotee ista operantibus, ut eos quoque ipsos in suae fabricae constructione componat, quo currunt lapides vivi, fide formati, spe solidati, caritate compacti. Ubi sapiens ille architectus Apostolus fundamentum posit Christum Iesum (cf. 1 Cor 3,10.11), summum ipsum lapidem angularem, sicut et Petrus de prophetica Scriptura commemorat: ab hominibus quidem reprobatum, a Deo autem electum et honorificatum (1 Petr 2,4). Huic adhaerendo, pacamur; huic incumbendo, firmamur. Simul enim est et fundamentalis, quia ipse nos regit; et angularis, quia ipse coniungit. Mt 7,24.25). Ipse est et pax nostra, qui fecit utraque unum (Eph 2,14); in ipso enim ñeque circumcisio quidquam valet, ñeque praeputium, sed nova creatura (Gal 6:15). Hi enim duo tanquam parietes ex diverse venientes, longe ab invicem fuerant, doñee ad illum, tanquam ad angulum ducti, etiam in illo sibimet copulati sunt. CAPUT II.—2. Aedificatio in labore, dedication in laetitia.—Itaque sicut hoc aedificium visibile factum est nobis corporaliter congregandis; ita illud aedificium, quod nos ipsi sumus, Deo spiritualiter habitaturo

inhabit it spiritually. The temple of God is holy, says the Apostle, and that temple is you. As we build this one with earthly pieces, in the same way we must build the other with well-arranged customs. This is dedicated now, on the occasion of my visit; the other, at the end of the world, when the Lord comes, when this corruptible of us puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality, because our humble body will be modeled after the body of his glory. See, then, what it says in the dedication psalm: You turned my tears into joy, you tore my coat and girded me with joy so that my glory may sing to you and I may not feel sad. While we are edified, our humility groans before him; When we are dedicated, he will sing our glory, because building requires fatigue and dedication requires joy. While the stones and beams of the forests are extracted from the mountains, while they are shaped, carved and adjusted, there is no lack of fatigue and worry; But, when the dedication of the completed building is celebrated, the fatigue and worries will be replaced by joy and security. In the same way, the spiritual construction, which will have God as its inhabitant, will not be temporary, but eternal; while men are separated from a life of infidelity and led to faith; while what is not good and lost in them is cut off and destroyed; As long as the assemblies are carried out in the proper manner, in peace and piety, how many temptations are not feared, how many tribulations must be endured! But when the day of the house dedication comes

eternal and we are told: Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom, prepared for you from the beginning of the world, what will be the joy and security! Glory will sing and weakness will not feel sad. When He who loved us and gave Himself for us appears to us and He who appeared to men born of a mother appears to them as the creator God who was in the Father; When the eternal dweller enters his finished and adorned house, founded on unity and clothed with immortality, he will shine in all so that God may be all in all. 3. This vision was the only thing that a certain person asked the Lord for; that person who, if we want, is us. Moved by that desire, he tired himself out amid groans, washed his bed every night and watered the platform with his tears. Thinking of that vision, tears were his bread day and night, while he was continually told: Where is your God? He, in effect, said: One thing I have asked of the Lord, that will I seek: to dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life to contemplate the delight of the Lord and to keep his temple safe. protected as his temple and hidden in the hiding place of his face. This is our hope; we do not yet see the reality. If we wait for what we do not see, through patience we wait for it.

If you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of the Father; Taste things above, not things on earth. Joyfully, therefore, work out your salvation with fear and trembling. God is the one who works in us to will and to act according to the good will. Do everything without murmuring. Topic: Good works. Location: Unknown. Date: The dedication of a Church. In the year 412.

1. When good works are shown to men, even those done for God, since they are works of pious and good men, human praise is not demanded, but rather they are proposed to be imitated. The good work contains a double merciful action: one spiritual and another corporal. With corporal mercy the hungry, the thirsty, the naked and the pilgrims are helped; But, when these same works are shown, while they provoke imitation, they also feed the spirits and minds. One is fed by a good work and the other by a good example, for both are hungry. One wants to receive food and the other wants to see something to imitate. The gospel reading that has just been read tells us about this truth. [1] Liturgical reading of the "passions" of the martyrs.—The reading of the passiones of the martyrs, or stories of their martyrdoms, in liturgical celebrations is a fact well attested in Augustinian texts. The practice was only limited by the scarcity of the passiones themselves, a fact that Augustine laments (serm.315,1). Evidently, of the great multitude of martyrs, only a few were privileged to have the memory of their heroism perpetuated in a faithful account, official or not, of their death. From the Augustinian sermons it is clear that the following passiones were read: first of all, that of Saint Stephen, contained in the canonical book of the Acts of the Apostles (6,8-7,60; serm.315,1); that of the Scylitan martyrs (serm.37,1; 299 D 7 [ = DENIS 16]), Saints Perpetua and Felicity (serm.280,1; 282,2), Saint Cyprian (serm.313 A 3 [ = DE NIS

This case concerned proconsular acts), those of Saint Vincent (serm.274; 275,1), those of Saint Fructuoso (serm.273,2.3), those of Saint Crispina (Commentaries on the psalms 120,13; 137,3) and those of the twenty martyrs of Hippo (serm.325,1; 326,2). This praxis had been regulated in a conciliar assembly. Thus, in canon 5 of the Council of Hippo in the year 393 we read: "The bishops as a whole said: 'It pleases everyone that not only the canonical Scriptures read, but even the passiones of the martyrs in their respective places are preached in the Churches.'" And in the Breviarium hipponense (36d): "Permit the reading of the passiones of the martyrs when the anniversary of their death is celebrated." But this practice was not universal. In the East, canon 26 of the Council of Laodicea is contrary, which does not admit any readings other than the canonical ones. But not even in the West did all the Churches act in an identical way. In Rome, Pope Gelasius I (492-496) witnesses that they were not read: "Likewise, the acts of the martyrs... since the names of those who wrote them are completely unknown, they are not read in the holy Roman Church, in order not to give even the slightest occasion for ridicule" (DENZ. 165). As can be seen, the cause is the unreliability of the stories; nothing strange when they had begun to proliferate in an exorbitant manner, without the slightest historical guarantee. As far as the Church of Milan is concerned, it can only be stated that Saint Ambrose used in his sermons the passiones of Saints Agnes and Cecilia; presumably reading it. For Gaul there are texts by Arnobius the Younger (Commentaries on Psalms 108), which can be interpreted as referring to the passiones. As far as Spain is concerned, a text found in the Gallican liturgy (I 3,9) speaks of how Saint Braulio of Zaragoza wrote a life of Saint Emiliano precisely so that it could be read in liturgical celebrations (PL 70,122). What has been said refers, as has already been indicated, to the liturgical readings; For spiritual reading they were always esteemed texts. See Cassiodorus (Institutions 32). [2] The "confessio".—In Christian Latin, the meaning of the term confessio is varied. It always includes the notion of proclaiming, of making public; but it has a triple object: the praise of God, one's own sins, one's own faith. Augustine uses the term, personally, throughout the

richness of its mentioned Christian content, as shown in its most famous work, the Confessions, although not all authors are able to agree on whether or not the work includes the confession of faith. In modern religious language, the second object has become so predominant that it has displaced the other two; to the first, absolutely, and to the third, considerably. "Confession" refers, almost exclusively, to the "confession of sins." In reality, this displacement is not surprising. On the one hand, there is already evidence of this from the same time as Augustine. Numerous texts of the Saint attest to this. One is enough for us: «I remind you that the confession in Scripture, when one confesses to God, is usually double: either of sins or of praise. No one ignores the confession of sin, but few notice the confession of praise. The confession of sin is so well known that, when it is heard in any text of Scripture: I will confess You, Lord, or We will confess You, immediately, out of the habit of understanding like this, the hands run to beat the chest; and to such an extent this happens that men only tend to understand by 'confession' that of sins" (Commentary on Psalm 137,2; also 141,19). On the other hand, we must not forget that the meaning of "praise" is not originally from the Latin language, but is a result of biblical influence. Indeed, in classical Latin, the term meant, primarily, the recognition of one's own fault or guilt in a trial. Quintilian defines it as any pronouncement against one's own person, always in a judicial context (Declamations 314; see also CICERÓN, The Invention I I 33,101). The confessio, confession, is precisely the opposite of defensio, defense; confession never or almost never voluntary, but forced, and, consequently, accepted as a misfortune and dishonorable situation. It is easy to see the step from here to the Christian meaning of recognition of one's own sins, a step that maintains, yes, the negative material content, but with a different ethical assessment: on the one hand, it is a Voluntary confession, and on the other, the only honorable attitude before God. From this judicial context the third meaning also emerged, precisely in relation to the literature of martyrdom. The Christian presented before the courts recognized his "crime", that is, professing the faith of the Church.

But here the ethical assessment radically changes, since objectively what is declared is no longer a crime, but the truth; The court and the judges are not the guilty and the innocent respectively, but on the contrary: the court is the innocent, and the judge or judges are the guilty. Hence the tone of exaltation that is associated with the "confession of faith" and the theology of martyrdom. The martyr, that is, the witness of faith, is the follower of Christ, the first witness of the truth before wicked judges, and will participate in his own glorification. See J. RATZINGER, Originalitat und Überlieferung in Augustins Begriff der Confessio: Revue des Études Augustiniennes 3 (1957) 375-392. [3] Evemerism.—The name “evemerism” is designated to a doctrine on the origin of the gods, of which the Greek philosopher Evemerus, a native of Messene and friend of King Cassander (311-298), was the author. In his most important work, at least for our knowledge, the 'lepa ówaypaipri (Sacred Record), he describes a fabulous trip to the island of Pancaya, in the Indian Ocean, and tells how, entering the temple of Zeus, he saw written on a column the exploits of Zeus himself and his ancestors, Uranus and Cronus, also the work of Zeus. There he could see that the gods of popular religion had originally been great kings or conquerors who, in reward or gratitude for the benefits received from them, humanity had attributed the category of god to them and had begun to worship them. The theory, which brings the plans so close

divine and human that practically denies the distinction between them, is not original from Evemero himself; He limited himself to giving it a systematic shape influenced by the East, especially Egyptian. The work had a notable success among the Romans thanks to the translation that Ennio made of it with the title of Sacred History. Christians also knew it, and made abundant use of it, evidently in the service of Christian apologetics, against pagan polytheism, as Judaism had done before. Even the pagans themselves recognized that pagan gods are not gods! See LACTANTIUS, The divine institutions I 11,13. Augustine mentions it explicitly in The Concordance of the Evangelists I 23,32 and in The City of God VI 7,1 and VII 27,1. In the first work it says like this: «Does not the poet Evemero also relate that both Jupiter and Saturn, his father, and Pluto and Neptune, his brothers, were, without a doubt, men? In this way, their worshipers must give thanks particularly to the poets, because they gave wings to their imagination not to dishonor them, but to adorn and beautify them. And in the second: «What did those who placed his nurse in the Capitol think of Jupiter? Isn't it true that they all agreed with Evemero, who wrote not with mythical charlatanism, but with history in hand, that all the gods were men and mortals? (VI 7,1). In sermon 273,3, which gave rise to this note, he clearly explains the origin of the gods. It should be noted that Augustine, here as well as in The City of God, attributes historical value to Evemero's work, which he explicitly distinguishes from the inventions of the poets. [4] The punishment and the cause.—"The martyr is not made by the punishment, but by the cause"; that is, not what suffers, but why he suffers it. This is a statement that constantly appears in Augustine's mouth when he speaks or writes about martyrdom (serm.94 A 1 [ = CAILLAU 2, 6 ]; 53 A 13 [ = MORIN 11 ]; 274; 275,1; 285,2; 306 A 1 [ = MORIN 14 ]; 335 C 2 [ = LAMBOT 2 ]; 335 G [ = LAMBOT 15 ]; Comments on Psalms 34

I I 13; 43.1; 68 I 9, etc.). Before God, only he who has a just cause is a martyr, he who dies for Christ, he who dies for faith, for justice. The fact of having suffered a lot is not a criterion, simply, for granting the title of martyr, since the same thing that one martyr has suffered may have been suffered by another for a nefarious cause. This insistence of Augustine has its explanation in the existence of the circumceliones (see complementary note 63 of vol. VII p.766: The circumceliones). Among the many atrocities they committed was killing themselves. Augustine testifies to this in numerous texts: Reply to the letter of Petiliano I I 20,46; Heresies 69; Reply to Cresconius I I I 49,54; Against Gaudentius I 31,36-39; account185,4,15; serm.62,17 and 313 E 4 (= GUELF. 28). Opiatus of Milevi also informs us of this (The Schism of the Donatists I I I 4). Filastrio calls them "the lovers of death" (Book on the various heresies 57,85). The practice was common to men and women (Against Gaudentius I I I 31,37). The most common and frequent way of dying was by falling into ravines or throwing oneself into water or fire (Las heresías 69; cta.185,4,15). They never used the rope, because that would be imitating Judas (serm.313 E 4 [ = GUELF. 28]. Other times they were not the ones who personally killed themselves, but rather they forced others to give it to them, under the threat of taking their lives if they did not do so (The Heresies 69), or they provoked the imperial forces to give it to them (cta.185,4,15). Sometimes, Augustine had to defend the Catholics from the accusations made by the Donatists of having killed, through imperial power, Donatists by throwing them into ravines, when in reality they had

thrown themselves. Augustine will argue with them with the unusual nature of the punishment, not contemplated in the Roman Penal Code, and the frequency with which the circumcelions themselves resort to the act (Reply to Petiliano's letter I I 20,46; Reply to Cresconius I I I 49,54). The motivations for such deaths are placed in a piety that exalted martyrdom to the maximum; With such deaths, their authors sought to be considered martyrs; in fact they received worship, which Augustine designates as sacrilegious and profane (Reply to the letter of Petilian I 24,26). They believed they found biblical support in the exploits of Razias, who is spoken of with praise in 2 Mac 14:37-46. Augustine will endeavor to show them how little the two cases are alike and how they cannot seek support in him (Against Gaudentius I I I 31,36). In conclusion, if it is not torment or violent death that makes a martyr, but rather the just cause, it follows that heretics are not martyrs, and, therefore, neither are circumcelions (serm.313 E 7 [ = GUELF.

On the other hand, clear proof that it is not the torment that counts, but the cause, is found in Augustine's events at Calvary, where Christ was crucified between two thieves. If the penalty is considered, that is, the fact of being crucified, Christ was in no way distinguished from his companions (serm.331,3). But Christ, although he was hanged like them, was not equally debased (serm.327,2). In this case, as in all others, it is the cause that serves as a criterion to evaluate the fact. In the person of Jesus, the cause gave a positive value to the fact, in itself negative, that God had suffered the ignominy of the cross. In such cases, Augustine uses the comparatio of the rhetors (CICERONE, The Invention I 11,15; I I 25,75; QUINTILLIAN, The Oratory Formation V I I 4,9), identifying the cause for which he is on the cross with the benefit that follows for us: Christ died for our benefit (serm.331,2; also 325,2; 335,2; 53 A 13 [ = MORIN 11]). See P. de Luis VIZCAÍNO, THE acts of Jesus in the preaching of Saint Augustine. Classical rhetoric at the service of patristic exegesis: Agustinian Study (Valladolid 1983) p.l30ff. [5] Death brought about by the tongue.—Who were responsible for the death of Jesus: the Jews or Pilate? Apart from purely occasional indications, Augustine deals with the issue explicitly and with some detail in several texts; e.g.: Treatises on the gospel of Saint John 114,4; Comments on Psalms 56; 63; serm.223 C (= GUELF. 6). The most important are the two first mentioned. They are from different times, but the ways of reflecting on the events are identical despite the fact that they are two formally different questions: in one, whether it was the Jews or Pilate who killed Jesus, and in the other, whether the Jews truly killed Jesus. For Augustine, there is no doubt that the Jews were the authentic authors of the death of the Lord. In both texts he resorts to the argument of a person: their bad faith, their cunning actions, that already in the way they acted they wanted to excuse themselves or absolve themselves of such a crime. In fact, they handed him over to Pilate so they could appear innocent before the people.

Within the arguments to person, he resorts to the previous facts and sayings (ante acta dictaque), showing a series of facts that by their nature are directed to death in the appreciation of any person: «Boast that you did not kill him if you did not want his death, if you did not stalk him, if you did not bribe him to be handed over to you, if you did not arrest him, if you did not chain him, you brought him before the judge; if you did not hand him over with your own hands to be murdered, if you did not ask for this with your cries" (Treaties..., 114,4). In the long enumeration of heQho§

prior to the central act, adds the evidence of the witnesses. None other better than. the prophet, through whom Christ speaks. "Hear what the prophet cries against you: Sons of men, his teeth are weapons and arrows, and his tongue is a sharpened sword (Ps 56:5)." With these words the instruments of crime are indicated. There is no longer any doubt; although not with their own hands, the Jews were the real murderers of Christ. “Just as the chief priests did not arrest Christ personally, but through those whom they sent to do it—did they not themselves come in the authority of their command?—so all those who with their impious cries cried for Christ to be crucified, they put Him to death; not certainly by themselves, but they through him who by their cries was driven to such a nefarious thing" (ibid.). So the Jews put him to death when they shouted, "Crucify him, crucify him!" He is so convinced of this that he uses this interpretation to resolve the divergence between Me and John regarding the time of the crucifixion: one evangelist noted the time of his physical death, while the other refers to the time when the Jews cried out for his death, since that fact meant death for Jesus. «It is written in John that Pilate sat down on the judgment seat at the beginning of the sixth hour, and certainly when the Lord was lifted up on the cross it was the sixth hour. But the other evangelist, seeing the intention of the Jews, who wanted to appear innocent of the death of the Lord, with his narration demonstrated that they were guilty by saying that the Lord was crucified at the third hour... The ministers of power crucified the Viora sixth; the transgressors of the law cried out at the third hour; What they did with their hands at the sixth hour, the same they did with their tongues at the third hour. Those who hurt by shouting are more guilty than those who carried out what they had been ordered to do” (Comments on Psalms 63:5). Once this thesis has been proven, he paints the characters according to it. The Pilate that he paints for us is the man that corresponds to the thesis: he presents him as a weak man overcome by fear (Treaties...116,7), highlighting the contrast between that fear and the high power he represents (Comments...63,8); everything he does or orders to be done is under pressure from others (Treaties...114,4); unintentionally (Comments...56,12); reluctantly (ibid., 63.2).

Furthermore, their reprehensible actions were carried out for humanitarian reasons, to soften the hearts of the Jews (Treaties...116,2). This is the Pilate that Augustine paints for us: a man worthy of others, who has many extenuating circumstances for his crime, although he cannot be relieved of all responsibility (Comments...56,12). Quite the opposite of the Jews, who, instead of mitigating circumstances, have aggravating circumstances. [6] The minister of the sacraments.—The differences between Augustine and the Donatists were fundamentally ecclesiological. One of the aspects in which both positions clashed was that which refers to the minister of the sacraments. Historically, the controversy centered on the sacrament of baptism. The position of the Donatists can be formulated as follows: the holiness of the minister is an essential requirement for the validity of the sacrament. If the minister is unworthy, his administration has no effect. They relied on San Cipriano. The holy bishop of Carthage had maintained that the sacraments were only valid if they were administered in the unity of the one Church. Only in it is grace found; Therefore, he who is not inside cannot possess grace, and, if he does not possess it, he cannot communicate it (ct.69,2; 73,10-11). Outside the Church, then, there are no sacraments. In this theology, the problem lies in knowing who is properly united to the Church, in elucidating what is meant

for the sanctity of the minister. The Donatists do not define it positively, but negatively. In practice, only those who had committed the "crimes" that separated them from the Church were deprived of the sanctity required to validly administer the sacraments: the concrete fact of having handed over the sacred books in persecution, the persecution of the Church itself, heresy and schism. A consequence of this theology was the Donatist schism itself (see complementary note 62 of vol. VII p.765: The origin of the Donatist schism). According to them, Caecilian was invalidly ordained; Therefore, all his ecclesial acts, all the sacraments derived from that initial flawed act, were invalidated; Furthermore, those who remained in communion with him also remained outside the Church. The result: the true Church was only in Africa, in the sect, the party of Donatus. Augustine's position was the opposite. The holiness of the minister means nothing in terms of the validity of the sacrament. For him, the authentic giver is God; the human minister is only a minister, a servant. Beyond the action of the human minister we must see the action of Christ, who is the one who truly confers grace (Reply to the letter of Parmenian II 14,22; Baptism against the Donatists IV 1,1). He distinguishes between donor and minislrator (serm.266,3). Augustine's position also had an immediate predecessor, in this case Optatus of Milevi, who highlights the validity of the sacraments by themselves, not depending on the men who administer them (The Schism of the Donatists 5,7), since the human minister is a worker, not a lord of grace (ibid.). Augustine refutes the theses of the Donatists. and at the same time defends -own. If the condition to be able to validly administer the sacraments, he tells them, is to be within the Church, man will always remain uncertain, since it cannot be known. Certainly, the Donatists relied on visible sins; But that was not enough for Augustine, since presence in the Church must be total. It is impossible to know who is a Christian and who is not (Reply to Cresconius IV 12,14). Therefore, a greater guarantee is required (acta.93,11,46.48). Making the validity of the sacrament depend on the holiness of the minister is to condition the action of God (ct.89,5; 93,9,48). With their doctrine, the Donatists usurp the position of Christ. «They say: 'I am Christ'; not with words, but—what is worse—with actions.

His audacity does not extend to pronouncing such words... Thus, he does not say explicitly: 'I am Christ', but he says it in another way... In a hidden way he says: 'I am the one who baptizes.' If you are referring to your status as a minister, I dare to assent. Let's not add anything else... But he doesn't hesitate to do so. What does it add? 'I am the one who justifies, I the one who does good'” (serm.292,6). For the Donatists, the subject of the sacrament was the Church; For Augustine it is God. He is the giver of grace, not she. The minister is a servant, not a giver. The minister is for the one who gives, not the one who gives (serm.266,1). The phrase is already famous: «Does Peter baptize? It is Christ who baptizes. Does Judas baptize? It is Christ who baptizes” (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 4:12; 5.17; serm.292,6; 46,17). [7] The gratuitousness of grace.—Grace receives this name because it is granted freely. Such is the resounding and constant affirmation of Saint Augustine. Every gift from God to man is free; both those conferred on him in the first creation and those granted in the second creation or recreation in Christ. The man has not deserved them. The statement becomes overwhelming in the Pelagian controversy. The attitude and doctrine of Pelagius and his followers were at the antipodes of Augustinian thought. To refer to them, Augustine seems not to have found

more exact expression than this: "enemies of the grace of God" or "enemies of the grace of Christ." In Reply to the Two Letters of the Pelagians (I 24,42) he says: "It is not without reason that we also condemn the Pelagians, who are so enemies of the grace of God given to us in Christ, that they affirm that it is not given to us freely, but according to our merits." See also I 1,2; I I 6,11. Augustine spoke not only from doctrinal positions, but also from his own experience. Years before he had narrated in the Confessions his conversion as a work of grace. His was the experience of a convert. He had not deserved conversion, and the Lord granted it to him. The justice with which God makes us just is a pure gift of his benevolence, since nothing human can be worthy of divine grace. No one has anything to boast about before God, because the only merits they have before God are demerits. «What does man have that he has not received? And if he has received it, what does he glory in? (Rom 3:27; 1 Cor 1:31)» (grace and free will 5:12). The best synthesis of the Saint's thought has been left to us by himself in two now famous phrases: "Give me what you ask of me and ask me for what you want" (Confessions X 29,40); and: "God does not crown your merits as your merits, but as his gifts" (Grace and free will 6,15; serm.131,8; 170,10; 299 A 2 [ = MAI 19 ]; 299 B 5 [ = GUELF. 23 ]; 299 C 5 [ = GUELF. 24 ]; account 194,5.19). Evi-

Clearly, this is directly opposed to the doctrine of the Pelagians, deniers of that gratuitousness; According to them, the grace that God grants us is a reward for our merits. God grants it or not according to whether the man has deserved it or not (The Acts of Pelagius 14,30.32). According to them, the need to affirm freedom in man entailed the denial of grace (The Acts...23,47). Furthermore, God does not command the impossible. If man were ordered to do something that he was incapable of doing on his own, God would be unjust (Nature and Grace 43,50; The Consequences and Forgiveness of Sins I I 3,3). The Pelagians do not completely deny grace. They even speak of it in laudatory terms, but they refer to it to other realities other than those thought by Augustine. For them, as for Augustine, the fact of creation, the gift of freedom, divine law, the Gospel, the good example of Christ and the saints, etc. are the grace of God. But they remain silent about the grace that Augustine was most interested in defending: internal grace. In reality, they did not completely deny it either, but they reduced it to complementary help, in no way necessary and even less essential. That is, God grants it to man so that he can do more easily what he could do alone equally, although with more effort (The grace of Christ and original sin I 27,28). But for Agustín that is not enough. For him, everything is grace, and, if it is grace, it is free; Well, if it is not free, it is not grace (serm.160,1; Comments on Psalms 30 I I 1,6). The most manifest example of this grace is the grace of Christ. What did the human nature of Christ do to deserve union with the person of the Word? See supplementary note 3 of vol. X p.884: The grace of Jesus. [8] The origin of death.—Regarding temporary death, Augustine distinguishes three states or situations of humanity. Adam's situation was that of someone who could not die; that of man in his current state, already a victim of sin, that of who cannot not die; that of man after the resurrection, that of whom he can no longer die (The city of God XXII 30,3). This means that, for him, physical death was a fateful consequence of Adam's sin. But this vision was directly opposed by the new thesis that appeared in Carthage after the arrival there of Pelagius and Celestius. Indeed, the problem of death
Additional notes

It appears already at the very beginning of the Pelagian controversy. It was one of the first theses to be propagated in Carthage by Celestio. Augustine became aware of it thanks to a writing by Marcellinus, who, while informing him, asked for his opinion (The consequences and forgiveness of sins I 2,2). This thesis was the first to be answered to Celestius in the synod of Carthage (The Acts of Pelagius 11,23). The new point of view boiled down to the following statement: death is a completely and totally natural event, not a consequence of Adam's sin. Adam would have died even if he had not sinned, as a condition of human nature itself, not as punishment for guilt. According to its promoters, if death were a consequence of Adam's sin, whoever believes in Christ should no longer suffer death, since Christ has brought us greater good than Adam has brought us evil. «Where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more (Rom 5,20)» (The consequences... I I 30,49). In this perspective they had to explain the death that the biblical texts speak of. Regarding Gen 2,17, the problem was not difficult for them to solve, because they applied it to the soul, not the body (The consequences... I 2,2). The Pauline text of Rom 5:12 was interpreted either from the naturalness of death, or from the imitation of Adam's sin (Incomplete Work against Julian VI 31). See in serm.299,10 the different argument of Tina and another part regarding Enoch and Elijah, of whom the Scripture says that they ascended to heaven without passing through death. [9] The name "Christian."—The term "Christian" was applied in ancient times not only to those who were baptized, but also to those who were simply catechumens. "Ask a man: 'Are you a Christian?' If he is a pagan or a Jew, he will answer: 'No.' If he answers in the negative, you still ask him if he is a catechumen or already faithful (that is, baptized)» (Treatise on the Gospel of Saint John 44,2; also serm.46,31;
A 8 [ = DENIS 17];
302.3; 97 A 3 [ = BIBLIOTH. CASIN. I I

115]). Thus, catechumens, by virtue of being catechumens, acquired the right to bear the glorious name of "Christian" (Commentaries on Psalms 36 I I 4). Based on what? As it could not be otherwise, Augustine derives the name "Christian" from "Christ." «Hence we are Christians because he is Christ. Christ is derived from 'chrism', that is, from 'anointing'. In ancient times, kings and priests were anointed. He was anointed king and priest. As king, he fought for us; as a priest, he offered himself for us” (Comments on Psalms 149:6). But it is the case that the catechumens are not yet anointed, since the anointing takes place at baptism. We must therefore look for another criterion that constitutes Christians. Obviously, it is not faith, because, although Augustine admits that catechumens already believe in Christ, his terminology goes in other directions: only the baptized is faithful (has faith). In fact, fidelis is usually synonymous with baptized (serm.301 A 8; 59,2; Treatises...44,2, etc.). If Augustine refuses to call catechumens faithful even if they believe in Christ, it is, in all probability, because he was prevented from doing so by the theology of baptism, which is the sacrament of faith. From Augustine's way of expressing himself, we must conclude that what gives the catechumen the right to be called Christian is precisely the fact of having been signed with the sign of the cross: "He already bears the sign of Christ on his forehead, he now enters the church, he is already invoked by such a sublime name, but he still carries the weight of his sin" (serm.97 A 3; Treatises...3,2; 44,2; 118,5; The catechesis of beginners 20,34). To the extent that it applies equally to the catechumen and the baptized, the name "Christian" therefore does not include the idea of ​​anointing. It refers, rather, to the cross of

Christ, formerly an object of shame and now a title of glory (Comments...36 I I 4). The signation that opened the catechumenate, and, above all, the baptismal consecration, constitute a kind of mark of belonging to Christ; With the idea of ​​belonging, Augustine also develops the theology of imitation. He who is marked with the sign of the cross must follow his teacher, and in particular commune with his passion (serm.107,7; 301 A 8; Treatises...43,9; Comments...36 II 4; 50,1). However, it must be noted that the terminology is not constant, as it sometimes expressly contrasts catechumens with Christians: "The catechumens do not know what Christians receive" (Treaties...11,4). In any case, Augustine invites his listeners to delve deeper into the mystery of the Christian name. Read E. LAMIRANDE, La signification de «christianus» dans la théologie de saint Augustin et la tradition ancienne, in Études sur l'Ecclésiologie de saint Augustin (Ottawa 1969). [10] The right of asylum.—One of the few data known from the Council of Carthage in the year 399 informs us that in it the bishops Epigonius and Vincent were commissioned to implore from the emperors a law in favor of those who took refuge in the church, regardless of the guilt that weighed on their shoulders, so that no one would dare to remove them from it. This tells us that in fact there was a custom of seeking asylum in churches by criminals or those persecuted by justice, but that the necessary legal protection was still lacking. The right of asylum, that is, the condition of certain places or things that granted impunity to those who sought refuge in them, is very old. It is already known in the Bible (Ex 21,13-14; Núra 35,6 and 11-34; Dt 4,41-43). It was widely spread in Greece, where most of the temples were places of refuge, although their number was later reduced; It also existed in the Roman Empire, but with even greater limitations. When Christianity achieved peace, it claimed for its temples and sacred places the same rights that pagan temples had enjoyed. In fact, this happened, even before there was explicit legislation on the matter. In the case of Christianity, the sacredness of the places was combined with the protective function of the bishop.

A constitution from the year 419 extends the privilege up to 50 steps away from the doors of the basilica; In the year 431, an edict by Emperor Theodosius further extended the territorial scope that granted impunity. As time went by, on the one hand, exceptions were made regarding criminals who could resort to that right and, on the other, defining the conditions for extracting the sacred precinct and handing over the guilty, as well as the penalties that fell on those who violated said right. Read in The City of God (I 4; I 34; V 17,2) the comparison that Augustine establishes between the right of asylum of the ancient pagans and the right of asylum granted by Christian times and places. In addition to the text of serm.302 (appendix), present in this volume, see serm.162 A 2 (= DENIS 19). [11] Saint Augustine and eloquence.—When speaking of eloquence and of Augustine we are not going to refer to his personal skills as an orator, which were recognized by everyone, whether they were friends or enemies; These were pagans, like Maximus (ct. 16,3); Manicheans, like Secundino (Letter from the Manichaean Secundino to Augustine 3), or Donatists, like Cresconio (Against Cresconio, Donatist grammarian I 1,2). Let us, then, dwell on the theoretical aspect of the question. Whoever has only read the Confessions and the negative judgments that he drops in the work about his profession (IV 2,2; IX 2,2.4), may arrive at a false judgment. Although there are some statements that can be understood in that sense ("We are asked

faith, not eloquence»: serm.260 E 2 [ = GUELF. 19]), Augustine cannot be classified within the classical anti-culture vein that ran through ancient Christianity, whose philosophy can be summarized in Tertullian's famous phrase: «What does Jerusalem have to do with Athens? "What harmony can there be between the Academy and the Church?" (The prescription against heretics 7). Without needing to resort to the work The Christian Doctrine, in whose book IV, written at the end of his life, he attempts to recover for the Church, like the gold of the Egyptians, all classical eloquence, putting it at the service of the exposition of Scripture, relativizing its necessity, while proclaiming its usefulness, in the same sermons we have Augustine's position perfectly outlined. In serm.335 K 5 (= LAMBOT 21) he introduces us to the eloquence of this world, by which the minds of men are subjugated, as symbolized in the most cruel sword of Goliath. But in the same text, following the biblical story, that same sword passes into the hands of David, and with it he kills Goliath. That is, eloquence, which was originally in the power of evil, passes into the service of good. It is an instrument that receives its value from whoever uses it and that can be used even against its former owners. In serm.312,3, Augustine returns to the same idea regarding Saint Cyprian as before as well. Following his conversion, a substantial change occurred in him: the instrument of his noble eloquence, through which he had manufactured ornaments that did not deserve the destructive doctrines of demons, was put at the service of the edification of the Church, whose growth meant their decay; and in this way, the trumpet of his great voice, which used to stimulate the battles of lies in the forum, began to defeat the devil with the precious death of the saints who fought in the service of Christ and to inflame the devout martyrs who placed their glory in him. In eloquence, Augustine only condemns the misuse that can be made of it, the misuse that paganism actually made and putting it as an end in itself. Obviously, it is neither necessary nor essential, but it is always a useful instrument that must be put at the service of a noble cause. [12] Saint Cyprian, defender of unity.—During the Donatist controversy, Saint Cyprian is, for Augustine, the prototype of the bishop defender of unity.

The recourse to the holy bishop of Carthage had more force from the moment that it was him on whom the Donatists relied to defend their theses. In fact, Saint Cyprian had to suffer, during his life as pastor of the Church, the tear of unity, and he had to continually strive to maintain it or reestablish it in the flock of the Lord. This unity was threatened or broken on a double front: on the one hand, within his Carthaginian diocese (I), and on the other, in relation to the Christian community of Rome (II). I. On the occasion of the escape of Saint Cyprian following the persecution of Decius, two Roman presbyters, Novatus and Felicisimo, began to intrigue against him. Of the first the Saint said, with no small dose of rhetoric, the following: «Novice, always eager for alterations and carried away by an insatiable greed and rapacity, swollen by a haughty arrogance and a senseless pride, always unfavorably unknown here by the bishops, always fond of betraying, a flatterer to deceive, never loyal in affection, he is a burning torch to fan the fire of sedition, a storm and torrent to make shipwreck of faith, challenger of peace, adversary of tranquility and enemy of peace” (ct.52,2,1; also v.50). Felicisimo attempted to disrupt the legitimate election of the clergy and people in favor of Cyprian, and went so far as to declare that he would not recognize those who obeyed Cyprian as part of his communion.

(ct.41,1; 43,2). They were then joined by five other priests who had poorly received Cyprian's election. He, at the beginning, was patient with them, reiterating his warnings to the clergy and people (ct. 15,1; 16,1). But, to maintain unity, he ended up excommunicating them, an excommunication that was confirmed by the Council of Carthage in the year 251. But it is not this aspect that Augustine usually refers to when he speaks of the holy bishop as a defender of unity, but rather the following. I I. After the martyrdom of Pope Fabian there was a schism in the Roman Church. The Novatian priest opposed the chosen Cornelius. In the dispute, the Church of Carthage ruled in favor of him. Shortly after, another conflict arose that pitted the two sees against one another: the conflict over the rebaptism of heretics. Faced with Rome, which maintained the thesis of non-iterability, Cyprian admitted that the baptism of heretics was invalid (see complementary note 6: The Minister of the Sacraments p.778), and that, therefore, it had to be repeated; but not all members of the African episcopate seemed to share his opinion. Cyprian preferred, above all, peace, maintaining it with those who thought differently, because of the great health he saw in it (Baptism against the Donatists V 17,3), and at the Council of Carthage on that subject he allowed everyone to give their opinion freely, without breaking communion with those who separated from his way of thinking. Cyprian is for Augustine, as a promoter of unity, the person who did not separate himself from those who did not share his ideas, and that is why he constantly invites the Donatists to address him and imitate his behavior. Nor should we forget that Saint Cyprian wrote a work on The Unity of the Church. Augustine calls the times of Saint Cyprian the times of unity, unity itself, ipsa unitas (Reply to Parmenian's letter I I I 2,8). [13] The relics of Saint Stephen.—The cult of the holy protomartyr reached gigantic dimensions in the fifth century. Apart from the widespread extension of the cult of the martyrs, the discovery of their remains and the narration of the same discovery made by the author, which was later translated into several languages, including Latin, by the work of Avitus of Braga (can be seen in PL 41,807-818), contributed to this. The discovery of the remains took place in the year 415 by the presbyter Lucian, in Kefargamla, near Gaza, thanks to a dream in which Gamaliel, the teacher of Saint Paul, appeared to him and indicated the place where they rested.

Its authenticity, always according to the aforementioned story, was confirmed by other revelations to other characters and by numerous miracles. Most of the remains remained in Jerusalem and were deposited in the church of Zion, waiting for a basilica to be built on the site of the stoning by Juvenal, bishop of the city; basilica that was inaugurated in the year 439, in a ceremony presided over by Saint Cyril of Alexandria. A small part of the Saint's relics remained in the possession of the author of the discovery, Luciano, who donated them to acquaintances and friends, among them Orosio, bishop of Menorca, who was in the Holy Land sent by Augustine. In this way, the relics reached the West, specifically to Africa, where they were received clamorously, seeing in the Saint a powerful intercessor before God, as confirmed by the numerous prodigies that occurred when his relics passed by, "a handful of dust" (serm.317,1). Augustine himself was enthusiastic, and with him the bishops of all the cities or villages through which the remains were triumphantly passed: in Uzala, where Evodio was bishop, and in Calama, seat of Posidio, both close friends of Augustine; in the Tibilitan baths, in Sinite, in private properties and, finally, in Hippo,

where in 324 the priest Heraclius built a chapel to house such a precious treasure. The result of this enthusiasm was that Augustine ordered a list of all the miracles that occurred and, in addition, a report of them to be read in public, in the liturgical assembly. A long series of them has been left to us written in The City of God (XXII 8), some of which we are also aware of through sermons 320-324. In this way, Augustine, who at the beginning of his Catholic period came to doubt the current existence of miracles because they were unnecessary, since the world had already believed, and the greatest miracle that induced faith had to be precisely the one that the world had believed (ibid., XXII 8,1), now celebrates them in the most solemn way, because what he has seen and heard has made him change his mind. [14] The meaning of "cupiditas".—It is difficult to find an equivalent in Spanish for the Latin term cupiditas. Generically, it can be translated as desire or desire, which is later specified according to the object of the desire. That object can be good or bad; but normally, if it is not specified, custom causes it to be interpreted in a negative sense (The City of God XIV 7,2). When it comes to getting closer to the concept, Augustine defines it as concupiscence, encompassing the triple concupiscence spoken of in 1 Jn 2,16 (The grace of Christ I 20,21); In fact, it summarizes the three temptations that Christ suffered (Comments on Psalms 30 II 1,10); In other texts he defines it as love for this world, for this century, in opposition to charity, as love for God and neighbor (Comments...31 I I 5); it is the evil that resides in man, the work of man, not of God (ibid., 18 I I 13); It is the manifestation of man's evil, which moves him to sin (ibid., 32 II 2,12). The cupiditas is, for the soul, viscous that attaches its wings to the earthly, temporary goods from here below; visco from which it can only be freed by charity (ibid., 138,13). It has aspects of greed, lust, revenge, etc. In any of these nuances, Augustine usually contrasts the concept of cupiditas with that of charity. Perhaps from that contrast it can be understood more easily. Both realities are opposed as virtue and vice, but both have in common that they are roots (Comments...9,14-15; 90 I 8; 110,8; The grace of Christ I 20,21, etc.); the one, charity, of goods, and the other, cupiditas, of evils, according to 1 Tim 6:10.

Both can nest in man, making charity a good tree and cupiditas a bad tree. Another difference exists between the two: cupiditas has man as its author, while charity does not come from us, but from God, as witnessed by Saint John (1 Jn 4:7-8). Consequently, when one sins, one acts not according to charity, but according to cupiditas (The grace of Christ I 20,21-21,22). Cupiditas is moved by pernicious delight; to charity, the fruitful (Comments...9,15); the first moves in the mud; the second, in the light (serm.34,5); the former seeks the lower, the latter the higher (serm.74,6). The attitude of man towards cupiditas must be that of one who seeks to destroy it, eliminate it, not that of one who tries to satisfy it (Comments...110,8), since it is insatiable; It is water that whoever drinks it, instead of seeing their thirst quenched, sees it increase (Comments...105,13). [15] The “ordo amoris.”—To greater or lesser extent, Augustine speaks explicitly about the ordo amoris (order in love) relatively frequently. We remember in chronological order: The customs of the Catholic Church I 15,25; Christian education I 22,21; 27,28; account.140.4; 155,4,13; serm.335 C (LAMBOT 2), Manual of faith, hope and charity 117,31; The city of God XII 8; XV 22, etc. S.Ag. 25
Additional notes

For Augustine, the Christian life is reduced to putting order in love. The virtues are all reducible to love (The Customs of the Church I 15,25), as well as the vices to a perverse love (The City of God XII 8). In turn, virtue, in the singular, is nothing other than "order in love" (The City of God XV 22). The problem for man is not so much, although also, between loving and not loving as between loving one way or another, or between loving more and loving less. In the sermon that gave rise to this note, Augustine clearly formulates one of those parts of the order of love, in which the dialectic is established between loving more and loving less: «I don't want you to not love anything, but I want you to order your love. Put heavenly goods before earthly ones, the immortal ones over the mortal ones, the eternal ones over the temporal ones. Put the Lord before all of them, not praising him, but loving him. But there are also other rules, which are summarized in The Christian Doctrine (I 27,28): «He who estimates all things at their just value lives justly and holily, that is, he who has love so ordered that he neither loves what should not be loved nor fails to love what should be loved; neither love more what should be loved less nor love equally what requires more or less love; nor, finally, love less or more what should be loved equally. He then gives examples: «No sinner should be loved as a sinner; Every man must be loved for God, and God for himself. And since God must be loved more than all men, each one must love God more than himself. We must also love every man more than our body, because all things must be loved for God, and the man who is strange to us can enjoy God with us, which our body is not capable of, which lives from the soul with which we will enjoy God. A dialectic is therefore established that takes these directions: yes-no (good as such); more-less (God-man; soul-body); rightly-not rightly (by God-not by God). Depending on the contexts, Augustine will accentuate one aspect more or less. But what does not change is his standard or criterion for judging the goodness of people: "When you ask if a man is good, you investigate not what he believes or hopes, but what he loves" (Manual...117,31). «Our customs are usually judged not by what one knows, but by what one loves. And it is good and bad loves that make customs good or bad” (cta.155,4,13).

Virtue is nothing other than loving what should be loved and how it should be loved, according to a hierarchy. «What is there to love more if not what is best? That's God. If in our love we put something before it or equate it with it, we do not know how to love ourselves, because it will be so much better for us the closer we get to him who is the best of all" (ct.155, 4,13). Obviously, this moral ordo amoris is based on a metaphysical ordo rerum. Creation is already a "cosmos", something ordered, and in love that order must be respected; but above that order is its creator, God. Everything must be postponed to him, and outside of him the degrees established by him must be respected. See R. FLÓREZ, Reflections on the “ordo amoris”: Revista Agustiniana de Spiritualidad 3 (1962) 137-168.
